children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.integral_equations
children.doc:
Closed-form solutions of the integral-equation presets (``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets.integral``).

Each entry of :data:`ANALYTIC` is ``(name, matcher(problem) -> bool, factory(problem) -> fn(X) -> (N, 1))``, the same
shape :mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.electromagnetics` uses, so ``pp.solve(problem, "analytic")`` resolves these
problems like any other preset.

The pairs here are *source and solution together*. For an integral equation the closed form is only half the case: the
free term ``f`` has to be the one that makes that ``u`` a solution, and if the two drift apart the preset silently
stops testing anything. So every case exposes both, and each pair is checked against a numerical integral in
``tests/test_integral_presets.py``.

The four cases, with ``lambda`` kept off the eigenvalue at ``lambda = 1`` (the Fredholm alternative: there the unit
kernel makes the system singular, so no finite comparison means anything):

``fredholm_unit_exp``       K = 1, f = exp(x) - lambda (e - 1), u = exp(x)
``fredholm_separable_exp``  K = x s (degenerate, rank one), f = exp(x) - lambda x, u = exp(x), since
                            int_0^1 s e^s ds = 1
``volterra_unit_exp``       K = 1, f = 1, u = exp(x)
``log_kernel_linear``       K = ln|x - s|, u = a + b x, f = u - lambda int_0^1 ln|x - s| u(s) ds, with the integral
                            written out below so the source stays elementary

functions.name: fredholm_unit_exp
functions.sig: (x, lam: float = 0.5)
functions.doc: ``u = exp(x)``, for ``u(x) = f(x) + lambda int_0^1 u ds`` with :func:`fredholm_unit_exp_source`.

functions.name: fredholm_unit_exp_source
functions.sig: (x, lam: float = 0.5)
functions.doc: ``f = exp(x) - lambda (e - 1)``: the integral of ``exp`` over ``[0, 1]`` is ``e - 1``.

functions.name: fredholm_separable_exp
functions.sig: (x, lam: float = 0.5)
functions.doc: ``u = exp(x)``, for the degenerate kernel ``K(x, s) = x s``.

functions.name: fredholm_separable_exp_source
functions.sig: (x, lam: float = 0.5)
functions.doc:
``f = exp(x) - lambda x``: with ``K = x s`` the integral is ``x int_0^1 s e^s ds = x``, since
``int s e^s ds = e^s (s - 1)`` gives ``0 - (-1) = 1``.

functions.name: volterra_unit_exp
functions.doc: ``u = exp(x)``, for ``u(x) = 1 + int_0^x u ds``.

functions.name: log_kernel_moment0
functions.doc: ``int_0^1 ln|x - s| ds = x ln x + (1 - x) ln(1 - x) - 1``, with ``0 ln 0 = 0`` at the ends.

functions.name: log_kernel_moment1
functions.doc:
``int_0^1 s ln|x - s| ds``, from ``u = s - x``::

int (u + x) ln|u| du = [u^2/2 (ln|u| - 1/2)] + x [u (ln|u| - 1)],  u from -x to 1 - x

functions.name: log_kernel_linear
functions.sig: (x, a: float = 1.0, b: float = 0.5)
functions.doc: ``u = a + b x``: non-constant, so a model cannot pass by learning a constant.

functions.name: log_kernel_linear_source
functions.sig: (x, lam: float = 0.5, a: float = 1.0, b: float = 0.5)
functions.doc: ``f = u - lambda (a M0 + b M1)`` with the two exact moments of ``ln|x - s|``.

children.summary: Closed-form solutions of the integral-equation presets (pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets.integral).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.membrane_diffusion
children.doc:
Real, closed-form membrane-controlled diffusive transport (Fick's
first law) -- the same real, standard model used in real reservoir-
type transdermal drug patches (e.g. scopolamine, clonidine,
fentanyl-class patches; see Robinson & Lee, *Controlled Drug
Delivery*), and generically applicable to any steady-state, membrane-
rate-limited diffusive release/transport problem:

    Steady-state flux/rate:  Rate = D * K * C_res * A / L
    Reservoir capacity:      M    = C_res * A * L_res
    Depletion time:          t_dep = M / Rate = L_res * L / (D * K)
    Concentration profile:   C(z) = K*C_res * (1 - z/L),  z in [0, L]
                             (linear at steady state, sink conditions
                             at z=L; d^2C/dz^2 = 0)
    Post-depletion decay:    k = D*K / (L * L_res)   (= 1/t_dep)
                             C(t) = C0 * exp(-k*(t - t_dep))  for t >= t_dep

``D`` (diffusion coefficient) and ``K`` (partition coefficient) are
generic real-order-of-magnitude transport parameters -- callers supply
real, citable values for their specific drug/polymer (or other
solute/membrane) pair; this module implements only the real physics,
not any particular substance's measured data.

First used in, and ported back from, PINNeAPPle-apps' ``patchdose_ai``
(a transdermal-patch design tool).

functions.name: steady_state_release_rate_mg_day
functions.sig: (diffusion_coeff_m2_s: float, partition_coeff: float, reservoir_conc_kg_m3: float, area_m2: float, membrane_thickness_m: float) -> float
functions.doc:
The real, closed-form ground-truth steady-state release rate
(mg/day) through a rate-limiting membrane, Fick's first law.

Returns
-------
rate : float [mg/day]
    Steady-state release rate.

functions.name: depletion_time_days
functions.sig: (diffusion_coeff_m2_s: float, partition_coeff: float, membrane_thickness_m: float, reservoir_thickness_m: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Real consequence of this model: depletion time depends ONLY on
membrane thickness -- area and reservoir concentration cancel out
(both the release rate and the total reservoir mass scale with
them identically). A genuine derived property of the physics, not
a simplification error.

Returns
-------
t : float [day]
    Time to deplete the reservoir.

functions.name: concentration_at_membrane_depth
functions.sig: (reservoir_conc_kg_m3: float, partition_coeff: float, membrane_thickness_m: float, z_from_reservoir_m: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Real steady-state concentration profile *inside* the same
Fick's-first-law model the release rate is built on -- not a
separate/invented formula. Steady-state diffusion through a
membrane with a fixed concentration at one face and sink
conditions (~zero concentration) at the other is, by definition,
linear in position:

    C(z) = K * C_res * (1 - z/L),   z in [0, L]

Its constant gradient is exactly what the release-rate formula
assumes: |J| = D*dC/dz = D*K*C_res/L -- the same D*K*C*A/L already
in the rate formula, confirming this field is consistent with (not
a contradiction of) the scalar model.

Returns
-------
C : float [kg/m3]
    Concentration at ``z_from_reservoir_m``.

functions.name: post_depletion_decay_rate_constant_per_day
functions.sig: (diffusion_coeff_m2_s: float, partition_coeff: float, membrane_thickness_m: float, reservoir_thickness_m: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Real derived first-order decay constant for the phase after the
reservoir's solid/excess drug is exhausted: the remaining
dissolved drug is removed through the membrane at a rate
proportional to how much is left, using the same real membrane
transport coefficient (D*K/L) that governs steady-state release,
normalized by the reservoir's own real volume:

    k = D*K*A / (L * V_reservoir),   V_reservoir = A * L_res

Area cancels algebraically:  k = D*K / (L * L_res)

-- exactly 1 / depletion_time_days (not a coincidence: the same
quantity is depletion time's own reciprocal).

Returns
-------
k : float [1/day]
    First-order decay constant.

functions.name: simulate_release_timeseries
functions.sig: (diffusion_coeff_m2_s: float, partition_coeff: float, reservoir_conc_kg_m3: float, area_m2: float, membrane_thickness_m: float, reservoir_thickness_m: float, duration_days: float | None = None, n_points: int = 100) -> list[dict[str, float]]
functions.doc:
Real time-domain simulation of release/depletion over the
device's wear life, combining only the real formulas above plus
the one derived decay-tail formula -- no invented dynamics.

Phase 1 (zero-order, t < depletion_time_days): the reservoir still
holds excess drug, so the membrane (the rate-limiting step)
sustains the full, constant steady-state rate -- the real,
standard "zero-order release" pattern real reservoir-type
transdermal patches are designed around.

Phase 2 (first-order decay tail, t >= depletion_time_days): the
reservoir is out of excess drug, so its concentration decays as
C(t) = C0*exp(-k*(t-t_dep)) and the achievable rate follows the
same Fick's-law formula, now time-varying only because C(t) is.

* :func:`schiller_naumann_cd`: L. Schiller and A. Naumann, Z. Ver. Dtsch. Ing. 77 (1933) 318-320,

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.pcb_thermal
children.doc:
PCB thermal building blocks (closed form, citable).

* Laminate properties: copper/FR-4 layers with copper coverage; per-layer
  in-plane and through-plane conductivity from the parallel (area-fraction)
  rule, board-level effective values from the parallel (in-plane) and
  series (through-plane) rules -- the standard compact treatment used by
  JEDEC JESD51-7 style board models.
* Thermal vias: plated barrels add copper area in parallel through the
  dielectric under a footprint.
* Surface heat transfer from a flat board, both faces:
    - natural convection, vertical plate: Churchill & Chu (1975),
      L = board height;
    - natural convection, horizontal plate: hot face up Nu = 0.54 Ra^1/4 /
      0.15 Ra^1/3, hot face down Nu = 0.27 Ra^1/4 (Incropera & DeWitt),
      L = A / P;
    - forced parallel flow: flat plate, laminar 0.664 Re^1/2 Pr^1/3,
      mixed (0.037 Re^0.8 - 871) Pr^1/3 above Re = 5e5;
    - radiation to surroundings at ambient, linearised:
      h_rad = eps sigma (Ts^2 + Ta^2)(Ts + Ta).
* JEDEC JESD15-3 two-resistor component model (theta_JC to the case top,
  theta_JB to the board).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.pipe_flow
children.doc:
Fully developed pipe and channel flow: Darcy friction factors, pressure drop and near-wall cell sizing.

Darcy friction factor ``f`` is defined by ``dp = f (L / D) rho U^2 / 2`` with U the bulk (mean) velocity and D the
(hydraulic) diameter (White, *Fluid Mechanics*, 7th ed., 2011, §6.6). The correlations are empirical and only hold
in their range; outside it they emit a ``RuntimeWarning`` (non-physical inputs raise ``ValueError``):

========== ==================================== =========================================
function   formula                              range
========== ==================================== =========================================
laminar    64 / Re (Hagen-Poiseuille)           Re < 2300
blasius    0.316 Re^-1/4 (Blasius 1913)         smooth pipe, 4e3 <= Re <= 1e5
colebrook  implicit (Colebrook 1939)            turbulent, Re >= 4e3
haaland    explicit (Haaland 1983)              4e3 <= Re <= 1e8, eps/D <= 0.05
curved_    White (1929) laminar curved pipe,    11.6 < De < 2000 (De = Re sqrt(D / 2 Rc))
pipe_ratio fully developed f_curved / f_straight
========== ==================================== =========================================

References: C. F. Colebrook, "Turbulent flow in pipes...", J. Inst. Civil Eng. 11 (1939) 133-156;
S. E. Haaland, "Simple and explicit formulas for the friction factor in turbulent pipe flow", J. Fluids Eng. 105
(1983) 89-90; H. Blasius, "Das Aehnlichkeitsgesetz bei Reibungsvorgaengen in Fluessigkeiten", Forschungsheft 131,
VDI (1913); F. M. White, *Fluid Mechanics*, 7th ed. (2011), §6.4-6.8; C. M. White, "Streamline flow through
curved pipes", Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 123 (1929) 645-663 (the correlation as given in P. Naphon and S. Wongwises,
"A review of flow and heat transfer characteristics in curved tubes", Renew. Sustain. Energy Rev. 10 (2006) 463-490).

functions.name: laminar
functions.sig: (Re: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Darcy friction factor of laminar fully developed pipe flow, ``f = 64 / Re`` (Hagen-Poiseuille; White
eq. 6.49). Warns for ``Re >= 2300``.

Returns
-------
f : float [-]
    Darcy friction factor.

functions.name: blasius
functions.sig: (Re: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Blasius (1913) smooth-pipe correlation ``f = 0.316 Re^-0.25`` (White eq. 6.55). Warns outside
``4e3 <= Re <= 1e5``.

Returns
-------
f : float [-]
    Darcy friction factor.

functions.name: colebrook
functions.sig: (Re: float, rel_rough: float = 0.0, tol: float = 1e-14, max_iter: int = 100) -> float
functions.doc:
Darcy friction factor from the Colebrook (1939) equation (White eq. 6.48),

    1 / sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (eps/D) / 3.7 + 2.51 / (Re sqrt(f)) ),

solved by fixed-point iteration on ``1 / sqrt(f)`` (a contraction for turbulent Re) from ``f = 0.02`` until the
update is below ``tol``. ``rel_rough`` = eps / D. Warns for ``Re < 4000`` (laminar / transitional flow) and
``eps / D > 0.05`` (beyond the Moody chart).

Returns
-------
f : float [-]
    Darcy friction factor.

functions.name: haaland
functions.sig: (Re: float, rel_rough: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Explicit Haaland (1983) approximation of Colebrook (White eq. 6.64), within about 2 % of it:

    1 / sqrt(f) = -1.8 log10( ((eps/D) / 3.7)^1.11 + 6.9 / Re ).

Warns outside ``4e3 <= Re <= 1e8`` or ``eps / D > 0.05``.

Returns
-------
f : float [-]
    Darcy friction factor.

functions.name: dean_number
functions.sig: (Re: float, D: float, Rc: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Dean number ``De = Re sqrt(D / (2 Rc))`` of a pipe of diameter D bent to a centre-line radius Rc (same
units).

Returns
-------
De : float [-]
    Dean number.

functions.name: curved_pipe_ratio
functions.sig: (De: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Fully developed laminar friction factor of a curved pipe over that of a straight one at the same Re, White
(1929): ``f_c / f_s = 1 / (1 - (1 - (11.6 / De)^0.45)^(1 / 0.45))``; 1 for De <= 11.6. Warns above De = 2000
(beyond White's data).

Returns
-------
ratio : float [-]
    ``f_c / f_s``.

functions.name: friction_factor
functions.sig: (Re: float, rel_rough: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc:
``laminar(Re)`` below Re = 2300, ``colebrook(Re, rel_rough)`` otherwise (the transitional band 2300-4000 is
uncertain; Colebrook is used there without a warning).

Returns
-------
f : float [-]
    Darcy friction factor.

functions.name: darcy_pressure_drop
functions.sig: (f: float, L: float, D: float, rho: float, U: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Darcy-Weisbach pressure drop [Pa] ``dp = f (L / D) rho U^2 / 2`` (White eq. 6.10) over a length L [m] of a
duct of (hydraulic) diameter D [m], density rho [kg/m^3], bulk velocity U [m/s].

Returns
-------
dp : float [Pa]
    Pressure drop over ``L``.

functions.name: parallel_plates_pressure_drop
functions.sig: (mu: float, L: float, h: float, U: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Laminar pressure drop [Pa] between infinite parallel plates a gap ``h`` [m] apart (plane Poiseuille flow),
``dp = 12 mu L U / h^2`` with U the mean velocity [m/s] and mu the dynamic viscosity [Pa s] (White §6.6).

Returns
-------
dp : float [Pa]
    Pressure drop over ``L``.

functions.name: first_cell_height
functions.sig: (y_plus: float, Re: float, D: float, U: float, nu: float, f: float | None = None, rel_rough: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Wall-normal height y [m] of the first cell such that ``y+ = y u_tau / nu`` equals ``y_plus`` (the usual
y+ estimate; a cell-centred code puts the first centroid at y / 2).

Wall shear from the friction factor of fully developed flow, ``tau_w = f rho U^2 / 8`` (White eq. 6.17), so the
friction velocity is ``u_tau = U sqrt(f / 8)`` and ``y = y+ nu / u_tau``. ``f`` defaults to
:func:`friction_factor` (laminar below Re = 2300, Colebrook with ``rel_rough`` above) at ``Re``; D [m] is only
used to check that ``Re`` is consistent with ``U D / nu`` (a mismatch above 1 % warns).

Returns
-------
y : float [m]
    Height of the first cell.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.pipe_insulation
children.doc:
Heat loss through an insulated pipe and the economic insulation thickness (ISO 12241 / VDI 2055 method).

Steady radial conduction through the insulation, whose conductivity is linear in temperature
``k(T) = k0 + k1 T``. Integrating the conductivity gives the exact Kirchhoff transform, so the mean of k over
[Ts, Ti] applies exactly:

    q' = 2 pi k_m (Ti - Ts) / ln(D_e / D_i)

The pipe wall and the inner film are neglected: steam or hot liquid is at the wall temperature, which errs on the
safe side. The outer surface coefficient follows ISO 12241:2008 sec. 4.1:

* radiation ``h_r = eps sigma (Ts^4 - Ta^4) / (Ts - Ta)`` (ISO 12241 sec. 4.1.2);
* convection on a horizontal cylinder in air (properties at the film temperature, Incropera Table A.4): natural by
  Churchill & Chu (1975, Incropera eq. 9.34), forced cross-flow by Churchill & Bernstein (1977, eq. 7.54), and
  mixed as ``Nu^3 = Nu_F^3 + Nu_N^3`` (Incropera eq. 9.66).

The surface temperature is found by bisection on the energy balance of the outer surface.

:func:`radial_fd` solves the same layer by finite volumes with k(T). Because it does not use the Kirchhoff
transform, it is an independent check. :func:`economic_thickness` minimises the annual cost, which is the lost
energy plus the annualised installed cost of the insulation (VDI 2055-1 sec. 6), over the standard thicknesses.

Heat loss per metre (W/m), surface temperature and coefficients of an insulated (or bare: thickness 0)

functions.doc:
Temperature across the insulation by finite volumes in r with k(T), Picard iterations. The inner and outer
temperatures are given. Returns r, T and the heat flow per metre at the inner and outer faces.

functions.doc: Capital recovery factor ``i (1+i)^n / ((1+i)^n - 1)``.

functions.sig: (d_pipe: float, t_in: float, t_amb: float, thicknesses: Sequence[float], *, k0: float, k1: float, eps: float, wind: float, hours: float, energy_price: float, efficiency: float, cost_per_m3: float, cost_per_m2: float, rate: float, years: float, t_surface_max: float = float('inf')) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Annual cost per metre (energy + annualised installed insulation) for each thickness. ``energy_price`` is
the price per kWh of fuel, which ``efficiency`` converts to heat. ``cost_per_m3`` is charged on the insulation
volume, ``cost_per_m2`` on the cladding area. Returns the table, the economic thickness and the thinnest
thickness that meets ``t_surface_max``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.plate_fin_heatsink
children.doc:
Plate-fin heat sink thermal/hydraulic model (closed form, citable).

Straight rectangular fins on a flat base, cooled either by ducted forced
air or by natural convection with vertical fins. Every relation below is a
published engineering correlation, not a fitted/invented formula:

* Air properties at 1 atm: tabulated (Incropera & DeWitt, Table A.4),
  linearly interpolated, ideal-gas density.
* Forced convection, parallel-plate channels (developing + fully developed
  composite): Teertstra, Yovanovich & Culham, "Analytical forced
  convection modeling of plate fin heat sinks", J. Electronics
  Manufacturing 10(4), 2000::

      Re_b* = Re_b * b / L,   Re_b = V_ch * b / nu
      Nu_b  = [ (Re_b* Pr / 2)^-3
               + (0.664 sqrt(Re_b*) Pr^(1/3) sqrt(1 + 3.65 / sqrt(Re_b*)))^-3 ]^(-1/3)

  ``h`` is referenced to the INLET air temperature: the ``Re* Pr / 2``
  limit is exactly the energy balance of air leaving at the wall
  temperature, so air heating is already accounted for.
* Pressure drop: Muzychka & Yovanovich apparent-friction model with the
  Shah & London fully developed ``f Re`` for rectangular ducts, plus
  Kays & London contraction/expansion losses.
* Natural convection, vertical isothermal parallel plates: Bar-Cohen &
  Rohsenow, J. Heat Transfer 106, 1984::

      El   = g beta dT b^4 / (nu alpha L)
      Nu_b = [ 576 / El^2 + 2.873 / sqrt(El) ]^(-1/2)

* Fin efficiency: :mod:`.fin_array_conduction` (Incropera, adiabatic-tip
  corrected length).
* Base spreading resistance (source smaller than the base, including 1D
  conduction through the base): Lee, Song, Au & Moran, "Constriction/
  spreading resistance model for electronics packaging", ASME/JSME
  Thermal Engineering Conf., 1995.

Limitations are reported, not hidden: every result carries ``warnings``
when a correlation is used outside its stated range or an assumption
(ducted flow, laminar channels, no radiation) may not hold.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.pump_npsh
children.doc:
Centrifugal pump on a suction / discharge system: duty point, NPSH available against required, cavitation margin.

* Water saturation pressure: IAPWS-IF97 region 4 saturation-pressure equation (IAPWS R7-97(2012), eq. 30). It
  reproduces the release's verification values (Table 35) to 9 digits, and it is valid from 273.15 to 647.096 K.
* Liquid density: Incropera, *Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*, Table A.6 (saturated water), interpolated
  linearly.
* Atmosphere: ISO 2533 standard atmosphere in the troposphere.
* Suction and discharge losses: Darcy-Weisbach with Colebrook (:mod:`.pipe_flow`) plus minor-loss coefficients.
* Pump: the head and required-NPSH curves are quadratic fits through the catalogue points the caller gives
  (shut-off head, best-efficiency point and so on). The duty point solves ``H_pump(Q) = H_static + K_sys Q^2``.
* NPSH available: ``(p_surface - p_v) / (rho g) + z_s - h_f,suction``, where z_s is positive when the liquid level
  is above the pump (flooded suction) and negative for a suction lift (Karassik et al., *Pump Handbook*, ch. 2).
  The margin follows ANSI/HI 9.6.1-2017: NPSH_a / NPSH_3 >= 1.1 to 2.5, depending on the application.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.rocket_nozzle
children.doc:
Ideal rocket nozzle: 1-D isentropic flow of a calorically perfect gas through a converging-diverging nozzle.

Exit Mach number from the area ratio (inverse of the area-Mach relation, supersonic or subsonic branch, by
bisection), choked mass flow, characteristic velocity c*, thrust coefficient C_F (momentum + pressure terms) and
specific impulse. Sutton & Biblarz, *Rocket Propulsion Elements*, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 3 (eqs. 3-16, 3-23, 3-24,
3-30, 3-32, 3-33); Anderson, *Modern Compressible Flow*, 3rd ed. (2003), ch. 5 and Table A.1. The forward
area-Mach and pressure ratios come from :func:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.compressible.isentropic_ratios`.

Assumptions: constant gamma, isentropic (no shocks, friction or heat loss), 1-D section averages, flow attached
and expanded to the given area ratio. Those are what a CFD run checks next; this is a screening estimate.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``rocket_nozzle_screening`` product (``isentropic.py``); the checks of its
``verify_analytical.py`` are ``tests/test_closed_form_rocket_nozzle.py``.

A/A* at Mach ``M`` (both branches).

functions.sig: (ratio: float, gamma: float, *, supersonic: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-12, max_iter: int = 300) -> float
functions.doc:
Invert A/A*(M) = ``ratio`` (>= 1) on the supersonic (default) or subsonic branch, by bisection.

Returns
-------
M : float [-]
    Mach number.

functions.sig: (M: float, gamma: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Static over stagnation pressure p/p0 at Mach ``M``.

    Mass flow, for SI inputs (Pa, m2, J/(kg K), K).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.closed_form.thin_airfoil
children.doc:
Closed-form 2-D section aerodynamics: thin-airfoil lift of a NACA 4-digit camber line and a profile-drag
correlation for a streamlined section.

Lift (inviscid, small angles; Anderson, *Fundamentals of Aerodynamics*, 6th ed., sec. 4.8, the Glauert
Fourier-series solution of the cambered thin airfoil)::

    x = (1 - cos theta0) / 2
    A0 = alpha - (1/pi) int_0^pi dz/dx dtheta0
    A1 = (2/pi) int_0^pi dz/dx cos(theta0) dtheta0
    Cl = pi (2 A0 + A1)                     (symmetric section: Cl = 2 pi alpha)

Profile drag (viscous, attached flow): the turbulent flat-plate skin friction ``Cf = 0.074 / Re^0.2`` (Prandtl's
1/7-power law, Schlichting, *Boundary-Layer Theory*, ch. 21) times Hoerner's thickness form factor for a
streamlined 2-D section, both surfaces wetted (Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic Drag*, 1965, ch. 6)::

    Cd = 2 Cf (1 + 2 t/c + 60 (t/c)^4)       (referred to the chord)

Scope: no thickness effect on lift, no camber or lift effect on drag, no stall, no compressibility, no transition
(fully turbulent). Use a panel method (``pinneapple_design.aero.panel``) or RANS for anything beyond trends.

children.doc:
Real, closed-form (non-PDE) engineering physics models.

``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment`` targets full PDE/FEM problems
(a ``ProblemSpec`` a real solver like FEniCS or a PINN then solves).
Not every real, citable engineering model needs that machinery --
classical lumped-parameter and 1D analytical results (fin-array
conduction, beam bending/fatigue, membrane diffusion, Helmholtz
resonance, ...) are real, standard, textbook physics in their own
right, useful as fast surrogates, training-data generators, or
independent verification ground truth without a PDE solve.

This subpackage exists so those closed-form models are shared,
tested, real PINNeAPPle code -- instead of being re-derived and
duplicated inside every downstream product that needs one. It started
from formulas originally written standalone inside five
``PINNeAPPle-apps`` products (heatsink/brakecool/ridetune/soundshape/
patchdose design tools) and was ported back into the platform so
future products can import them directly rather than re-deriving them.

Sub-modules
-----------
fin_array_conduction
    Extended-surface (fin) conduction + convection, real closed-form
    result (Incropera & DeWitt) generalized over any fin-array
    geometry (straight rectangular fins, radial vanes, ...).
cantilever_fatigue
    Cantilever-beam bending stress + Basquin stress-life fatigue.
membrane_diffusion
    Fick's-first-law membrane-controlled diffusive release/transport.
helmholtz_resonator
    Helmholtz-resonator (bass-reflex port) tuning equation.
plate_fin_heatsink
    Plate-fin heat sink: forced (Teertstra) / natural (Bar-Cohen)
    convection, spreading resistance (Lee), pressure drop.
pcb_thermal
    PCB stack-up conductivity, thermal vias, JEDEC two-resistor packages
    and board-surface convection + radiation.
burgers
    Viscous (Cole-Hopf) and inviscid (characteristics) Burgers solutions
    for the sine initial condition.
pipe_flow
    Darcy friction factors (laminar, Blasius, Colebrook, Haaland), pressure
    drop and first-cell height for a target y+.
heat
    Transient 1-D slab conduction (Fourier series, Carslaw & Jaeger).
compressible
    Isentropic ratios, normal shock, Pitot pressure, modified-Newtonian Cp_max.
particle_drag
    Sphere drag coefficient (Clift, Grace & Weber 1978; Schiller & Naumann 1933).
rocket_nozzle
    Ideal rocket nozzle: exit Mach from the area ratio, choked mass flow, c*, thrust coefficient, Isp.
ideal_reactors
    Ideal isothermal first-order reactors: plug-flow and stirred-tank conversion, tube volume and residence time.
children.summary: Real, closed-form (non-PDE) engineering physics models.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.codegen
pinneapple_physics.codegen.fdm_script_generator
children.doc:
Standalone finite-difference *script* generator for PINNeAPPle.

This is a different artifact from ``pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.SymbolicPDE``:
that module compiles a SymPy PDE residual into an in-memory autograd
*closure* (``residual_fn(coords) -> tensor``) for PINN training, evaluated
inside the same Python process. Nothing here reuses or wraps that closure.

``FDMScriptGenerator`` instead renders a **complete, self-contained Python
source file** — text you can ``open(path, "w").write(...)`` — that solves a
PDE with an explicit finite-difference scheme and writes its result to a
``.npz`` file. The generated file imports nothing from this package (or
from ``pinneapple_physics`` at all): it is meant to be handed to someone
else, run with a bare ``python generated_solver.py``, or executed inside
``pinneapple_tools.sandbox.custom_solver_runner.run_custom_solver`` in a
separate process with resource limits.

Scope (curated, not general)
-----------------------------
This covers exactly three PDE forms, chosen to match the ``ProblemSpec``
presets already shipped in ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets``:

  * 1D heat/diffusion equation   (``pde.kind`` contains "heat" or "diffusion")
  * 1D viscous Burgers equation  (``pde.kind`` contains "burgers")
  * 2D Poisson/Laplace equation  (``pde.kind`` contains "poisson" or "laplace")

There is no attempt at a general symbolic-PDE-to-FDM compiler here — that
is explicitly out of scope. Any other ``pde.kind``, or a matching kind with
an unsupported coordinate layout (e.g. 2D heat), raises ``NotImplementedError``
with a message naming exactly what is and isn't covered, rather than
silently guessing.

Numerical schemes mirror the hand-written ones already in
``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.fdm`` (FTCS/upwind for Burgers,
an explicit CFL-limited step for heat) so the generated code reads like
idiomatic PINNeAPPle FDM code, not a foreign style. It is independent
code, though: the generated file cannot import ``pinneapple_simulation``
(it must run with nothing but the stdlib + NumPy), so the stencils are
re-expressed standalone rather than imported. The Poisson solver here
deliberately does NOT copy
``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.fdm._sor_2d``'s vectorized
simultaneous-update scheme: that scheme is a weighted-Jacobi update
despite being called "SOR" (all neighbor reads come from the previous
sweep), and it was found to diverge here for omega>1 on the exact
manufactured problem this generator's own test suite checks against.
This module uses a real (checkerboard red-black) Gauss-Seidel SOR
instead — see ``_POISSON_2D_BODY`` for the details and the convergence
check performed while writing it.

Usage
-----
    import pinneapple_physics as pp
    from pinneapple_physics.codegen import FDMScriptGenerator

    spec = pp.burgers_1d_default(nu=0.01)
    path = FDMScriptGenerator().write(spec, "burgers_solver.py", nx=256, nt=4000)
    # `python burgers_solver.py --out solution.npz` now runs standalone.

Output convention
------------------
The generated script's ``solve(params: dict) -> dict`` returns a dict with
a ``"coords"`` key (mapping coordinate name -> 1D array) plus one entry per
PDE field (e.g. ``"u"``/``"T"``) holding the solution array — the same
``solve(params) -> dict`` shape used by
``pinneapple_tools.sandbox.custom_solver_runner.run_custom_solver`` and by
the generated FEniCS scripts in
``pinneapple_physics.codegen.fenics_script_generator``, so all
codegen-produced solvers share one calling convention. ``main()`` saves
that same dict, flattened, to a ``.npz`` file via ``numpy.savez`` — one
top-level array per coordinate/field name, following the flat-array-per-key
convention used elsewhere in this repo (e.g.
``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.irk_gauss_legendre``'s cached
``.npz`` files) rather than a single opaque blob.

Deliberately narrow: this is a classifier over a fixed, documented set

It reuses the ``ProblemSpec``/``PDETermSpec`` vocabulary already defined
in ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment`` rather than inventing a new

children.name: pinneapple_physics.codegen.fenics_script_generator
children.doc:
Standalone UFL/dolfinx *script* generator for PINNeAPPle.

Like ``fdm_script_generator.py``, this renders complete, human-readable
Python source files — not in-memory closures — for a curated set of finite
element physics problems:

  * "diffusion"  -- steady linear diffusion / Poisson-like scalar field:
                    -div(k * grad(u)) = f
  * "stokes"     -- steady Stokes flow (Taylor-Hood P2/P1 velocity-pressure)
  * "elasticity" -- linear elasticity, optionally with a penalty-method
                    rigid-obstacle contact term

Physics-shape selection
------------------------
``classify_physics_shape(spec)`` inspects a ``ProblemSpec``-like object's
``pde.kind`` string and ``fields`` tuple and picks one of the three shapes
above: a displacement-looking field set (or "elasticity" in the kind
string) -> elasticity; a velocity+pressure field pair (or "stokes"/
"navier_stokes" in the kind string) -> stokes; anything else (the default)
-> diffusion. This is a 3-way heuristic classifier, not a general
PDE-shape inference engine — anything that doesn't obviously look like one
of these three families is treated as "diffusion" by default, which is the
right conservative fallback (a scalar Poisson-like solve) rather than a
guess at something more exotic.

Relationship to pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fenics
----------------------------------------------------------------
``pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fenics.FEniCSWorkflow.solve()``
does not execute an arbitrary script at all — it takes a ``FEniCSConfig``
(``pde`` name string + ``domain``/``bcs``/``params`` dicts) and forwards it
to the hardcoded variational forms in
``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.fenics_bridge.FEnicsBridge``
(``_form_heat_equation``, ``_form_linear_elasticity``). Those hardcoded
forms cover exactly two of this generator's three shapes:

  * "diffusion"  -> ``FEnicsBridge``'s ``"heat_equation_steady"`` kind
  * "elasticity" -> ``FEnicsBridge``'s ``"linear_elasticity_plane_stress"``/
                    ``"linear_elasticity_plane_strain"`` kinds

so scripts generated for those two shapes ALSO get a
``build_fenics_config(params=None) -> FEniCSConfig`` function, letting the
exact same problem run either standalone (``python script.py``) or through
the existing bridge:

    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fenics import FEniCSWorkflow
    sample = FEniCSWorkflow(build_fenics_config()).solve({"k": 2.0})

Two honest caveats about that integration, found while wiring it up (both
pre-existing, in files this module does not touch):

1. ``solve_and_package()`` in
   ``pinneapple_simulation/external_solvers/fenics/solver.py`` does
   ``from pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.fenics_bridge import
   FEniCSBridge`` — but the class actually defined in that module is named
   ``FEnicsBridge`` (lowercase "nics"). That import raises ``ImportError``
   today whenever dolfinx or legacy FEniCS is actually installed, entirely
   independent of anything in this codegen package.
2. ``FEnicsBridge._SUPPORTED_KINDS`` is
   ``{"heat_equation_steady", "linear_elasticity_plane_stress",
   "linear_elasticity_plane_strain"}`` — it does not include
   ``"navier_stokes_stokes"``, even though
   ``FEnicsBridge._build_variational_form`` has a dispatch branch for it
   (``_form_navier_stokes``); that branch is unreachable through
   ``FEnicsBridge.forward()`` today because the kind whitelist rejects it
   first, and no contact-term hook exists on any kind.

Because of (2), "stokes" scripts and contact-enabled "elasticity" scripts
get NO ``build_fenics_config()`` — there is nothing in the existing bridge
for them to plug into yet. They are standalone-only: run them with
``python script.py`` / call their own ``solve(params)``.

dolfinx availability in this environment
------------------------------------------
dolfinx/ufl are NOT importable in the environment this generator was
written and tested in (``import dolfinx`` raises ``ModuleNotFoundError``).
The generated scripts are therefore validated here only via
``ast.parse()`` (syntactically valid Python) and a string/AST check that
the expected UFL/dolfinx API surface is present (see
tests/test_codegen.py) — NOT by actually running a real finite-element
solve end to end. If dolfinx becomes available, that same test file runs
the diffusion case for real and checks it against an analytic solution;
until then, treat the FEM physics here as "written to match the exact API
already used successfully elsewhere in this repo
(pinneapple_simulation/numerical_solvers/fenics_bridge.py)", not as
independently numerically verified.

children.doc:
pinneapple_physics.codegen — automatic physical-code generation.

Different in kind from ``pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde``: that module
compiles a SymPy PDE residual into an in-memory autograd *closure* used
during PINN training in the same process. Everything in this package
instead renders a **complete, standalone, saveable Python source file**
(text you write to disk with ``open(path, "w").write(...)``) that runs on
its own, with no import of this package, via a bare ``python script.py``.

Sub-modules
-----------
fdm_script_generator
    ``PDEParser`` + ``FDMScriptGenerator``: curated finite-difference
    scripts (1D heat, 1D Burgers, 2D Poisson/Laplace) written in NumPy
    only.

fenics_script_generator
    ``FEniCSScriptGenerator`` (+ ``classify_physics_shape``): curated
    UFL/dolfinx finite-element scripts (linear diffusion, Stokes flow,
    linear elasticity with an optional penalty-method contact term).

Both generators emit scripts that expose a ``solve(params: dict) -> dict``
function returning at least a ``"coords"`` key — the same convention used
by ``pinneapple_tools.sandbox.custom_solver_runner.run_custom_solver``,
which can execute any of these generated scripts (or a hand-written one
following the same convention) in a separate, resource-limited process.

Scope
-----
Both generators are curated over a small, explicitly documented set of
PDE/physics forms — not general symbolic-PDE-to-code compilers. See each
module's docstring for exactly what is (and isn't) covered.

Usage
-----
>>> import pinneapple_physics as pp
>>> from pinneapple_physics.codegen import FDMScriptGenerator
>>> spec = pp.burgers_1d_default(nu=0.01)
>>> FDMScriptGenerator().write(spec, "burgers_solver.py")
'burgers_solver.py'
children.summary: Automatic physical-code generation.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.compile_api
children.doc:
``pp.compile``: optimise a physics problem once, solve it faster, with the same results.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> compiled = pp.compile("burgers_1d", optimize="physics")           # doctest: +SKIP
>>> sol = compiled.solve("pinn", epochs=2000)                          # doctest: +SKIP
>>> print(compiled.benchmark(epochs=100))                              # doctest: +SKIP

What ``optimize="physics"`` does today: the PDE residual is built from several derivative calls on the same
field (the time derivative and the convective term of Burgers both differentiate ``u``; Navier-Stokes and the
elasticity and Euler kernels do it more). The compiled problem memoizes first derivatives within one loss
evaluation, so each field is differentiated once per step instead of once per term. The losses are the same;
the weights after training agree to floating-point summation order. The gain is the share of derivative graphs
saved, so it depends on the PDE (measured numbers in ``docs/core_concepts/solver.md``).

Not done: operator fusion beyond derivative reuse, kernel-level batching and memory planning. Forward-mode and
batched second derivatives were measured and were not faster on CPU (see the docs), so they are not used.

methods.name: identical
methods.doc: True when trained weights of the two runs agree within ``rtol`` of the largest weight.

classes.sig: (problem: PhysicalProblem, optimize: str = 'physics') -> None
classes.doc: A problem with its optimisations decided. ``solve`` and ``loss_fn`` use them.

methods.name: loss_fn
methods.doc: The PINN loss ``loss_fn(model, y_hat, batch)`` of this problem, compiled.

methods.name: solve
methods.doc: ``pp.solve(problem, method)`` with the optimisations on (only the ``pinn`` method has any).

methods.name: benchmark
methods.sig: (epochs: int = 100, repeats: int = 3, *, n_collocation: int = 2048, hidden_dim: int = 64, n_layers: int = 4, num_threads: Optional[int] = 1, seed: int = 0, **pinn_options) -> Benchmark
methods.doc:
Train the same PINN with and without the optimisations, alternating runs, and report the best CPU time
of each plus how far the trained weights differ. ``num_threads=1`` keeps the timing stable.

functions.doc:
Prepare a problem (a ``PhysicalProblem``, a ``ProblemSpec`` or a preset name) for faster solving.

``optimize="physics"`` turns on the physics-aware optimisations (derivative reuse); ``"none"`` is the
uncompiled baseline with the same interface, which is what ``benchmark`` compares against.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.conservation
children.doc:
Conservation as a hard constraint on model outputs: project a predicted field so that its weighted integral
(total mass, energy, charge, water) equals a prescribed value exactly.

Neural surrogates trained with a conservation penalty only conserve approximately, and the error accumulates when a
surrogate is rolled out in time. A projection after the network removes the error by construction and stays
differentiable, so it can sit inside training:

* ``"additive"``: f + (T - <w, f>) / <w, 1>; the smallest correction in the w-weighted L2 norm (a uniform shift);
* ``"multiplicative"``: f * T / <w, f>; keeps the sign and the relative pattern (zero stays zero);
* ``"positive"``: clip negatives, then multiplicative; for fields that must be non-negative (density, humidity,
  concentrations), the standard global mass fixer of tracer transport.

``weights`` are the quadrature weights of the grid (cell areas or volumes, Gauss weights times radius^2 on the
sphere), so <w, f> is the discrete integral. :class:`ConservationProjection` wraps a model; the target comes from the
input (e.g. the mass of the previous state, plus sources).

classes.name: ConservationProjection
classes.sig: (model: nn.Module, weights: Tensor, mode: str = 'additive', target_fn: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor] | None = None)
classes.doc:
``model`` followed by an exact projection. ``target_fn(x, y_pred)`` gives the conserved total for each batch
entry (e.g. ``lambda x, y: integral(x_state, w)`` for a closed system); by default the integral of the input field
``x`` itself (same grid as the output).

functions.name: integral
functions.sig: (field: Tensor, weights: Tensor, dims: int = 1) -> Tensor
functions.doc: Weighted sum over the last ``dims`` dimensions (``weights`` has that trailing shape).

functions.name: project_integral
functions.sig: (field: Tensor, weights: Tensor, target: float | Tensor, mode: str = 'additive', dims: int | None = None, eps: float = 1e-30) -> Tensor
functions.doc: Return ``field`` corrected so that ``integral(field, weights) == target`` (per leading batch entry).

children.summary: Conservation as a hard constraint on model outputs: project a predicted field so that its weighted integral (total mass, energy, charge, water) equals a prescribed value exactly.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.constraint_engine
children.doc:
Um objeto de restrição, aplicado nos três lugares onde uma resposta pode violar um limite (#221, roadmap X34).

A biblioteca já sabia recusar um projeto por uma exigência dura (#172, ``pinneapple_design.design_gate``), medir
conservação e condição de contorno (#159, ``pinneapple_physics.conservation``) e carregar incerteza numa frente de
Pareto (#80, ``pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.robust``). Cada uma dessas coisas checava o seu próprio limite, do
seu próprio jeito: um limite escrito para o portão de projeto não era o mesmo número que o otimizador recebia, e
nenhum dos dois era o que a guarda de deploy perguntava. O resultado prático é o pior possível -- um modelo que passa
no treino, converge no otimizador e é servido violando o limite que o cliente escreveu.

Este módulo é a ponte que faltava: **um** :class:`pinneapple_physics.physical_problem.Constraint`, o mesmo objeto,
com **uma** aritmética (:func:`residual`), entregue em três pontos de aplicação:

``penalty`` / ``Trainer(constraints=...)``
    o limite entra no laço de treino como termo diferenciável da perda, então a rede aprende a respeitá-lo;
``optimizer_constraints`` / ``PhysicsOptimizer(constraints=...)``
    o mesmo limite vira ``ineq``/``eq`` do ``pinneapple_core.optim``, então o otimizador o trata como restrição de
    verdade (SQP, Lagrangeano aumentado, evolução) e não como penalidade disfarçada;
``ConstraintGuard``
    o mesmo limite, checado sobre a predição no momento em que ela é servida, recusando em vez de corrigir.

E, fora dos três, a mesma função :func:`check_all` responde "quantas vezes este limite foi violado" sobre um ensemble,
que é o que o relatório de decisão (#219) precisa: a probabilidade de violação de uma restrição é a média de
:func:`check` sobre as realizações, não uma estatística inventada em outro módulo.

A aritmética é uma só, e é a do ``PhysicsOptimizer``: **residual** ``g`` com ``g <= 0`` significando "satisfeita".
``g`` é ``quantidade - limite`` para ``<=``, ``limite - quantidade`` para ``>=`` e ``|quantidade - limite|`` para
``==``; para uma restrição escrita como expressão (``"mass_kg - payload_kg >= 2"``) é a mesma subtração com o sinal da
comparação dobrado dentro, lida pelo avaliador seguro de ``pinneapple_data.expressions`` (nada de ``eval``). Um ``g``
negativo é folga: é ele que o relatório ordena para dizer *qual* caso dirige o risco.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> from pinneapple_physics.constraint_engine import check
>>> T = pp.Constraint("temperatura", quantity="T_max", op="<=", value=85.0, unit="degC", family="safety")
>>> check(T, {"T_max": 92.5}).violated
True
>>> round(check(T, {"T_max": 92.5}).margin, 3)          # 7.5 degC above the limit
7.5

A família (``physical``, ``conservation``, ``operational``, ``material``, ``actuator``, ``safety``) **não** muda a
aritmética: é o rótulo que o relatório agrupa, que o otimizador usa para nomear a restrição e que a guarda põe na
recusa. Fingir que seis famílias se checam de seis maneiras diferentes seria criar seis motores de novo.

classes.name: ConstraintCheck
classes.doc:
One constraint asked once: satisfied or not, by how much, and against which limit.

``margin`` keeps the sign that :func:`residual` uses (``<= 0`` satisfied), so ``slack`` -- ``-margin`` -- is how
far inside the limit the answer sits. An answer exactly at the limit has zero slack, which is a tie and not a
margin: a report that rounded it to "satisfied" would hide the case that is next to fail.

classes.name: ConstraintReport
classes.doc: Every constraint asked over one answer (or over one ensemble member).

methods.name: ok
methods.doc: True when no **hard** constraint is violated. A soft constraint never blocks.

classes.name: ConstraintViolation
classes.sig: (report: ConstraintReport, where: str = '')
classes.doc: A hard constraint was violated. Carries the :class:`ConstraintReport` that says which one and by how much.

classes.name: ConstraintGuard
classes.sig: (constraints: Sequence[Any], *, on_violation: Any = 'raise', where: str = '', values: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, tol: float = TOL)
classes.doc:
The same constraints as a guard around a prediction, so a deployment refuses instead of serving.

A constraint is cheap enough to evaluate per prediction, and that is the point: the guard asks the constraint
object itself -- not a copy, not a re-implementation in the serving code -- and raises
:class:`ConstraintViolation` with the report when a **hard** constraint is violated. A soft constraint is reported
and let through: the answer is still off, and stopping a production call over a number that was declared
non-fatal would be worse than the number.

``on_violation="raise"`` (default) refuses; ``"report"`` evaluates, records ``last_report`` and returns the
prediction anyway (a shadow mode, for measuring a limit in production before enforcing it); a callable is called
with the report and then the violation is raised -- a metric, a log line or an alert.

Usage
-----
>>> guard = ConstraintGuard([T], where="serve /predict")
>>> predict = guard.wrap(model_predict)          # or: @guard
>>> predict(x)                                   # raises ConstraintViolation on a hot prediction

methods.name: check
methods.sig: (out: Any, values: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> ConstraintReport
methods.doc: Ask every constraint about ``out``, record the report on ``last_report``, and act on a violation.

methods.name: wrap
methods.doc: ``predict`` with the guard in front: same call, same return value, or a refusal.

functions.name: residual
functions.sig: (constraint: Any, values: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Any
functions.doc:
The signed margin of ``constraint`` over ``values``: ``<= 0`` satisfied, ``> 0`` violated by that much.

``values`` maps quantity name -> number or field. A field (a numpy array or a torch tensor) gives an elementwise
margin -- one per cell -- and :func:`check` takes the worst of them; with a tensor the result is a tensor and
carries its graph, which is what lets the same object be a training penalty.

functions.name: check
functions.sig: (constraint: Any, values: Mapping[str, Any], *, tol: float = TOL) -> ConstraintCheck
functions.doc:
Ask one constraint about one answer, and record the answer (satisfied, margin, value, limit).

A field-valued quantity is reduced to its worst element before the comparison: the report then says "the hottest
cell is 7.5 degC above the limit", which is the statement a designer can act on.

functions.name: check_all
functions.sig: (constraints: Iterable[Any], values: Mapping[str, Any], *, tol: float = TOL) -> ConstraintReport
functions.doc:
Every constraint asked about one answer. This is also how a probability is measured: :func:`check_all` per
ensemble member, then the fraction of reports that violate each constraint.

functions.name: penalty
functions.sig: (constraints: Sequence[Any], out: Any, values: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, *, reduction: str = 'mean')
functions.doc:
The constraints as one differentiable loss term: ``sum(weight * mean(relu(g) ** 2))``.

``out`` is what the model produced -- a tensor (the predicted field is then the quantity every ``kind="bound"``
constraint is about) or a mapping of quantity name -> value. ``values`` carries anything else the constraints
name, typically the batch (the design parameters of an expression constraint).

A satisfied constraint contributes exactly zero, and the ``relu`` keeps a non-zero gradient at the boundary, so a
network that already respects the limit is not pushed away from it. The square makes the term quiet for a small
violation and dominant for a large one, which is what a hard limit deserves.

A field-valued quantity is penalised **cell by cell**, not reduced to its worst cell: :func:`check` reduces because
a report has to answer "is this satisfied", decided by the hottest cell, while a penalty has to push back
everywhere the field is over the line -- reducing to one cell would spend a whole step's gradient budget on a
single point.

Returns a torch scalar. With no constraints it returns ``torch.zeros(())``, so a training loop can add it
unconditionally.

functions.name: optimizer_constraints
functions.sig: (constraints: Sequence[Any], names: Sequence[str] | None = None)
functions.doc:
The same constraints as ``pinneapple_core.optim`` objects, for ``PhysicsOptimizer(constraints=...)``.

``names`` names the optimizer's parameter vector, in order, so a constraint written as ``"mass_kg <= 50"`` or
``"chord - 2 * thickness >= 0.01"`` finds its variables. Without ``names`` the optimizer's own
``argument="dict"`` convention is assumed. A bound constraint with ``op="=="`` becomes an equality constraint;
everything else is an inequality ``g <= 0``, which is the convention both sides already use.

children.summary: Um objeto de restrição, aplicado nos três lugares onde uma resposta pode violar um limite (#221, roadmap X34).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.darcy_checks
children.doc:
Physics checks of a 2-D Darcy field, ``-div(a grad u) = f`` on the unit square with ``u = 0`` on the boundary.

Every check works on a predicted field alone (no reference solution) and uses the same discretisation as the
reference solver ``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` and the zoo dataset
``darcy_2d_li2021``: cell-centred values on an ``n x n`` grid, ``h = 1/n``, two-point flux finite volumes with
harmonic-mean face coefficients and half-cell Dirichlet faces. A field that solves that discrete problem passes all
of them to round-off; a surrogate's prediction passes them only as far as it respects the physics.

``darcy_residual``
    ``f - A_a u`` per cell (``A_a`` the finite-volume operator): the PDE residual, consistent with the solver.
``residual_error_bound``
    a guaranteed bound on the error of ``u`` in the energy norm of the discrete problem, from the residual only:
    ``||u_h - u||_A <= ||r||_{L^-1} / sqrt(min a)``, with ``L`` the constant-coefficient (``a = 1``) operator, whose
    inverse is applied by a fast sine transform. It holds because ``A_a - min(a) L`` is positive semi-definite
    (every face coefficient is a harmonic mean, never below ``min a``). Returned relative to ``||u||_A``.
``boundary_flux_balance``
    net outward flux through the four sides (``2 a u`` per boundary face, the solver's own boundary flux) against
    the integral of the source: the discrete conservation statement.
``boundary_values``
    the value of ``u`` on the boundary, extrapolated linearly from the first two cells (second order).
``check_nodal_darcy_batch`` (and ``nodal_*``, ``solve_nodal_darcy``)
    the same kind of checks for training data stored at the nodes of a finite-difference grid (PhysicsNeMo's
    ``Darcy2D`` datapipe layout), before anyone trains on the data: residual of the documented equation in that
    layout, boundary values, a control-volume flux balance, positivity, and the diversity measures of
    ``pinneapple_data.audit``. For cell-centred data in the layout of ``darcy_2d_li2021``, use ``audit_dataset``.
``residual_l2_bound``
    the same certificate for the error of the field itself (discrete Poincare inequality).
``PROFILES`` / ``profile_verdicts``
    use profiles, set a priori with the reason for each limit: ``fields`` (maps of ``u``: L2 bound, ``u = 0``,
    positivity) and ``fluxes`` (flow rates and wall gradients: energy bound, flux balance); per profile the
    decision and the graded ratio value / limit.
``sample_checks`` / ``sample_verdict``
    the checks of one prediction exactly as ``pinneapple check`` runs them, so a verdict shown next to a
    prediction is the CI's verdict.
``estimated_error`` / ``estimated_flux_error`` / ``regional_errors`` / ``use_verdicts``
    where the error is, from the residual alone: (uncertified) error maps of ``u`` and of the flux ``a grad u``, its size near the walls and in the
    interior, and which uses a prediction can serve and why (interior field values; walls and boundary fluxes;
    inputs inside the training envelope).
``physics_metrics`` / ``calibrate_tolerances``
    the per-sample values of the physics checks, and limits calibrated on a model's own predictions for held-out
    in-distribution inputs (no labels): a drift monitor that flags inputs where the model is less physical than
    where it was validated.
``darcy_checks`` / ``darcy_trust_report``
    the checks above (plus positivity, the maximum principle for ``f >= 0``, an optional reference comparison and
    an optional applicability check of the coefficient against the training data) for one field or a batch, as
    :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report.Check` objects and a deploy decision.

numpy and scipy only (the checker of ``pinneapple check`` loads this module without torch).

classes.name: CoefficientEnvelope
classes.doc:
What the training coefficients looked like: the values ``a`` took and the range of the field statistics.

``fit(a_train)`` records the extreme values of ``a`` and the ``[q, 1 - q]`` quantiles of the contrast, high
fraction and interface density; ``contains(a)`` says, per sample, whether a new coefficient lies inside.

methods.name: violations
methods.doc: Per sample, the descriptors outside the envelope (empty list = inside).

methods.name: to_check_config
methods.doc: The ``envelope`` table of a ``pinneapple check`` result (``physics = "darcy"``).

methods.name: from_check_config
methods.doc: Inverse of :meth:`to_check_config`.

classes.name: DarcyCheck
classes.doc: One check over a batch: the per-sample values, the aggregate compared with the limit, pass / fail.

classes.name: UseProfile
classes.doc:
What a prediction is used for, and the physics limits that use needs. ``limits``: metric (a key of
:func:`physics_metrics`) -> limit; ``reasons``: why each limit, written before any model is checked.

functions.name: darcy_operator_apply
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``A_a u``: the finite-volume operator of ``-div(a grad u)`` (with ``u = 0`` on the boundary) applied to ``u``.

``u``, ``a``: ``(n, n)`` or ``(batch, n, n)`` at the cell centres. Identical, cell by cell, to the matrix that
``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` assembles.

functions.name: darcy_residual
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Finite-volume residual ``f - A_a u`` per cell (same shape as ``u``); zero for the solver's own solution.

functions.name: residual_error_bound
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Certified relative error of ``u`` in the energy norm of the discrete problem, from its residual alone.

Returns ``||r||_{L^-1} / sqrt(min a) / ||u||_A`` per sample (a scalar for one field), an upper bound on
``||u_h - u||_A / ||u||_A`` where ``u_h`` is the exact finite-volume solution on the same grid. Inner products
carry the cell area ``h^2``. The bound is about the discrete solution: the discretisation error of ``u_h`` itself
(about 0.5 % in L2 at 128 x 128 for the zoo dataset) is not included.

functions.name: residual_l2_bound
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Certified relative L2 error of ``u`` (to the discrete solution), from its residual alone.

``||u_h - u||_2 <= ||r||_{L^-1} / (min a * sqrt(lambda_min(L))) / ||u||_2``: the energy bound of
:func:`residual_error_bound` with the discrete Poincare inequality ``v^T A v >= min(a) lambda_min(L) ||v||^2``,
``lambda_min(L) = (8 / h^2) sin^2(pi / (2 n))`` (about ``2 pi^2``). It bounds the error of the field itself, the
quantity a map of ``u`` is judged by, where the energy bound bounds the error of its gradient (the flux).

functions.name: boundary_flux_balance
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Net outward flux through the boundary against the integral of the source (per sample).

The outward flux through a boundary face of cell ``c`` is ``a_c (u_c - 0) / (h/2) * h = 2 a_c u_c``, as in the
solver. Returns ``{"outflow", "source", "imbalance"}`` with ``imbalance = |outflow - source| / |source|``.

functions.name: boundary_values
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``u`` on the four sides, ``1.5 u_0 - 0.5 u_1`` from the two cells next to each face: ``(batch, 4, n)``
(order x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max; ``(4, n)`` for one field).

functions.name: coefficient_stats
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Per-sample descriptors of a coefficient field used for the applicability check.

``a_min``, ``a_max``, ``contrast`` (max / min), ``high_fraction`` (share of cells above the mid value) and
``interface_density`` (share of interior faces across which ``a`` jumps: inversely proportional to the
correlation length of the field).

functions.name: darcy_checks
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0, *, reference: np.ndarray | None = None, envelope: CoefficientEnvelope | None = None, tolerances: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, quantile: float = 0.9, physics_kind: str = 'physics') -> list[DarcyCheck]
functions.doc:
Physics checks of predicted Darcy fields ``u`` for coefficients ``a`` (``(n, n)`` or ``(batch, n, n)``).

Each check is computed per sample and aggregated with the ``quantile`` over the batch (0.9: nine samples in ten
must pass); the per-sample values are kept. Physics checks (no reference needed): certified energy-error bound
from the residual, boundary condition, flux balance, positivity (``f >= 0`` only). ``reference`` adds the
relative L2 error; ``envelope`` adds the applicability of the coefficients (inside the training envelope).
``physics_kind`` labels the physics checks (e.g. ``"drift"`` when ``tolerances`` come from
:func:`calibrate_tolerances`).

functions.name: physics_metrics
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Per-sample values of the physics checks, keyed like :data:`DEFAULT_TOLERANCES` (``energy_bound``,
``l2_bound``, ``bc``, ``flux``, ``positivity``); no reference solution needed.

functions.name: calibrate_tolerances
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0, *, quantile: float = 0.99, floor: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Limits for :func:`darcy_checks` from a model's own predictions ``u`` on held-out in-distribution inputs ``a``.

The fixed :data:`DEFAULT_TOLERANCES` say whether a prediction obeys the physics to an engineering tolerance.
These say whether a new prediction is as physical as the model was where it was validated: per check, the
``quantile`` of the per-sample values on the calibration inputs (at least ``floor``, default 1e-12). No
reference solution is used, so the limits can be refreshed on any batch of in-distribution inputs. With the
default aggregation of :func:`darcy_checks` (the 0.9 quantile of a batch), a batch from the calibration
distribution passes, and a batch that departs from it is flagged.

functions.name: profile_verdicts
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0, *, profiles: Mapping[str, UseProfile] | None = None, quantile: float = 0.9) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Per use profile, over a batch: each metric's ``quantile`` value, its limit and ``ratio = value / limit``,
the profile's ``ratio`` (the worst one, 1 = at the limit) and its decision (APPROVED when every metric is
within its limit, else REJECT).

functions.name: sample_checks
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float = 1.0, *, tolerances: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, envelope: CoefficientEnvelope | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
The checks of one prediction (``(n, n)``), each ``{"key", "value", "limit", "passed"}``, as ``pinneapple
check`` runs them (``physics = "darcy"``): the physics metrics against ``tolerances`` (default
:data:`DEFAULT_TOLERANCES`) and, with ``envelope``, the coefficient against the training envelope (values of
``a``, contrast, high fraction, interface density). A figure that shows a verdict next to a prediction uses this
function, so it says what the CI says.

functions.name: sample_verdict
functions.sig: (checks: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> str
functions.doc: PASS when every check of :func:`sample_checks` passes, else FAIL (the exit status of ``pinneapple check``).

functions.name: estimated_error
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Map of the error of ``u`` estimated from its residual alone: ``e ~ L^-1 r / a_h``.

``A_a e = r`` holds exactly for the error ``e = u_h - u`` to the discrete solution. Replacing ``A_a`` by the
constant-coefficient operator ``a_h L`` (``a_h`` the harmonic mean of ``a``, one fast sine transform) gives this
estimate. It is not a certified bound (see :func:`residual_error_bound` for that), but it says where the error
is. With the harmonic mean it tends to over-estimate: on the PhysicsNeMo Darcy example it is 1.4 to 2.7 times the
true error, with a correlation of 0.7 to 0.85 to the true error map.

functions.name: flux_magnitude
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``|a grad u|`` per cell from the solver's own face fluxes (harmonic-mean faces, half-cell Dirichlet faces):
each component is the mean of the cell's two face flux densities.

functions.name: estimated_flux_error
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Map of the error of the flux ``a grad u`` estimated from the residual alone (:func:`estimated_error`),
relative to the largest flux of ``u``: ``|a grad e| / max |a grad u|``.

functions.name: region_masks
functions.sig: (n: int, wall_cells: int = 2, interior_from: int = 8) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Boolean masks of an ``n x n`` cell grid: ``wall`` (cells closer than ``wall_cells`` to the boundary) and
``interior`` (at least ``interior_from`` cells away).

functions.name: regional_errors
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0, *, wall_cells: int = 2, interior_from: int = 8) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Relative error estimated without a reference (:func:`estimated_error`) in the ``wall`` and ``interior``
regions of :func:`region_masks`, per sample: ``||e||_region / ||u||_region``.

functions.name: use_verdicts
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float = 1.0, *, envelope: CoefficientEnvelope | None = None, wall_cells: int = 2, interior_from: int = 8) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
For one prediction (``(n, n)``): which uses it can serve, and why (:data:`USES`), from the residual alone,
plus ``inputs`` (the coefficient inside the training envelope). Each entry: ``ok``, the measured ``values``, the
``limits`` and a one-line ``reason``.

functions.name: trust_report
functions.sig: (checks: Sequence[DarcyCheck], *, model: str = '', kinds: Sequence[str] | None = None)
functions.doc:
The deploy decision (``TrustReport``: APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT) of a list of :class:`DarcyCheck`, e.g. the
checks of several :func:`darcy_checks` calls (fixed limits and calibrated ones); ``kinds`` keeps only those.

functions.name: darcy_trust_report
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0, *, model: str = '', kinds: Sequence[str] = ('physics', 'reference', 'applicability'), **kwargs)
functions.doc:
``(TrustReport, checks)``: the deploy decision (APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT) of :func:`darcy_checks`.

``kinds`` selects which checks enter the decision (``("physics",)`` gives the verdict the physics alone reach,
without labels or the training envelope).

functions.name: save_darcy_npz
functions.sig: (path, a: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, **extra)
functions.doc:
One Darcy field as the grid result ``pinneapple check`` reads (``physics = "darcy"``): cell-centre axes
``x``, ``y`` of the unit square, coefficient ``a`` and solution ``u`` (float32).

functions.name: check_config_entry
functions.sig: (name: str, path: str, *, f: float = 1.0, tolerances: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, envelope: CoefficientEnvelope | None = None, coefficient: str = 'a', solution: str = 'u') -> str
functions.doc:
One ``[[result]]`` table of a ``pinneapple-check.toml`` for a Darcy prediction saved with
:func:`save_darcy_npz`: ``physics = "darcy"``, the source, the tolerances (metric keys of
:func:`physics_metrics`) and the coefficient envelope (bounds of ``a`` and the envelope statistics).

functions.name: nodal_darcy_residual
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, k: np.ndarray, f: float = 1.0, dx: float = 1.0, *, cropped: int = 1, cross_denominator: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``-(k lap u + grad k . grad u) - f`` at the stored nodes whose four neighbours are known: ``(batch, m, m)``
with ``m = n - 1`` when the high side is cropped, ``n`` otherwise.

functions.name: nodal_boundary_values
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, *, cropped: int = 1) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``u`` extrapolated linearly from the two nearest stored nodes to the zero-ghost nodes on the four sides:
``(batch, 4, n)`` (x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max). Low ghost at index -1, high ghost at index ``n + cropped``.

functions.name: nodal_flux_balance
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, k: np.ndarray, f: float = 1.0, dx: float = 1.0, *, cropped: int = 1) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Relative imbalance of a control-volume budget around the stored nodes (whole block if not cropped, all but
the last row and column if cropped): net outward flux (harmonic-mean face coefficients) against ``f`` times the
area. Zero for a conservative solution; per sample.

functions.name: solve_nodal_darcy
functions.sig: (k: np.ndarray, f: float = 1.0, dx: float = 1.0, *, cross_denominator: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Direct solve of ``-(k lap u + grad k . grad u) = f`` on an ``n x n`` node block with zero ghosts at index -1
and ``n`` (coefficient clamped at the edges): the reference for :func:`nodal_darcy_residual` with ``cropped=0``.

functions.name: check_nodal_darcy_batch
functions.sig: (k: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, f: float = 1.0, dx: float = 1.0, *, cropped: int = 1, alt_cross_denominators: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, tolerances: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, floor_factor: float = 2.0, n_reference: int = 8) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Physics checks of a batch of node-based Darcy training pairs ``(k, u)`` before anyone trains on them.

Residual of the documented equation (relative RMS over the batch, ``residual`` limit), boundary condition
(``bc``), control-volume flux balance (``flux``), positivity and the diversity of the coefficient samples. For
reference, the same equation solved directly for up to ``n_reference`` distinct coefficients
(:func:`solve_nodal_darcy`, coefficient clamped over the cropped edge) is put through the same checks; the boundary and flux limits are at least
``floor_factor`` times what that exact solve reaches on the same grid. ``alt_cross_denominators`` (name -> value) gives the
residual of other stencils, to say which equation the data do satisfy. Returns a JSON-able dict with the values and pass / fail.

children.summary: Physics checks of a 2-D Darcy field, -div(a grad u) = f on the unit square with u = 0 on the boundary.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge
pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge.adapter
children.doc:
``ProblemSpec`` -> real DeepXDE ``dde.Model`` translation and training.

Translates a real PINNeAPPle :class:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.ProblemSpec`
(coords, fields, :class:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.PDETermSpec`,
and :class:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.conditions.ConditionSpec`
boundary/initial conditions) into DeepXDE's own real objects -- a
``dde.geometry`` geometry, a ``dde.data.PDE``/``dde.data.TimePDE``, a
``dde.nn.FNN``, and a ``dde.Model`` -- and actually runs DeepXDE's own
``.train()`` on it. This is a genuine alternative solving backend, not a
re-implementation of PINN training: DeepXDE does the sampling, the network,
the optimizer loop, and the loss bookkeeping; this module only does the
one-time translation at the boundary.

Only two ``pde.kind`` values are translated for real here: ``"burgers"``
(1D viscous Burgers, e.g. the ``burgers_1d`` preset) and ``"poisson"`` (2D
Poisson, e.g. the ``poisson_2d`` preset) -- both residual forms are taken
directly from ``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.compile`` so the
sign conventions match PINNeAPPle's own native compiler
(``u_t + u*u_x - nu*u_xx = 0`` for Burgers; ``laplacian(u) - f = 0`` for
Poisson, ``f`` defaulting to zero). Any other ``pde.kind`` raises a clear
``NotImplementedError`` naming the unsupported kind rather than silently
mistranslating it -- generalizing this to every PDE kind PINNeAPPle's own
compiler supports is future work, not something this bridge fakes.

Condition translation (``ConditionSpec`` -> ``dde.icbc.*``) supports
``"dirichlet"``, ``"neumann"``, and ``"initial"`` conditions whose
``selector_type`` is ``"all"``, ``"callable"``, or ``"tag"`` with
``tag == "boundary"`` (the convention used by e.g. ``poisson_2d``'s BC,
meaning "the geometric domain boundary", which is exactly what DeepXDE's
own ``geom.on_boundary`` already computes). Other tags, condition kinds
(``"robin"``, ``"interface"``, ``"data"``), or multi-field conditions raise
``NotImplementedError`` rather than being silently dropped.

Optional dependency
--------------------
``deepxde`` is genuinely optional: importing this module never requires it.
Only :func:`solve_with_deepxde` (and :func:`require_deepxde`) perform a real
``import deepxde`` and raise a clear, actionable ``ImportError`` if it is
missing.

classes.name: DeepXDESolveResult
classes.doc:
Outcome of :func:`solve_with_deepxde`.

Attributes
----------
deepxde_model:
    The real, trained ``dde.Model`` (call ``.predict(x)`` on it directly).
spec:
    The :class:`ProblemSpec` that was translated and solved.
final_loss:
    Sum of the training-loss components (``train_state.loss_train``) at
    the last recorded training step.
train_time_s:
    Wall-clock seconds spent in ``dde.Model.train()``.

functions.name: require_deepxde
functions.sig: () -> Any
functions.doc:
Import ``deepxde``.

Raises a clear, actionable ``ImportError`` if it is not installed. This
is the ONLY place in :mod:`pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge` that
performs a real ``import deepxde``.

functions.name: is_deepxde_available
functions.sig: () -> bool
functions.doc: Return ``True`` if ``deepxde`` can be imported.

functions.name: solve_with_deepxde
functions.sig: (spec: ProblemSpec, *, n_domain: int = 2000, n_boundary: int = 200, n_initial: int = 100, layers: Sequence[int] = (50, 50, 50, 50), epochs: int = 10000, activation: str = 'tanh', kernel_initializer: str = 'Glorot normal', optimizer: str = 'adam', lr: float = 0.001, source_fn: Optional[Callable[[np.ndarray, dict], np.ndarray]] = None, verbose: int = 0, **deepxde_kwargs) -> DeepXDESolveResult
functions.doc:
Translate ``spec`` into a real DeepXDE problem and train it for real.

Builds a ``dde.geometry`` geometry from ``spec.coords``/``domain_bounds``,
a residual callable from ``spec.pde`` (see :func:`_build_pde_residual`
for the supported ``pde.kind`` values), boundary/initial conditions from
``spec.conditions`` (see :func:`_translate_conditions`), a
``dde.data.PDE``/``dde.data.TimePDE``, a ``dde.nn.FNN`` sized
``[len(coords)] + list(layers) + [len(fields)]``, and a ``dde.Model`` --
then calls DeepXDE's own ``model.compile()``/``model.train()``.

Parameters
----------
spec:
    The problem to solve. Only ``spec.pde.kind in {"burgers", "poisson"}``
    is translated; anything else raises ``NotImplementedError`` naming
    the unsupported kind.
n_domain, n_boundary, n_initial:
    Passed through to ``dde.data.PDE``/``TimePDE`` as
    ``num_domain``/``num_boundary``/``num_initial``. ``n_initial`` is
    ignored for time-independent problems (no ``dde.data.PDE`` argument
    for it).
layers:
    Hidden-layer widths of the ``dde.nn.FNN``.
epochs:
    Training iterations, passed to ``model.train(iterations=epochs)``.
activation, kernel_initializer:
    Passed to ``dde.nn.FNN``.
optimizer, lr:
    Passed to ``model.compile()``.
source_fn:
    For ``pde.kind == "poisson"`` only: ``f(X, ctx) -> array`` giving the
    RHS forcing (``laplacian(u) - f = 0``); defaults to
    ``spec.pde.meta.get("source_fn")`` and then zero, matching
    ``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.compile``'s convention.
verbose:
    Passed to both ``model.compile()`` and ``model.train()``.
**deepxde_kwargs:
    Forwarded to ``model.train()`` (e.g. ``display_every``, ``callbacks``).

Raises
------
ImportError
    If ``deepxde`` is not installed.
NotImplementedError
    If ``spec.pde.kind``, a condition kind/selector, or the geometry
    shape cannot be honestly translated.

children.summary: ProblemSpec -> real DeepXDE dde.Model translation and training.

children.doc:
pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge -- DeepXDE <-> PINNeAPPle integration glue.

Bridges a real PINNeAPPle
:class:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.ProblemSpec` (as produced by
e.g. ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets.get_preset``) to real
DeepXDE (Lu Lu, Xuhui Meng, Zhiping Mao, George Em Karniadakis, "DeepXDE: A
Deep Learning Library for Solving Differential Equations," SIAM Review,
63(1):208-228, 2021; https://github.com/lululxvi/deepxde) training, so a
PINNeAPPle problem can be solved with DeepXDE as an alternative solving
backend to PINNeAPPle's own native compiler
(``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler``) -- without reimplementing any
of DeepXDE's geometry sampling, network, optimizer loop, or loss bookkeeping.

Sub-modules
-----------
adapter
    :func:`~pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge.adapter.solve_with_deepxde`
    translates ``spec.coords``/``spec.domain_bounds`` into a real
    ``dde.geometry`` geometry, ``spec.pde`` into a real DeepXDE residual
    callable, ``spec.conditions`` into real ``dde.icbc.DirichletBC`` /
    ``NeumannBC`` / ``IC`` objects, builds a real ``dde.nn.FNN`` and
    ``dde.Model``, and actually calls DeepXDE's own
    ``model.compile()``/``model.train()`` -- returning the trained model
    wrapped in :class:`~pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge.adapter.DeepXDESolveResult`.

    Only two ``pde.kind`` values are translated for real: ``"burgers"``
    (e.g. the ``burgers_1d`` preset) and ``"poisson"`` (e.g. the
    ``poisson_2d`` preset), matching the residual sign conventions of
    PINNeAPPle's own native compiler exactly. Any other ``pde.kind``, an
    untranslatable condition, or an unsupported geometry shape raises a
    clear ``NotImplementedError`` naming what is unsupported, rather than
    silently mistranslating the problem.

Optional dependency
--------------------
``deepxde`` is genuinely optional: importing this package, or anything in
it, never requires deepxde to be installed. Only
:func:`~pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge.adapter.solve_with_deepxde` (and
:func:`~pinneapple_physics.deepxde_bridge.adapter.require_deepxde`) perform
a real ``import deepxde`` and raise a clear, actionable ``ImportError``
(with an install hint) if the package is missing.
children.summary: DeepXDE <-> PINNeAPPle integration glue.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.dimensions
children.doc:
Dimensional consistency of a PDE, checked before anything is trained (#205).

A PDE whose terms do not share a dimension is not a modelling subtlety: it is a unit mistake, and a network trained
on it fits the residual of a statement that cannot be true. The failure shows up later as an error floor nobody can
explain. This reads the equation the way a reader does — ``dT/dt = alpha * laplacian(T) + q / (rho * cp)`` — assigns
a dimension to every term from the units the problem already declares, and says which term broke it:

    >>> from pinneapple_physics.dimensions import check_dimensions
    >>> report = check_dimensions("dT/dt = alpha*laplacian(T) + q/(rho*cp)", units={
    ...     "T": "K", "t": "s", "x": "m", "alpha": "m^2/s", "q": "W/m^3", "rho": "kg/m^3", "cp": "J/(kg*K)"})
    >>> print(report)                                    # doctest: +SKIP
    dT/dt -> K/s, alpha*laplacian(T) -> K/s, q/(rho*cp) -> m^2/s^2/K: inconsistent
    >>> [str(p) for p in report.problems]                # doctest: +SKIP
    ["'q/(rho*cp)' is m^2/s^2/K, the other terms of the equation are K/s"]

What it will not do: guess a unit. A name it does not know is refused by name, because a checker that assumed the
missing unit would pass exactly the equation it was written to catch.

Notation it understands, so the equation can be written the way the paper writes it:

======================  ============================================================================
``dT/dt``, ``∂T/∂t``    time derivative: the field's unit over the time coordinate's unit
``d2T/dx2``, ``∂²T/∂x²`` second spatial derivative
``laplacian(T)``, ``lap(T)``, ``∇²T``   field over a length squared
``grad(T)``, ``div(u)``  field over a length
