``d_dt(T)``, ``dt(T)``, ``d_dx(T)``, ``dx(T)``, ``d2_dx2(T)``   the same three, in call form
======================  ============================================================================

Units come from the problem when one is given (``problem.units`` and each parameter's ``unit``), from ``units=`` when
not, and ``units=`` wins where both say something.

classes.name: Term
classes.doc: One additive term of the equation, with the unit it works out to.

classes.name: DimensionReport
classes.doc: What the checker found: the terms and their units, and every reason the equation cannot hold.

methods.name: raise_if_inconsistent
methods.doc: Refuse to go on: the message is the report, so the failing term is the first thing read.

functions.name: unit_dim
functions.sig: (text: str) -> Dim
functions.doc: The dimension vector of a unit string; ``"m^2/s"`` -> m²·s⁻¹. Raises ``ValueError`` for a unit it cannot read.

functions.name: format_dim
functions.sig: (dim: Dim) -> str
functions.doc:
A readable unit for a dimension: ``K/s``, ``m^2/s``, ``W/m^3``, ``dimensionless``.

A short base product wins (``K/s`` reads better than ``Hz·K``). A longer one is named after the derived unit it
contains, because that is the unit the term is quoted in: ``W/m^3``, not ``kg/(m·s^3)``.

functions.name: check_dimensions
functions.sig: (equation: str, *, problem: Any = None, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, space: str | None = None, time: str | None = None) -> DimensionReport
functions.doc:
Check that every term of ``equation`` shares a dimension.

``equation`` is one statement, ``"dT/dt = alpha*laplacian(T) + q/(rho*cp)"``. Units come from ``problem`` when one
is given and from ``units`` in either case, with ``units`` winning. ``space`` and ``time`` name the units behind
``laplacian``, ``grad``, ``div`` and the derivatives; without them they are taken from a coordinate whose unit is a
length or a time, and the checker refuses rather than assuming metres and seconds.

children.summary: Dimensional consistency of a PDE, checked before anything is trained (#205).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.domain_checks
children.doc:
Physics checks per domain, for models that were trained somewhere else: does the prediction still obey the
structure the domain demands, where no truth is available?

A pre-trained model is accurate on its training distribution and quiet outside it; the checks here ask the three
questions a domain asks of any field, and answer them with a number that needs no reference:

* **weather** — :func:`advection_residual`: a tracer that is advected satisfies ``dc/dt + u.grad c = 0``, so the part
  of its 6-hour change that the wind cannot explain is a measure of how far the prediction has left the dynamics.
  :func:`global_drift`: the area-weighted integral of a conserved total (dry static energy ``cp T + g z``) must not
  wander: its drift per day, in units of the field's own spatial spread, is a model-independent number that a
  physical forecast keeps near the one the analysis has.
* **flood masks** — :func:`hand` (height above nearest drainage) and :func:`flood_mask_score`: water on a cell that
  the terrain does not drain into is impossible; a mask that wets terrain far above the water surface, or that wets a
  downstream cell while leaving its upstream donors dry, is inadmissible whatever the model.
* **video** — :func:`temporal_residual`: between two frames of a physical scene, intensity moves with the scene
  (brightness constancy), so the part of the frame-to-frame change that no displacement within ``max_speed`` can
  explain is the flicker, the reshuffle or the teleporting content.

Every check is a :class:`~pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.monitor.ValidityCheck` (value, tolerance, the evidence
string of the monitor) and :func:`as_prediction_check` turns it into the ``(score, reason)`` callable that
``PhysicsEnsemble(prediction_checks=...)`` tilts the weights with.

functions.name: sphere_gradient
functions.sig: (field: np.ndarray, lat: Sequence[float], lon: Sequence[float]) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Eastward and northward gradient on a latitude-longitude grid in 1/m: central differences, periodic in
longitude, one-sided at the first and last row; the metric ``R cos(lat)`` divides the eastward difference, so a
gradient near a pole is not inflated by the converging meridians.

functions.name: advection_residual
functions.sig: (field: np.ndarray, u: np.ndarray, v: np.ndarray, hours: float, lat: Sequence[float], lon: Sequence[float], weights: np.ndarray | None = None) -> float
functions.doc:
Relative part of the time change of ``field`` that the advection by ``(u, v)`` does not explain.

``field``: ``(steps + 1, lat, lon)``; ``u``, ``v``: the advecting wind in m/s, ``(steps + 1, lat, lon)`` or
``(lat, lon)`` (one analysis wind for the whole window). ``hours`` is the interval between two steps. The value is
``||dc/dt + u.grad c|| / max(||dc/dt||, ||u.grad c||)`` with the area weights ``weights`` (cosine of latitude by
default): 0 for a field that is exactly advected, ~1 for a change with no advective structure -- or for a tracer
that sits still under a wind that should carry it, which is the same failure from the other side -- and it needs
no reference field. The denominator is the larger of the two terms so that a field which does not change at all is
judged against the advection that should have moved it, instead of dividing by zero.

functions.name: advection_check
functions.sig: (wind_of: Callable[[Any], tuple], tolerance: float, lat: Sequence[float], lon: Sequence[float], hours: float = 6.0, select: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], np.ndarray] | None = None, weights: np.ndarray | None = None, name: str = 'advection_consistency') -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc:
``wind_of(query) -> (u, v)`` is the wind that should advect the prediction of that query (the analysis wind at
the initial time is legitimate: it is known before the forecast). ``select(prediction, query)`` picks the field
out of the prediction when it is not one already.

functions.name: dry_static_energy
functions.sig: (temperature: np.ndarray, geopotential: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``cp T + g z`` (:math:`\Phi = g z` given as geopotential): the total energy of a dry parcel that a forecast
must not create or destroy globally.

functions.name: global_drift
functions.sig: (field: np.ndarray, lat: Sequence[float], hours: float = 6.0, weights: np.ndarray | None = None) -> float
functions.doc:
Change per day of the area-weighted mean of ``field``, in units of its own initial spatial spread
(area-weighted standard deviation about that mean). A conserved total gives ~0; a forecast that creates energy or
mass shows it here without any reference, and the scale-free value lets a temperature and a geopotential be
compared.

functions.name: energy_check
functions.sig: (tolerance: float, lat: Sequence[float], hours: float = 6.0, field_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], np.ndarray] | None = None, weights: np.ndarray | None = None, name: str = 'energy_drift') -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc:
Drift of the global total of the prediction (:func:`global_drift`); ``field_fn`` builds the conserved total out
of the prediction and the query (``dry_static_energy`` of two channels, for instance).

functions.name: flow_directions
functions.sig: (terrain: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Index of the steepest lower 8-neighbour of every cell, flattened; ``-1`` where the cell is a pit (no lower
neighbour). Edges are not connected across the boundary (the grid is a patch of terrain, not a sphere).

functions.name: hand
functions.sig: (terrain: np.ndarray, drainage: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Height above nearest drainage (m): for every cell, the elevation difference along the descending path
(steepest descent, :func:`flow_directions`) to the first cell of the drainage network it reaches. ``NaN`` where the
path ends in a pit that is not on the network: a filled DEM and a connected stream network reach everywhere, and a
cell that reaches nothing is reported rather than given a made-up height.

functions.name: flood_mask_score
functions.sig: (mask: np.ndarray, terrain: np.ndarray, drainage: np.ndarray, depth: float, check_upstream: bool = True) -> float
functions.doc:
Admissibility of a flood mask in [0, 1] (1 = admissible), from two violations of water-on-terrain:

* **above the water** — a wet cell whose height above the nearest drainage exceeds ``depth``: the water would have
  to sit above the terrain that drains away;
* **dry upstream of wet** — a dry cell that drains directly into a wet cell and lies below the water surface: a
  disconnected mask, water without the cells that feed it.

Normalised by the number of wet cells (a mask with none is admissible and uninformative: 1).

functions.name: hand_check
functions.sig: (terrain: np.ndarray, drainage: np.ndarray, depth: float, min_score: float = 1.0, select: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], np.ndarray] | None = None, name: str = 'water_on_terrain') -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc:
``flood_mask_score`` as a validity check: the value is ``1 - score`` (tolerance ``1 - min_score``), so it reads
like the other checks — 0 is a mask the terrain admits.

functions.name: lucas_kanade
functions.sig: (frames: np.ndarray, window: int = 3) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Dense one-step displacement between consecutive frames (Lucas-Kanade with a ``window`` half-size box filter):
``(u, v, residual)`` where ``u`` is along the last axis, ``v`` along the first, both in pixels per frame, and
``residual`` is ``|dI/dt + u dI/dx + v dI/dy|`` — the part of the change that the motion does not explain. The
gradients are averaged over the two frames of each pair, the discretisation that keeps the linearisation honest
for displacements of a pixel or two (the difference against the single-frame gradient is large: on a smooth
texture a one-pixel translation gives a residual of 0.16 here and 0.43 there).

functions.name: temporal_residual
functions.sig: (frames: np.ndarray, max_speed: float | None = None, window: int = 3) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
How much of a video's frame-to-frame change the motion cannot explain, plus the two things a physical sequence
does not do: move faster than ``max_speed`` (pixels per frame) and change its flow from one frame to the next.

``flow_residual``: ``||dI/dt + u.grad I|| / ||dI/dt||`` over the frames (0 for a scene that moves rigidly, 1 when
no displacement explains the change — a flicker, a gain change, shuffled frames); ``teleport_fraction``: fraction
of pixels whose estimated speed is above ``max_speed``; ``jerk``: mean change of the flow between frames divided
by the mean speed (a scene that moves smoothly keeps it near 0, a reshuffled one does not).

functions.name: temporal_continuity_check
functions.sig: (tolerance: float = 0.25, max_speed: float | None = None, window: int = 3, name: str = 'temporal_continuity') -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc:
``max(flow_residual, teleport_fraction)`` against ``tolerance``: the value is 0 for a sequence whose change is a
motion within ``max_speed`` and 1 when nothing about the change is motion.

functions.name: as_prediction_check
functions.sig: (check: ValidityCheck, strength: float = 1.0) -> Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], tuple]
functions.doc:
The ``(score, reason)`` callable ``PhysicsEnsemble(prediction_checks=...)`` expects, from a validity check:
a score of 1 inside the tolerance, falling linearly to 0 at ``strength`` times the tolerance (so a check that is
twice over its limit takes the expert out of the case, and one slightly over only tilts its weight).

children.summary: Physics checks per domain, for models that were trained somewhere else: does the prediction still obey the structure the domain demands, where no truth is available?

children.name: pinneapple_physics.embedded
children.doc:
Embedded execution: the model, its physics residual and its measurement check as **one** ONNX graph, with a
runtime a flight computer calls at tens to hundreds of hertz (#350).

The residual is cheap, which is what lets trust fly. A robot cannot afford a Python interpreter to tell it that the
prediction it is about to act on left the physics, so the whole decision goes into the graph:

* the **model** -- any ``torch.nn.Module`` mapping a fixed-size state ``(frames, H, W)`` to the next frame;
* the **residual** -- a finite-difference stencil written as convolutions, so it is arithmetic and not control flow:
  ``advection-diffusion`` (``u_t + c . grad u - alpha lap u``), ``advection``, or ``heat``, with periodic boundaries;
* the **measurement check** -- the sensor reading against the prediction, relative to its scale;
* the **decision** -- ``off_physics`` where the residual is above its tolerance, ``suspect`` where the measurement
  disagrees (which is what ``PhysicsEnsemble`` already knows how to discount), and ``trust`` as the residual judged
  against its tolerance, so a caller can threshold it at any level.

Nothing in the graph branches: ``torch.where``/comparisons export as arithmetic. :class:`EmbeddedRuntime` is the other
half -- it loads the graph, runs one step, and *measures* the latency, because "tens of hertz" is a claim only a
measurement supports.

    >>> import torch
    >>> from pinneapple_physics.embedded import EmbeddedSpec, export, EmbeddedRuntime, graph_summary
    >>> model = torch.nn.Conv2d(2, 1, 3, padding=1, padding_mode="circular")     # (2, H, W) -> (1, H, W)
    >>> spec = EmbeddedSpec(state_shape=(2, 32, 64), tolerance=0.05)
    >>> graph_summary(export(model, spec, "flight.onnx")).is_straight_line
    True
    >>> rt = EmbeddedRuntime("flight.onnx", threads=1)
    >>> out = rt.step(state, measurement)          # prediction, residual, trust, off_physics, suspect, error
    >>> rt.latency(state, measurement, n=200)["hz"]

What this is not: a quantised or pruned graph (the arithmetic is the model's own), a CUDA graph, or the PX4/ROS 2
bridge itself -- that needs a board with the flight stack on it. This ships the graph and the runtime it calls.

classes.name: EmbeddedSpec
classes.doc:
The fixed contract of the graph: what goes in, what comes out, and what each check is judged against.

``state_shape`` is ``(frames, height, width)``. The exported graph is fixed to this size, because a flight
controller allocates its buffers once. ``sensor_channels`` are the state channels a sensor measures (the
measurement check compares those), ``parameters`` are the equation's numbers, ``tolerance`` is the residual limit
and ``measurement_tolerance`` the relative disagreement a reading is allowed to have.

classes.name: EmbeddedOutput
classes.doc: One step of the embedded path: what the model says, what the physics says about it, what the sensor says.

classes.name: GraphSummary
classes.doc: What the exported file contains: the node types, whether any can branch, and its size.

classes.name: Composite
classes.sig: (model: torch.nn.Module, spec: EmbeddedSpec)
classes.doc: The whole decision as one straight-line graph: prediction, residual, trust, the two flags and the error.

classes.name: EmbeddedRuntime
classes.sig: (path: Any, *, threads: int = 1)
classes.doc:
One ONNX session, one step, and the latency measured -- the half a flight computer actually calls.

``threads`` is 1 by default: an embedded core is one core, and a latency measured on eight threads is not a
budget anybody can use.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: One decision for one fixed-size state.

methods.name: latency
methods.sig: (state: np.ndarray, measurement: np.ndarray, *, n: int = 200) -> dict[str, float]
methods.doc: Run ``n`` steps and report what the machine did: median, p95, worst, and the rate they imply.

functions.name: residual_fn
functions.sig: (spec: EmbeddedSpec) -> Any
functions.doc:
The residual as a torch function of ``(prediction, previous_frame)`` -- the same arithmetic the graph carries.

Kept public so the embedded number can be compared with the one computed in Python on the same arrays: a graph
that disagrees with its own reference is a graph nobody should fly.

functions.name: export
functions.sig: (model: torch.nn.Module, spec: EmbeddedSpec, path: Any, *, opset: int = 17) -> Path
functions.doc:
Write the composite graph: ``(state, measurement) -> (prediction, residual, trust, off_physics, suspect,
error)``.

Fixed shapes, no Python in the hot path: the exported file is arithmetic from the first node to the last.

functions.name: graph_summary
functions.sig: (path: Any) -> GraphSummary
functions.doc: What the file contains, and whether it is a straight line (no ``If``/``Loop``/``Scan`` anywhere).

children.summary: Embedded execution: the model, its physics residual and its measurement check as **one** ONNX graph, with a runtime a flight computer calls at tens to hundreds of hertz (#350).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.ensemble
children.doc:
Adaptive ensembles of physics models: PINNs, neural operators (FNO, DeepONet...), GNNs (MeshGraphNet...), numerical
solvers and closed forms, selected and combined online from the errors they make on new cases.

A query is one case: parameters, an initial or boundary condition, a geometry, a time step of a rollout. Every expert
turns the query into a prediction of the same field at the same points (adapters below handle the different inputs of
PINNs, operators and graph networks). When something reveals how good the predictions were, the weights are updated:

* a **reference** (a sensor reading, an experiment, a high-fidelity solver run on some of the cases): relative L2 error;
* the **physics residual** of each prediction (``residual_fn``), which needs no reference at all: models whose output
  violates the governing equations lose weight even in operation, where no truth is available;
* optionally the **cost** of each expert, so a cheap surrogate is preferred while it is accurate enough and the
  expensive solver takes over when it is not (adaptive fidelity).

The weighting is the prequential scheme of :mod:`pinneapple_physics.online_learning` (Fixed-Share per expert grid,
AdaHedge over the learning and switching rates): every update uses only cases already seen, so the choice of model
cannot overfit. Point-wise intervals are ensemble spread times a factor calibrated online by adaptive conformal
inference, so they are wide where the models disagree. :func:`fit_static_weights` gives the offline alternative
(convex weights fitted on a validation set, with a cross-validated estimate of their error).

classes.name: Expert
classes.doc:
``predict(query) -> array`` of the common output shape; ``cost``: fixed cost per call (any unit), or None to
use the measured wall time, or a callable ``cost(query)`` when it depends on the case (a forecast whose cost
grows with its lead time). ``provenance``: what the expert is and where it comes from — for a pre-trained model,
the record :func:`pinneapple_physics.pretrained.from_pretrained_expert` writes (source, licence, cost method).

methods.name: cost_of
methods.doc:
The cost of one call on this query, or None when it has to be measured (a callable cost that needs the
query gives None for ``query=None``: the cost is then only known per case).

fields: cost: float | Callable[[Any], float] | None = None

classes.name: PhysicsEnsemble
classes.sig: (experts: Sequence[Expert] | Mapping[str, Callable], mode: str = 'combine', etas: Sequence[float] = (0.5, 2.0, 8.0), alphas: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.01, 0.05), point_weights: np.ndarray | None = None, residual_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], float] | None = None, residual_weight: float = 0.0, cost_weight: float = 0.0, clip: float = 5.0, interval_level: float | None = 0.9, conformal_gamma: flo...
classes.doc:
Online selection / combination of physics models.

``mode``: "combine" (weighted average of the fields) or "select" (the field of the leading expert; with
``select_only_leader=True`` only that expert is evaluated, which is how the ensemble saves cost).
``point_weights``: quadrature weights of the output points (cell volumes) for the L2 norms. ``min_weight``: in
"combine" mode experts below this weight are left out of the average (still scored, so they can come back): a
model that has failed badly does not contaminate the combination through the fixed-share floor.
``residual_fn(prediction, query) -> float`` (>= 0): physics residual used as a label-free loss with
``residual_weight``; ``cost_weight`` penalises expensive experts. ``residual_lookahead`` (> 0, needs
``residual_fn``): before predicting, every expert's residual on the *current* query tilts the learned weights.
The residual needs no reference, so this reacts to a regime change on its first case instead of after the errors
of earlier cases pile up. ``lookahead_reference="self"`` (default) compares each expert's residual with its own
median over the last ``lookahead_window`` cases, ``w_i * (r_i / median_i) ** -residual_lookahead``: a jump means
the case left that expert's domain, while experts with different discretisations are never ranked by their
residual levels (a numerical scheme that satisfies its discrete equation can have a small residual and a larger
error than a neural operator). ``"experts"`` compares the residual levels across experts,
``w_i * exp(-residual_lookahead * r_i / scale)``; with large values it picks the smallest residual.
``residual_baseline`` ({expert: residual level in its own domain}, see :func:`residual_baseline`) replaces the
recent median as the reference of those experts: a model's recent history is out of domain right after a regime
change, so two models whose residuals both drop cannot be told apart by it, while their in-domain levels can.
``lookahead_persistence`` (N > 1): the tilt counts only when the last N residuals of an expert agree (all above
or all below its reference), and then by the smallest departure: a single noisy reading does not switch the
model, while a real regime change (which persists) still does, N - 1 readings later.
``measurement_check(query) -> bool``: True when the reading itself is physically suspect (a failed balance between
redundant sensors, an impossible jump, energy where a physical state has none). A suspect reading is predicted
with the learned weights only (no residual tilt) and teaches nothing: it does not update the weights, the
interval calibration or the residual history.
``conserve``: optional
``(weights, target_fn(query))`` to project the combined field onto the conserved total.
``router``: physics-aware routing (:class:`pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.PhysicsAwareRouter`, or any object
with ``prior(query, names) -> {name: log-weight}`` and ``awake(query, names) -> {name: bool}``). Before
predicting, the compatibility of each expert's assumptions and training envelope with the current case tilts the
learned weights; experts outside their physics are asleep for that case: not used, and not penalised by it (their
loss is set to the mixture's), so they keep their weight for when the case returns to their regime.
``prediction_checks``: label-free checks of each expert's prediction for the current case, run after the experts
and before choosing (``{name: fn(prediction, query)}``, or one ``fn(name, prediction, query)`` for all), each
returning a score in [0, 1] or ``(score, reason)``: a closure check of an LES, a cross-scale consistency check, a
conservation check. A score below ``check_threshold`` takes the expert out of this case (it is still scored, so
its weight learns from the failure); the others are tilted by ``score ** check_strength``. When every awake
expert fails, the router's ``escalate_from(query, names, failed)`` (a fidelity ladder, see
:class:`pinneapple_physics.multiscale.ScaleAwareRouter`) gives the experts to use instead, which are checked in
turn. ``error_tolerance``: an expert whose last reference error in the same context (``error_context(query)``,
e.g. the requested scale; one context if None) is above it fails the checks for this case too, so a fidelity
ladder escalates when the cheap rung is not accurate enough; it is still scored and comes back once its error
is within the tolerance again.

methods.name: provenance
methods.doc:
What each expert is and where it comes from, for those that declare it (see
:func:`pinneapple_physics.pretrained.from_pretrained_expert`): the source of the weights and their licence.

methods.name: licences
methods.doc: ``{expert: licence identifier}`` of the experts whose provenance records one.

methods.name: predict
methods.sig: (query: Any, select_only_leader: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Predict one case. With ``select_only_leader`` only the leading expert is run (to save cost), except every
``explore_every``-th call, when all experts run so the others' errors stay up to date.

methods.name: last_state
methods.doc:
Opaque record of the last :meth:`predict` call (expert fields, weights used, residuals, interval state).
Keep it and pass it to ``update(..., state=...)`` to score that prediction later, after other cases have been
predicted: the way to learn from a label that arrives with a delay (see :meth:`run_delayed`).

methods.name: update
methods.sig: (query: Any = None, reference: np.ndarray | None = None, state: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Score the last prediction (call :meth:`predict` first for the same query), or the prediction recorded in
``state`` (from :meth:`last_state`) when its label arrives later. Uses ``reference`` if given, the physics
residual if ``residual_fn`` is set, and the cost if ``cost_weight`` > 0.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (queries: Sequence[Any], references: Sequence[np.ndarray | None] | None = None, keep_predictions: bool = False) -> EnsembleRun
methods.doc:
Sequential evaluation: predict each case with the weights learned so far, then update with its reference
(if any) and residual. ``keep_predictions`` stores each case's fields (ensemble, interval, every expert) in
``EnsembleRun.predictions``, e.g. for ``pinneapple_physics.ensemble_viz.animate_ensemble``.

methods.name: run_delayed
methods.sig: (queries: Sequence[Any], references: Sequence[np.ndarray | None], available_at: Sequence[float], issue_times: Sequence[float] | None = None, keep_predictions: bool = False, flush: bool = True) -> EnsembleRun
methods.doc:
Prequential evaluation with delayed labels: the reference of case k exists only from time
``available_at[k]`` on (a forecast verified at its lead time, a lab result that takes days).

functions.name: relative_l2
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray, weights: np.ndarray | None = None) -> float

functions.name: from_callable
functions.sig: (name: str, fn: Callable[[Any], Any], cost: float | None = None, kind: str = 'numerical') -> Expert

functions.name: from_solution
functions.sig: (name: str, solution: Any, points: Callable[[Any], np.ndarray], cost: float | None = None, shape: Callable[[Any], tuple] | None = None) -> Expert
functions.doc: A ``pp.solve`` result (PINN, FEM, analytic, external solver...): evaluated at ``points(query)``.

functions.name: from_torch
functions.sig: (name: str, model: Any, to_input: Callable[[Any], Any], from_output: Callable[[Any, Any], Any] | None = None, cost: float | None = None, kind: str = 'neural') -> Expert
functions.doc:
Any ``torch.nn.Module`` (FNO, DeepONet, MeshGraphNet, a PINN network...): ``to_input(query)`` builds its input
(tensor, GraphBatch...), the output's ``.y`` is used if present, and ``from_output(y, query)`` maps it to the
common points (e.g. drop the batch and channel axes).

functions.name: residual_baseline
functions.sig: (experts: Sequence[Expert], domain_queries: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]], residual_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], float]) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Median physics residual of each expert on queries from its own domain (its training or validation cases),
known before operation: the reference for ``PhysicsEnsemble(residual_baseline=...)``. Experts missing from
``domain_queries`` are left out (they fall back to their recent history).

functions.name: fit_static_weights
functions.sig: (predictions: np.ndarray, references: np.ndarray, n_folds: int = 5, point_weights: np.ndarray | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Offline ensemble: convex weights (>= 0, sum 1) minimising the summed squared error on a validation set.

``predictions``: (n_cases, n_experts, ...) fields; ``references``: (n_cases, ...). Returns the weights fitted on all
cases and a K-fold cross-validated relative L2 error of the weighted ensemble next to each single expert's, so the
gain is measured on cases the weights did not see.

children.summary: Adaptive ensembles of physics models: PINNs, neural operators (FNO, DeepONet...), GNNs (MeshGraphNet...), numerical solvers and closed forms, selected and combined online from the errors they make on ...

children.name: pinneapple_physics.ensemble_viz
children.doc:
Animated view of an adaptive physics ensemble: prediction against the reference field, case by case, with the model
the ensemble chose and how its weights moved.

``animate_ensemble(run, references, "ensemble.gif")`` takes an ``EnsembleRun`` made with ``keep_predictions=True``.
Each case is shown over a few frames: for space-time fields ``(n_t, n_x)`` the frames step through time, so the waves
move; for 1-D fields ``(n_x,)`` the case is held. Panels:

* the field: reference (black), the ensemble's prediction in the colour of the chosen model with its interval, and
  every expert as a faint line;
* the current weights, interpolated between cases so the bars slide;
* the timeline: weights over all cases (revealed up to the current case), the chosen model as a coloured strip, and
  the ensemble's relative L2 error on a log axis next to the best single model on each case.

functions.name: animate_ensemble
functions.sig: (run: Any, references: Sequence[np.ndarray], path: str | Path = 'ensemble.gif', *, x: np.ndarray | None = None, times: np.ndarray | None = None, frames_per_case: int = 4, fps: int = 10, cases: Sequence[int] | None = None, regimes: Sequence[tuple[int, str]] | None = None, title: str = 'Adaptive physics ensemble', dpi: int = 80, colors: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> Path
functions.doc:
Write a GIF of the ensemble run. ``cases``: subset of case indices to animate (default: all). ``regimes``:
``[(first_case, label), ...]`` drawn as dashed lines on the timeline. Returns the path written.

children.summary: Animated view of an adaptive physics ensemble: prediction against the reference field, case by case, with the model the ensemble chose and how its weights moved.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.experiment
children.doc:
``Experiment``: one reproducible run of a method on a problem, with its metrics and provenance.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> exp = pp.Experiment("burgers_1d", method="pinn", options={"epochs": 3000}, reference="analytic", seed=1)
>>> result = exp.run()
>>> result.metrics["relative_l2"]["u"], result.wall_time_s
>>> result.save("runs/burgers_pinn")          # JSON record (+ model weights when there is a model)
>>> exp.save("runs/burgers_pinn")             # experiment.json: the definition, reloadable
>>> same = pp.Experiment.load("runs/burgers_pinn")   # runs again, same predictions

A run fixes every random source it controls (Python, NumPy, PyTorch, and PyTorch's deterministic-algorithms mode
while it runs), records the problem fingerprint, the library and dependency versions and the machine, and scores
the solution against ``reference`` when one is given. Running the same experiment twice on the same machine gives
the same predictions (``tests/test_solve_compare_experiment.py`` checks it bit for bit on CPU).

methods.name: save
methods.doc: Write ``result.json`` (and ``model.pt`` when the solution has a PyTorch model) to ``directory``.

methods.name: load_record
methods.doc: The saved JSON record (the solution object itself is not rebuilt; reload weights with ``torch.load``).

classes.name: Experiment
classes.doc:
A method applied to a problem, with a seed, options and an optional reference to score against.

``active`` turns the single solve into a **study over the problem's design box** (#34, #153): instead of one solve
the run spends ``budget`` simulations on the points that
:func:`~pinneapple_data.adaptive_sampling.adapt` picks, and the answer is the retrained surrogate over the box.
Its fields are the keywords of :class:`~pinneapple_physics.active_design.ActivePolicy`
(``budget``, ``n_initial``, ``batch``, ``signals``, ``quantity``, ``space``, ``target``, ``seed``); the axes are
the parameters whose role is ``"design"`` or ``"uncertain"`` and that carry bounds. ``active=True`` uses the
defaults, and the measured cost of that choice is in :func:`~pinneapple_physics.active_design.benchmark_active_design`.

methods.name: to_dict
methods.doc: The run's definition, JSON-ready: what :meth:`from_dict` rebuilds and :meth:`save` writes.

methods.name: from_dict
methods.doc:
Rebuild from :meth:`to_dict`. A problem that came from a preset comes back with its functions attached,
so a reloaded experiment runs and reproduces; one that did not keeps its described-only conditions and
fails loudly if it is solved.

methods.name: save
methods.doc: Write ``experiment.json`` to ``directory``; pair it with ``run().save(directory)``'s ``result.json``.

methods.name: load
methods.doc: Read a saved experiment: ``path`` is the directory :meth:`save` wrote, or the file itself.

methods.name: run_active
methods.doc: Spend the budget over the problem's design box instead of solving once (``active=...``, #34 and #153).

functions.name: run_all
functions.sig: (experiments: Sequence[Experiment]) -> Dict[str, ExperimentResult]
functions.doc: Run several experiments; keyed by experiment name.

children.summary: Experiment: one reproducible run of a method on a problem, with its metrics and provenance.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.experiments
children.doc:
Reproducing a recorded run: resolve, verify, run, compare, and say which of three things happened (#1480).

An experiment id from six months ago is not reproducible by re-running it: the package moved, the machine changed,
and nothing in the output says so. ``reproduce(exp_id)`` answers the question the re-run does not:

============  ==========================================================================================
``reproduced``  same versions, same inputs, every metric within the recorded tolerance
``divergent``   it ran, but the environment or the inputs differ, or a metric left its tolerance — and the
                differences are listed, so "why is this number different" has an answer
``refused``     it cannot be run faithfully: a dependency version, an artifact or an input is missing. The
                refusal names it instead of running on whatever happens to be present
============  ==========================================================================================

Refusal is a **result**, not an exception to work around: a caller that gets ``refused`` has learned something
about the record, and a caller that gets ``divergent`` decides whether comparing is still worth it.

Hardware is compared and reported separately from software. A run on another CPU is not the same run — the
metrics are compared within the tolerance instead of to the last bit — but it is not the same failure as a
version bump, and the report says which one happened.

Two kinds of record are reproduced, and more can register their own:

* an **experiment** — a directory with ``experiment.json`` and ``result.json``, what :meth:`Experiment.save` and
  :meth:`ExperimentResult.save` write;
* a **workflow run** — a directory with ``flow.json`` and ``run.json``, registered by :mod:`pinneapple_flow`.

    >>> import pinneapple as pp
    >>> r = pp.experiments.reproduce("runs/burgers_pinn")      # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> r.outcome, r.divergent                                  # doctest: +SKIP
    ('reproduced', False)
    >>> print(r.to_markdown())                                  # doctest: +SKIP

classes.name: Difference
classes.doc: One thing that is not what the record says: which kind, what it is, and both values.

classes.name: MetricComparison
classes.doc: One recorded metric against the value this run produced, with the tolerance it was judged by.

methods.name: ok
methods.doc:
Within tolerance. A metric the record has and this run does not is **not** ok, and neither is the
reverse: a silently missing metric is how a comparison passes without comparing anything.

classes.name: Measurement
classes.doc: What running the record again produced: the metrics to compare and the environment it ran in.

classes.name: Reproducer
classes.doc:
One kind of record that can be reproduced: how to recognise it and how to run it again.

``prepare`` returns ``(record, run)``, or raises :class:`Refused` naming what is missing. Everything after the
re-run — comparing the environment, the inputs and the metrics, and deciding the outcome — is shared, so a new
kind cannot invent its own definition of "reproduced".
fields: prepare: Callable[[Path], tuple[dict[str, Any], Callable[[], Measurement]]]

classes.name: Refused
classes.doc: The record cannot be run faithfully. Carries the sentence the caller reads.

classes.name: Reproduction
classes.doc: The answer: an outcome, the differences behind it, and the metrics compared.

methods.name: environment_recorded
methods.doc:
Whether the record says what it ran on. Without it the versions were not compared, and the report says so
rather than calling the run a reproduction because the numbers happened to match.

methods.name: to_markdown
methods.doc: The report a person reads: the outcome, why, and the two tables behind it.

functions.name: environment
functions.sig: () -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The environment fingerprint this library records with a run: python, versions, commit, machine.

Exposed because a kind of record that is not an :class:`Experiment` still has to record the same keys for its
reproduction to be comparable with the rest.

functions.name: register_reproducer
functions.sig: (reproducer: Reproducer) -> Reproducer
functions.doc:
Add a kind of record that can be reproduced. Re-registering the same kind with another meaning is refused,
so two packages cannot silently disagree about what "workflow" means.

functions.name: producers
functions.sig: () -> dict[str, Reproducer]
functions.doc: The kinds this installation can reproduce (the workflow one arrives with ``pinneapple_flow``).

functions.name: experiment_reproducer
functions.sig: () -> Reproducer

functions.name: reproducer_for
functions.sig: (directory: Path) -> Reproducer | None
functions.doc: The registered kind that recognises ``directory``, or ``None``.

functions.name: reproduce
functions.sig: (exp_id: str | os.PathLike[str], *, root: str | os.PathLike[str] | None = None, rtol: float | None = None, exact: bool = False, tolerances: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> Reproduction
functions.doc:
Re-run the recorded experiment ``exp_id`` and say whether it reproduced.

``rtol``: relative tolerance for every metric without its own; ``exact=True`` asks for bit-identical numbers
(``rtol = 0``) and is only honest for a deterministic method on the same machine. ``tolerances`` overrides per
metric, and the record's own ``tolerances`` override both — a record that declares how close is close enough is
the one that decides. Never raises for a record that cannot be run: that is ``outcome == "refused"``.

functions.name: cli
functions.sig: (argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int
functions.doc:
``pinneapple reproduce <path>``: the record, the verdict on stdout, and an exit code a job can read.

``0`` reproduced, ``1`` divergent, ``2`` refused or a bad invocation. The three are different answers and a
script that treats "refused" as "divergent" will pass a run it never reproduced.

children.summary: Reproducing a recorded run: resolve, verify, run, compare, and say which of three things happened (#1480).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.hemodynamics
children.doc:
Haemodynamics from 4D-flow MRI: Womersley's closed form as the reference, sparse samples of it as the
measurement, and a Navier-Stokes PINN asked for the two things the modality does not measure (#362).

4D-flow MRI gives velocity: a few planes across a vessel, twenty-odd cardiac phases, voxels of one to three
millimetres and noise. It does not give pressure, and it does not give wall shear stress (WSS) -- both are derivatives
of what it measures, taken at a wall where there is no sample. Whether a physics-informed network can supply them is
a measurable question, and it is measured here on a **synthetic phantom**: a rigid straight artery whose exact
solution is known in closed form. No patient data is involved at any point.

The reference is Womersley's solution of pulsatile laminar flow in a rigid straight tube. For a pressure gradient
``-dp/dz = Re[G e^{i w t}]`` the axial velocity is

    W(r) = (G / (i rho w)) [1 - J0(beta r/R) / J0(beta)],      beta = alpha sqrt(-i),   alpha = R sqrt(w / nu)

with ``alpha`` the Womersley number. Superposed over harmonics it is an exact solution of the axisymmetric
Navier-Stokes equations, which is what makes it a reference and not an approximation. Its wall shear stress is the
gradient at ``r = R`` and its pressure is linear along the axis, so both target quantities exist in closed form.

    >>> from pinneapple_physics.hemodynamics import BLOOD, Womersley, sample_4d_flow
    >>> wave = Womersley.from_flow_rate(radius=0.015, nu=BLOOD.nu, omega=2 * 3.141592653589793,
    ...                                 flow=[(1, 70e-6, -1.2)])
    >>> wave.alpha, wave.peak_velocity, wave.wall_shear(0.0)
    >>> four_d = sample_4d_flow(wave, n_radial=8, n_phases=24, noise=0.05, seed=0)

What the measurement leaves out is the point. The nearest voxel centre to the wall sits half a voxel away from it
(``voxel / 2``), and the boundary layer the wall shear stress lives in is ``R / alpha`` thick. When the first is
larger than the second -- a 15 mm aorta at 60 bpm, where ``R/alpha`` is 0.7 mm and a 3 mm voxel is 1.5 mm away -- the
data contain no information about the gradient at the wall, and only the physics can supply it. :func:`resolution_sweep`
measures what that costs, and the guide ``docs/guides/hemodynamics_4dflow.md`` reports the number.

What this is not: patient data, a real MRI scanner's sampling protocol (no slice profile, no partial volume, no
velocity aliasing), a curved or compliant vessel, or a validation against measured flow. The phantom is a straight
rigid tube because that is where a closed form exists.

classes.name: Blood
classes.doc:
Density and dynamic viscosity. The defaults are round textbook values for whole blood at 37 C, Newtonian:
1060 kg/m^3 and 3.5 mPa s, which is the assumption Womersley's solution is derived under.

methods.name: nu
methods.doc: Kinematic viscosity [m^2/s].

classes.name: Harmonic
classes.doc:
One frequency of the pressure gradient: ``-dp/dz = Re[gradient * exp(i (order*omega*t + phase))]`` [Pa/m].

The gradient is the amplitude of the *forcing*, not of the velocity: it is what Womersley's solution is written
in terms of. :meth:`Womersley.from_flow_rate` builds the harmonics from a flow-rate waveform instead, which is
the quantity a physiologist has.

classes.name: Womersley
classes.sig: (radius: float, nu: float, omega: float, harmonics: Sequence[Harmonic], rho: float = 1060.0) -> None
classes.doc:
Pulsatile laminar flow in a rigid straight tube, as Womersley (1955) wrote it.

``radius`` [m], ``nu`` [m^2/s], ``omega`` [rad/s] and the harmonics of the pressure gradient. Everything else --
velocity, flow rate, wall shear stress, pressure drop -- follows from the closed form; nothing is integrated
numerically.

The solution is linear in the forcing, so the harmonics superpose and any waveform that is a finite sum of
frequencies is exact. That is what makes this a reference: at every point of the tube and every instant the
velocity returned here satisfies the axisymmetric Navier-Stokes equations to roundoff.

methods.name: from_flow_rate
methods.sig: (radius: float, nu: float, omega: float, flow: Sequence[tuple[int, float, float]], rho: float = 1060.0, mu: float | None = None) -> Womersley
methods.doc: Build from a **flow-rate** waveform instead of a pressure gradient.

methods.name: alpha
methods.doc: Womersley number of the fundamental, ``R sqrt(omega/nu)``.

methods.name: velocity
methods.doc: Axial velocity [m/s] at ``y = r/R`` in ``[0, 1]`` and phase ``tau = omega*t`` [rad].

methods.name: radial_profile
methods.doc: Alias for :meth:`velocity` at one phase, for readability when a profile is meant.

methods.name: shear_rate
methods.doc: ``dw/dr`` [1/s] at ``y = r/R`` and phase ``tau``. Signed: negative near the wall for forward flow.

methods.name: wall_shear
methods.doc: Wall shear stress [Pa], ``-mu dw/dr`` at ``r = R``: positive when the wall feels a forward drag.

methods.name: flow_rate
methods.doc: Volume flow [m^3/s] through the cross-section at phase ``tau``.

methods.name: gradient
methods.doc: ``-dp/dz`` [Pa/m] at phase ``tau``.

methods.name: pressure_drop
methods.doc: Pressure difference ``p(z) - p(z + length)`` [Pa]: the gradient times the distance, gauge-free.

methods.name: peak_velocity
methods.doc: Peak of ``|w|`` over the cycle and the radius, from the closed form on an ``n``-point grid.

methods.name: state
methods.doc: The numbers that describe the case, for a record.

classes.name: FourDFlow
classes.doc:
A synthetic 4D-flow acquisition of one :class:`Womersley` case.

The samples are voxel centres, not a continuous profile: ``n_radial`` voxels across the radius put the ``j``-th
centre at ``y = (j + 1/2)/n_radial``, so the closest sample to the wall is **half a voxel away from it** and the
wall itself is never measured. ``n_planes`` planes along the axis repeat the same measurement with independent
noise (the flow is developed, so the planes differ only in their noise), and ``n_phases`` cardiac phases sample
the cycle.

``velocity`` is what the scanner would report: ``clean`` plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation ``sigma``,
which is ``noise`` times the peak velocity of the case (a 5 % velocity error, the usual order for 4D-flow).

methods.name: voxel
methods.doc: In-plane voxel size [m], ``R/n_radial``.

methods.name: wall_gap
methods.doc:
Distance from the nearest sample to the wall [m]: half a voxel, and the reason WSS is a derivative with no
support.

methods.name: phases
methods.doc: The cardiac phases present, in radians.

methods.name: profiles
methods.doc:
``(y, velocity)`` for one cycle, averaged over the planes: ``(n_radial, n_phases)``. Averaging the planes
is what a careful analyst does with repeated measurements, and it gives the finite-difference baseline its
best case.

classes.name: Vessel
classes.doc:
One synthetic phantom: a straight rigid tube with a radius and a flow-rate waveform.

The radii bracket the range of human arteries at 60 bpm; the waveforms are plausible round values, not
measurements. None of this is patient data -- the whole case is generated from the closed form.

classes.name: PINNConfig
classes.doc: How the network is built and trained. The defaults are the ones the guide's sweep was run with.

classes.name: WomersleyPINN
classes.doc: The model, built lazily so that importing this module does not import torch.

functions.name: stokes_layer
functions.sig: (radius: float, alpha: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Thickness of the oscillatory boundary layer [m], ``R / alpha`` -- the length the wall shear stress lives in.

It is the distance over which the velocity falls from its core value to zero at the wall, and the reason a coarse
voxel cannot see the gradient: with ``alpha = 20`` on a 15 mm radius the layer is 0.72 mm thick.

functions.name: sample_4d_flow
functions.sig: (wave: Womersley, *, n_planes: int = 3, n_phases: int = 24, n_radial: int = 8, noise: float = 0.05, seed: int = 0) -> FourDFlow
functions.doc:
Sample a :class:`Womersley` case the way a 4D-flow acquisition samples a vessel.

``n_radial`` voxels across the radius (so the wall is half a voxel from the first sample), ``n_phases`` cardiac
phases over the cycle, ``n_planes`` planes along the axis, and Gaussian noise of ``noise`` times the peak
velocity. Nothing else of the acquisition is modelled -- no slice profile, no partial volume, no aliasing.

functions.name: wss_from_profile
functions.sig: (y: np.ndarray, velocity: np.ndarray, radius: float, mu: float, order: int = 1) -> float
functions.doc:
Wall shear stress [Pa] read straight off a measured profile: fit a polynomial in ``y`` through the
outermost ``order + 1`` samples and extrapolate its slope to ``y = 1``.

``order = 1`` is the two-point difference every 4D-flow WSS pipeline starts from; ``order = 2`` fits a parabola
through three. Both are *data only*: the extrapolation runs over the gap between the last sample and the wall,
where there is no measurement, so the error they make is the honest floor of a velocity-only estimate and the
number a PINN has to beat.

functions.name: wss_from_4d_flow
functions.sig: (four_d: FourDFlow, mu: float, order: int = 1) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: The data-only estimate of the WSS waveform [Pa]: :func:`wss_from_profile` at every measured phase.

functions.sig: (wave: Womersley, four_d: FourDFlow, config: PINNConfig | None = None, progress: bool = False, w0: float | None = None) -> tuple[object, dict]
functions.doc:
Fit the network to one acquisition. Returns the model and a record of the training.

The data term is applied here rather than inside the compiled loss because it constrains one of the three fields
(``v``); the residuals come from :func:`_loss_function`. Everything is in the dimensionless variables, and ``W0``
is the largest measured velocity -- a scale that comes from the acquisition itself, not from the answer: what the
network has to find is the shape and the phase, and the gradient at the wall follows from those.

The scale is attached to the model as ``peak_velocity`` so that :func:`model_wall_shear` and
:func:`model_pressure_gradient` undo it without being told twice.

functions.doc: ``(u, v, g)`` at the given points, broadcast against each other and flattened.

functions.doc:
WSS [Pa] from the network: ``-mu dw/dr`` at the wall, the radial derivative taken by autograd.

It is the same operator the exact solution is closed-form in and the same one the data-only estimate
extrapolates towards; the difference is where the slope comes from.

functions.sig: (model, tau, wave: Womersley, w0: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``-dp/dz`` [Pa/m] from the network, in physical units.

functions.sig: (pred, ref) -> float
functions.doc: Relative L2 error, both arrays flattened: the metric every table in the guide is in terms of.

functions.name: ensemble
functions.sig: (wave: Womersley, four_d: FourDFlow, members: int = 5, config: PINNConfig | None = None, progress: bool = False) -> dict
functions.doc:
An ensemble of independently seeded fits: the mean and the spread of what they disagree about.

The spread is the uncertainty this module reports. It is a deep ensemble, not a variational posterior: it prices
the optimisation and the initialisation, not the model form, and a boundary layer none of the members resolves is
a bias all of them share and none of them reports. That limitation is measured in the guide rather than hidden.

functions.doc: ``n_phases`` phases over one cycle, in radians, excluding the repeat of ``2 pi``.

functions.doc: The :class:`Womersley` solution of one :class:`Vessel` at a heart rate of ``omega`` [rad/s].

functions.name: measure
functions.sig: (wave: Womersley, four_d: FourDFlow, ens: dict, *, segment_length: float | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Every error this module reports for one acquisition, against the closed form.

The two targets are the wall shear stress and the pressure. The pressure is compared as the difference between
two planes ``segment_length`` apart -- the only form in which an incompressible field has one -- and the wall
shear stress as the waveform over the cycle. Both are relative L2 over the cycle, so the number does not depend
on how long the studied segment is; the absolute peaks are reported beside them so that a 3 % error of 0.03 Pa
and a 3 % error of 3 Pa are not mistaken for each other.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.lithography
pinneapple_physics.lithography.design
children.doc:
Closed-loop optical proximity correction: imaging model, a learned operator only when it pays off, inverse
lithography, and the mask re-verified by the exact model over the process window (#1180).

1. **Exact model**: SOCS kernels at each focus of the process window (Hopkins, equal to Abbe when every kernel is
   kept; ``kernel_energy`` truncates them for speed and the final verification uses the full Abbe sum).
2. **Measure** the cost of one exact image; the evaluations are ``clips x ILT steps x corners`` (``clips``: how
   many layout clips this correction will run on).
3. **Ask** :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.architecture_recommendation.recommend_architecture` (a grid
   field): ``none`` when the exact model is cheap enough; otherwise a neural operator, trained on exact images and
   checked (held-out error, finer resolution, printed-pattern EPE) before it is used.
4. **ILT** through the exact kernels at every corner, or through the operator at best focus.
5. **Verify** the binarized mask with the full Abbe model: EPE at nominal against the uncorrected mask, the EPE
   over focus x dose (depth of focus, exposure latitude), the mask's smallest feature against the mask rule, and
   Abbe against the kernels on that mask.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.lithography.ilt
children.doc:
Inverse lithography (pixel OPC): the mask that prints a target, by gradient descent through the imaging model.

The mask is ``m = sigmoid(theta)`` per pixel; the printed resist is the smooth step ``sigmoid(a (T - dose I))``
for a dark-tone target (``sigmoid(a (dose I - T))`` for clear tone); the loss is the mean squared difference from
the target, summed over process corners (focus and dose), plus a small term pulling the mask to binary values
(Poonawala & Milanfar, *IEEE Trans. Image Process.* 16 (2007) 774; Granik, *J. Micro/Nanolith.* 5 (2006) 043002).
``imager`` maps a mask tensor to its aerial image at one focus: the exact model (SOCS kernels, differentiable) or a
learned operator. The final mask is binarized and **always** re-imaged by the exact model by the caller.

functions.name: optimise_mask
functions.sig: (target: np.ndarray, L: float, imager: Callable[[torch.Tensor, float], torch.Tensor], *, corners: list[tuple[float, float]] = ((0.0, 1.0),), threshold: float = 0.3, diffusion: float = 0.0, tone: str = 'dark', steps: int = 200, lr: float = 0.3, steepness: float = 50.0, binary_weight: float = 0.02, init: np.ndarray | None = None, filter_nm: float = 0.0, min_feature_nm: float = 0.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
``{"mask" (bool), "mask_continuous", "loss_history", "mrc_changed_px"}``; ``corners`` are ``(defocus nm, dose)``.

``filter_nm``: the pixel parameters are Gaussian-filtered before the sigmoid, so the mask cannot hold features
much smaller than the filter (a smooth, manufacturable mask). ``min_feature_nm``: the binary mask is then opened
and closed with a square of that size, the mask rule check (MRC) every mask shop applies; how many pixels it
changed is returned, and the caller verifies the mask after it.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.lithography.imaging
children.doc:
Scalar imaging of a periodic mask cell under partially coherent illumination (Abbe and Hopkins), in wafer units.

The mask is a transmission ``m(x, y)`` sampled on an ``N x N`` grid over a period ``L`` (nm). With the Fourier
coefficients ``M(f)`` of the cell, Abbe's method sums the coherent images of every source point ``s`` (a direction
of illumination, in units of ``NA / lambda`` as the partial-coherence factor sigma):

    I(x) = sum_s w_s | sum_f M(f) P(f + s NA/lambda) exp(2 pi i f.x) |^2 ,      sum_s w_s = 1

with the pupil ``P(f) = 1`` for ``|f| <= NA / lambda`` (zero outside) and the defocus phase
``exp(2 pi i z (sqrt(1/lambda^2 - |f|^2) - 1/lambda))`` (non-paraxial, in the medium of the image). A clear mask
images to ``I = 1``. Hopkins's form gathers the same sum into the transmission cross coefficient
``TCC(f1, f2) = sum_s w_s P(f1 + s) P*(f2 + s)``; its eigen-decomposition (sum of coherent systems, SOCS) keeps the
kernels that carry the image and is exact when all are kept.

Born & Wolf, *Principles of Optics*, 7th ed., sec. 10.5 (partially coherent imaging); Hopkins, *Proc. R. Soc. A* 217
(1953) 408; Mack, *Fundamental Principles of Optical Lithography* (2007), ch. 2-3; Cobb, PhD thesis, UC Berkeley
(1998) (SOCS). Scalar theory: polarization and the mask's 3-D topography are not modelled; at NA above about 0.7
the vector (high-NA) effects reduce the image contrast and are the next term to add.

Everything is a ``torch`` float64 computation, so the image is differentiable in the mask (inverse lithography).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.lithography.metrics
children.doc:
Resist and printed-pattern metrics: threshold resist with acid diffusion, CD, NILS, EPE, process window.

* **Resist**: the aerial image blurred by a Gaussian of length ``diffusion`` (nm, acid diffusion), then a constant
  threshold at the dose: a pixel clears (positive resist) where ``dose * I_blur >= threshold`` (Mack 2007, ch. 9:
  the threshold model is the simplest resist model; it ignores development kinetics).
* **CD** of a line along a cut: the width between the two threshold crossings, linearly interpolated.
* **NILS** at an edge: ``CD * |d ln I / dx|`` (normalized image log-slope).
* **EPE** of a 2-D pattern: the area where printed and target differ divided by the target's edge length, a mean
  edge-placement error in nm (pixel-exact for Manhattan patterns).
* **Process window**: the printed pattern over a focus x dose grid; the depth of focus is the focus range over
  which the EPE stays within a tolerance at the nominal dose, the exposure latitude the dose range at best focus.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.lithography.surrogate
children.doc:
A learned imaging operator: a Fourier neural operator from the mask to its aerial image, trained on exact images.

Training masks are random Manhattan clips (rectangles of the layout's sizes); labels are exact images (SOCS kernels
of :mod:`.imaging`, which equal Abbe's). The operator is checked before it is used:

* **held-out error**: relative L2 of the image on clips never trained on;
* **resolution**: the same physical cell sampled twice as finely (the FNO keeps its Fourier modes), against exact
  images at that resolution;
* **printed pattern**: the EPE of the pattern printed from the predicted image against the one printed from the
  exact image (what matters for OPC).

A mask optimised through the operator is re-imaged by the exact model by the caller: the operator never grades
itself (Li et al., *ICLR* 2021, FNO).

Measured with the defaults (64 x 64 clips of 1 024 nm, annular 0.6-0.9, NA 1.35, 192 training clips, 60 epochs,
171 s on four CPU cores): held-out relative L2 0.89 % (worst 1.7 %), 1.03 % at twice the sampling, printed-pattern
EPE 1.52 nm.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.maxwell_checks
children.doc:
Physics checks of electromagnetic fields from any source (a PINN, an FNO, a graph network, a solver, measured
data), without a reference solution: every check asks whether the fields obey Maxwell's equations and the
balance laws that follow from them.

Fields are components on a tensor grid. ``grid`` maps the axes present to 1-D coordinate arrays, in the order
``x, y, z, t`` (``indexing="ij"``, the layout ``pinneapple check`` reads); a field array has one dimension per axis
present. A direction that is absent is a direction of invariance (``d/dz = 0`` for a 2-D field). ``fields`` maps
component names to arrays: ``Ex, Ey, Ez``, ``Bx, ...`` (or ``Hx, ...``), ``Dx, ...``, ``Jx, ...`` and ``rho``.
Missing components are zero; ``B = mu H`` and ``D = eps E`` fill in whichever of the pair is missing. With
``omega`` the fields are complex phasors (``exp(+j omega t)``, no ``t`` axis) and ``d/dt`` is ``j omega``.

Residual checks (each relative: ``||sum of terms|| / sum of ||term||``, over interior points; 0 for an exact
field, 1 when the terms do not cancel at all; derivatives are second-order central differences):

``gauss_electric``      div D - rho
``gauss_magnetic``      div B
``faraday``             curl E + dB/dt
``ampere_maxwell``      curl H - J - dD/dt
``continuity``          d rho/dt + div J

A smooth field that obeys the law leaves a residual of order ``(k h)^2`` from the differences alone, so each
residual is also computed on the grid with every other point (``2h``): the ratio ``r(2h) / r(h)`` is about 4 when
the residual is discretisation error (the field is consistent with the law) and about 1 when the field itself
violates it. Both are reported; the extrapolated residual ``max(0, (4 r(h) - r(2h)) / 3)`` estimates the part
that does not vanish with ``h``.

Balance and network checks:

``poynting_balance``    d/dt int u dV + oint S.n dA + int J.E dV = 0 over the grid box (time domain), or
                        Re oint S.n dA + P_loss = P_source (phasors), relative to the largest term
``tangential_continuity`` n x (E1 - E2) = 0 (and n x (H1 - H2) = K) at an interface
``pec_boundary``        n x E = 0 on faces declared perfect electric conductors
``reciprocity``         ||S - S^T|| / ||S|| of scattering matrices
``passivity``           largest singular value of S <= 1 at every frequency (lossless: S^H S = I)

``maxwell_checks`` runs the checks the given fields allow and returns :class:`MaxwellCheck` objects;
``maxwell_trust_report`` turns them into a deploy decision; ``sample_checks`` is what ``pinneapple check`` runs
for ``physics = "maxwell"``. numpy only (the checker loads this module without torch).

References: Jackson, *Classical Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed., sec. 6.7 (Poynting's theorem) and 6.1 (the
equations); Pozar, *Microwave Engineering*, 4th ed., sec. 4.3 (reciprocal and lossless networks).

functions.sig: (grid, fields, *, eps = EPS0, mu = MU0, sigma = 0.0, omega: float | None = None, tol: float | None = None) -> MaxwellCheck
functions.doc:
Poynting's theorem over the grid box.

Time domain: ``U(t1) - U(t0) + int_t0^t1 [oint S.n dA + int J.E dV] dt = 0`` with ``U = int (E.D + B.H)/2 dV``
(linear, non-dispersive media; ``J`` includes ``sigma E``), relative to ``max(|U|) + int |flux| dt``.
Phasors: ``Re oint (E x H*)/2 . n dA + (1/2) int Re(J* . E) dV = 0`` with ``J`` the total current (impressed
and conduction; dielectric loss through a complex ``eps`` is added as ``(omega/2) int -Im(eps) |E|^2``),
relative to the sum of the absolute values of the terms.

functions.doc:
``n x (F1 - F2) = K`` at interface points: ``F1``, ``F2`` are (n, 3) fields on the two sides at the same
points, ``normal`` a unit normal (3,) or (n, 3) pointing from side 2 to side 1; ``K`` the surface current
(for H; zero for E). Value: RMS mismatch over RMS of the tangential fields.

functions.doc:
``n x E = 0`` on grid faces declared PEC (``"x_min"``, ``"y_max"``, ...): RMS tangential E on those
faces over RMS |E| in the whole field.

functions.doc:
``S = S^T`` for a reciprocal network (``S`` of shape (n, n) or (f, n, n)): max over frequencies of
``||S - S^T||_F / ||S||_F``.

functions.doc:
Passivity: ``I - S^H S`` positive semi-definite, i.e. the largest singular value of ``S`` is at most 1, at
every frequency; value = ``max(sigma_max - 1, 0)``. ``lossless=True`` checks unitarity ``||S^H S - I||``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.metrics
children.doc:
``pp.metrics``: the error metrics used everywhere in the library, with one convention.

Convention (applies to every function here):

* ``pred`` and ``true`` are arrays of the same shape ``(N,)`` or ``(N, F)``: N points, F fields.
  NumPy arrays, PyTorch tensors and nested lists are accepted; computation is in float64.
* For ``(N, F)`` inputs a function returns one value per field (shape ``(F,)``); use ``per_field`` to get a
  ``{field_name: value}`` dict. Fields are never mixed: a relative error of a velocity and of a pressure with
  different scales would be meaningless.
* Relative errors divide by the norm of ``true`` **for that field**. If that norm is zero the relative error is
  undefined and ``nan`` is returned (never a silently huge or zero number).

    >>> from pinneapple_physics import metrics
    >>> metrics.relative_l2([1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.0])
    0.0
    >>> metrics.per_field(metrics.rmse, pred, true, fields=("u", "p"))
    {'u': 0.012, 'p': 0.31}

functions.name: l2
functions.sig: (pred, true)
functions.doc: Euclidean norm of the error, per field: ``||pred - true||_2``.

functions.name: relative_l2
functions.sig: (pred, true)

functions.doc: ``{metric: {field: value}}`` for several metrics at once (the shape benchmark tables use).

functions.sig: (pred, true) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
One number per metric over every entry, all fields together: ``relative_l2``, ``rmse``, ``mse``, ``max_abs``,
``r2``. For leaderboards that rank models by a single value; use the per-field functions for anything reported
per quantity. When the shapes differ, a 1-D side gets a trailing axis and the two are broadcast, as the benchmark
suite always did.

functions.name: rollout_relative_l2
functions.sig: (pred_seq, true_seq, *, aggregate: str = 'steps') -> float
functions.doc:
Relative L2 error of a time rollout: ``pred_seq`` and ``true_seq`` have shape ``(T, ...)``, axis 0 is time.

* ``aggregate="steps"`` (default): the mean over steps of ``||pred_k - true_k|| / ||true_k||``, each norm over
  every entry of step ``k``. Steps where ``||true_k|| = 0`` are skipped; ``nan`` if no step is left.
* ``aggregate="trajectory"``: ``||pred - true|| / ||true||`` over the whole sequence at once (Frobenius norms),
  which weights steps by their magnitude.

Pass the predicted steps only (drop the initial condition when the rollout starts from the true state).
Unlike the per-field functions above, all fields of a step are pooled: use it on one field, or on fields
of comparable scale (e.g. normalised states).
