children.name: pinneapple_physics.multirotor
pinneapple_physics.multirotor.control
children.doc:
A cascaded controller, so the vehicle actually flies while its faults are being diagnosed.

Position -> desired acceleration -> a thrust vector and an attitude -> body rates -> torques -> the mixer. Each loop is
proportional (with damping on the velocity) because this is not the subject of the issue: what matters is that the
vehicle holds a trajectory under a fault until the fault is detected, so the residual is measured on a flying vehicle
rather than on an open-loop divergence.

The controller is deliberately given **no knowledge of the faults** -- it sees the nominal model and the sensors -- so a
payload or a degraded motor makes it work harder, which is exactly what shows up in the residual.

classes.name: Trajectory
classes.sig: (kind: str = 'hover', *, altitude: float = 5.0, radius: float = 4.0, period_s: float = 20.0, climb_rate: float = 0.5, yaw_rate: float = 0.0)
classes.doc: Where the vehicle is asked to be: hover, a circle, a climb, or a step -- enough to exercise the dynamics.

methods.name: at
methods.doc: ``(position, velocity, yaw)`` at time ``t``.

classes.name: Controller
classes.sig: (model: Multirotor, *, kp_pos: float = 2.0, kd_pos: float = 3.2, kp_att: float = 6.0, kp_rate: float = 0.12, ki_rate: float = 0.25, max_tilt_rad: float = 0.55, max_thrust_factor: float = 2.2)
classes.doc: The cascade. Gains are per loop and have units, so they can be read: ``kp_pos`` is 1/s, ``kp_att`` is 1/s.

methods.name: command
methods.sig: (state: State, target_position: np.ndarray, target_velocity: np.ndarray, yaw: float, dt: float) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: The four motor speeds (normalised to ``omega_max``) that chase the target.

functions.name: quaternion_error
functions.sig: (target: np.ndarray, current: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``conj(current) * target``: the attitude error as a rotation vector **in the body frame**.

The order matters and was measured: ``target * conj(current)`` gives the same error in the *world* frame, and using
it as a body-rate command couples a yaw error into roll and pitch -- the vehicle tumbles as soon as the heading
moves, which is exactly what the circle trajectory does.

children.summary: A cascaded controller, so the vehicle actually flies while its faults are being diagnosed.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multirotor.detect
children.doc:
The detectors, compared on equal terms, and the diagnosis that names the fault.

Three detectors on the same residual stream, because the issue's question is not "can a residual find a fault" but
"what does the residual buy over the two things people already do":

* :class:`ThresholdDetector` -- a fixed threshold on each residual channel. The baseline everybody starts with.
* :class:`KalmanDetector` -- a per-channel Kalman filter on a random-walk bias, alarming when the *innovation* leaves
  its own covariance. This is the classic innovation-based fault detector, and it is a fair one: it knows the noise.
* :class:`CusumDetector` -- a one-sided CUSUM on the same residuals, the standard change detector when the fault is a
  small persistent shift rather than a spike.

All three are tuned the same way and measured the same way: **the most sensitive setting that produces no false alarm
on the calibration flights**, then the detection delay is measured on flights it never saw. Anything else is a
comparison between three different false-alarm rates.

The diagnosis is not a classifier fitted to labels: it reads *which* channel moved. A payload pushes along body ``-z``;
a motor pushes along that motor's arm and spends power; a gust is horizontal in the world frame; a GPS glitch moves the
fix and nothing else.

classes.name: Calibration
classes.doc:
What the fault-free flights say each channel does.

``mean`` and ``std`` standardise a sample; ``allowance`` is the per-channel *reference value* a CUSUM needs, and it
is measured rather than assumed: a fixed allowance of one sigma lets the vibration channel -- which is rectified, so
half its samples sit at zero and the rest arrive in bursts -- fill an accumulator to fifty sigmas on a healthy
flight. Set at each channel's own 95th percentile, a healthy flight cannot fill it and a fault still crosses it in
a few samples.

classes.name: Detection
classes.doc: When a detector fired, on which channels, and how strong the evidence was at that moment.

classes.name: Detector
classes.sig: (*, sensitivity: float = 5.0, consecutive: int = 5)
classes.doc: Common ground: a calibration, a sensitivity, and a run over a flight that returns the first alarm.

classes.name: ThresholdDetector
classes.doc: A fixed threshold on each channel: ``|r - mean| > sensitivity * std`` for ``consecutive`` samples.

classes.name: KalmanDetector
classes.sig: (*, sensitivity: float = 5.0, consecutive: int = 5, bias_drift: float = 0.02)
classes.doc:
A per-channel Kalman filter whose innovation is the statistic.

The state is the residual's slowly varying bias (a random walk with variance ``q`` per sample, in units of the
calibrated sigma); the measurement is the residual sample, with variance 1 in those units. A fault is a change in
the bias, so the *normalised innovation* ``nu / sqrt(S)`` is a standard-score stream: a persistent run above
``sensitivity`` is an alarm. Noise that the filter already predicts does not fire it -- which is what it buys over
the fixed threshold.

classes.name: CusumDetector
classes.sig: (*, sensitivity: float = 5.0, consecutive: int = 5, drift: float | None = None)
classes.doc:
A two-sided CUSUM on the standardised residual, for the small persistent shift a chip or a payload makes.

Each channel carries its own *allowance* -- the reference value subtracted before accumulation -- measured as the
95th percentile of the standardised calibration data. That is not a refinement: with the textbook one-sigma
allowance the vibration channel alone fills its accumulator to 50 sigma on a healthy flight, because it is
rectified and arrives in bursts.

functions.name: calibrate
functions.sig: (flights, *, after_s: float = 2.0) -> Calibration
functions.doc: Mean and spread of every channel over the settled part of fault-free flights.

functions.name: tune
functions.sig: (detector_class, calibration: Calibration, fault_free, *, sensitivities = (2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 5.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0), **kwargs)
functions.doc:
The most sensitive setting of ``detector_class`` that raises no alarm on the calibration flights.

This is what makes the comparison fair: each detector is pushed to its own edge of usability and then measured on
flights it has never seen, instead of being given three different false-alarm budgets and one headline delay.

The grid runs to 40 on purpose. A CUSUM accumulates, so on a residual that is autocorrelated -- this one rings at a
few hertz -- its running sum crosses a 10-sigma bar during a *healthy* flight; the setting it actually needs to stay
quiet is far above the threshold detector's, and letting the grid stop at 10 would have reported a detector that
only looks worse because it was not allowed to be tuned.

functions.name: diagnose
functions.sig: (flight: Flight, detection: Detection, calibration: Calibration, *, window_s: float = 1.5) -> dict
functions.doc:
Name the fault from *which* channel moved, with the evidence in sigmas.

Two questions, in this order. **Is it the sensor or the vehicle?** A measurement check that is the dominant evidence
is a sensor fault -- and it has to be dominant, not merely large: the vibration channel's spread is 0.004 m/s^2, so
a payload's step in the accelerometer also moves it a little, and a rule that only asked "did vibration exceed
three sigma" answered "IMU vibration" for a payload. **If it is the vehicle, which part?** A vertical force with a
quiet torque is mass; a torque is a rotor, and its direction names the motor; a planar force is the air moving.

children.summary: The detectors, compared on equal terms, and the diagnosis that names the fault.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multirotor.faults
children.doc:
The faults a multirotor actually suffers, injected where they physically act, and the checks each one moves.

A payload is mass; a degraded motor is less thrust for the same command; a chipped blade is less thrust at *better*
efficiency, because the tip it lost was the part the induced losses punished most; a gust is wind; a GPS glitch is a
lie in the position fix; a
magnetometer interference is a heading that is wrong while everything else is right; vibration is noise the
accelerometer should not have.

Keeping them there -- and not as a label on a dataset -- is what makes the residual of :mod:`.residuals` able to tell
them apart: each one moves a different subset of the physics, so the signature is the diagnosis.

classes.name: Fault
classes.doc: One injected fault: what kind, when it starts (and stops, if it does), how big, and on which motor.

classes.name: FaultState
classes.doc: What the faults have done to the vehicle at one instant.

functions.name: chip_factors
functions.sig: (rotor: Rotor, omega: float, tip_loss: float = 0.1) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc:
``(thrust, torque)`` of a blade with its tip gone, over the intact one, both measured from BEMT at ``omega``.

A chip removes the outer stations, which are the ones moving fastest: thrust falls and the *torque per newton*
rises, because what is left of the blade has to work at a less favourable inflow. The numbers are measured here
rather than assumed -- the ratio depends on where the chip is and how fast the rotor turns.

functions.name: faulty_airframe
functions.sig: (base, *, mass_kg: float, battery_resistance_ohm: float)
functions.doc: The airframe with a fault's mass and battery change applied; the rotor table is shared, not rebuilt.

functions.name: apply_faults
functions.sig: (faults, t: float, *, base_airframe, base_resistance_ohm: float, rotor, omega_hover: float, frame: str = 'world') -> FaultState
functions.doc: The vehicle's state under ``faults`` at time ``t``: mass, motor gains, wind, battery, and what the sensors lie.

children.summary: The faults a multirotor actually suffers, injected where they physically act, and the checks each one moves.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multirotor.model
children.doc:
The 6-DoF airframe: four BEMT rotors, a battery that sags, drag, wind and ground effect.

The state is the one a flight controller estimates -- position, velocity, attitude, body rates -- plus what the vehicle
knows about itself: the four rotor speeds and how much charge is left. Every fault in :mod:`.faults` enters here and
nowhere else, which is what lets the residual of :mod:`.residuals` name it.

Frame conventions: body ``x`` forward, ``y`` right, ``z`` down; thrust along body ``-z``; attitude is a unit quaternion
``(w, x, y, z)`` rotating body to world; ``position[2] = -altitude``.

The rotor model is BEMT (:class:`~pinneapple_physics.multirotor.rotor.Rotor`), which costs milliseconds per call and
cannot live inside a 500 Hz loop, so :class:`RotorTable` tabulates it once and interpolates -- the same physics,
sampled: BEMT thrust follows ``T ~ omega^2`` to within 2 %, so the sampling is not an approximation of the answer.

classes.name: RotorTable
classes.sig: (rotor: Rotor, *, omega_max: float = 1300.0, climb = (-8.0, 8.0), n_omega: int = 27, n_climb: int = 9)
classes.doc: The BEMT rotor, tabulated on ``(omega, climb)`` and interpolated: the same numbers, cheap enough for 500 Hz.

methods.name: thrust_many
methods.doc: The same interpolation for an array of rotor speeds, in one numpy pass (the flight loop calls it 4x a step).

methods.name: total_power
methods.doc: Aerodynamic power of every rotor, summed.

methods.name: omega_for_thrust
methods.doc: The rotor speed that produces ``thrust_n`` on this table, by bisection (the mixer's inverse).

methods.name: dq_dt
methods.doc: ``dQ/dT`` at ``omega``: how much yaw torque a newton of differential thrust buys.

classes.name: Battery
classes.doc: A pack that sags: ``V = V_oc(SoC) - I R``, with the open-circuit voltage falling as the charge goes.

methods.name: voltage
methods.doc: The terminal voltage under load -- the sag a detector reads as "the pack is unhappy".

methods.name: current
methods.doc: The current that draws ``power_w`` at the terminal voltage of this state of charge.

classes.name: State
classes.doc: The state a flight controller estimates, plus the rotor speeds and the charge.

methods.name: rotation
methods.doc: Body-to-world rotation matrix from the quaternion.

methods.name: euler
methods.doc: ``(roll, pitch, yaw)`` in radians, for reporting only -- the dynamics never needs it.

classes.name: Telemetry
classes.doc: What the battery and the ESCs report at one instant.

classes.name: Airframe
classes.doc: The vehicle: mass, inertia, arm geometry, rotors, drag and the motor lag.

methods.name: hover_omega
methods.doc: The rotor speed that holds this vehicle up, straight from the BEMT rotor.

classes.name: Multirotor
classes.sig: (airframe: Airframe | None = None, *, table: RotorTable | None = None, motor_efficiency: np.ndarray | None = None, thrust_gain: np.ndarray | None = None, torque_gain: np.ndarray | None = None)
classes.doc:
The airframe, integrated: thrust from each rotor, the moments it makes, the drag it fights and the charge it
spends. :meth:`step` is one RK4 step of the whole thing, motors included.

methods.name: thrust_and_torque
methods.doc: Thrust per rotor (body ``-z``) and its aerodynamic torque, ground effect included.

methods.name: derivatives
methods.doc: ``(d_position, d_velocity, d_attitude, d_rates, d_rotors)`` -- the right-hand side RK4 integrates.

methods.name: step
methods.sig: (state: State, command: np.ndarray, dt: float, *, wind = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), disturbance = None) -> tuple[State, Telemetry]
methods.doc: One RK4 step forward, then the charge it spent. ``disturbance`` is an external body force in newtons.

methods.name: measure
methods.doc: The power, current and voltage of a state, without stepping it.

methods.name: allocate
methods.doc: ``(collective thrust, body torque)`` to four motor commands in ``[0, 1]`` -- the mixer.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multirotor.residuals
children.doc:
What the vehicle's sensors report, and what the physics says they should have reported.

The residual is the second half: with the *commanded* rotor speeds (an ESC reports them), the nominal airframe and the
measured specific force, Newton-Euler predicts what the accelerometer and the power draw should be. A fault is then a
disagreement between two numbers that should be equal -- not a machine-learning label.

The channels, and why each one is there:

* ``force_x/y/z`` -- the body specific force the nominal model predicts from the commanded rotors, minus what the
  accelerometer measured. In a hover this is ``g (m_true / m_nominal - 1)`` along body ``-z``: a payload makes the
  rotors work harder than the nominal mass explains. A degraded motor or a chipped blade points along *that motor's*
  arm instead, and a gust is horizontal in the world frame -- three different directions, which is the diagnosis.
* ``torque_x/y/z`` -- the body torque the commanded rotors imply, over the inertia, minus the angular acceleration the
  gyro measured. A payload does not make a torque; a motor does.
* ``power`` -- the electrical power the nominal rotor and pack predict, minus what the ESC and the pack report. A
  sagging pack and a chipped blade live here while leaving the force channel alone.
* ``gps``, ``heading``, ``vibration`` -- the three *measurement* checks: the fix against dead reckoning, the
  magnetometer against the integrated gyro, and the accelerometer's high-frequency content against the declared noise.
  A fault in these must not be diagnosed as a change of the vehicle, which is exactly what they are separated for.

Everything is computed from quantities a real flight controller has: the commands it sent, the IMU, the GPS, the pack
telemetry. It never sees the fault, and it never sees the true state.

classes.name: SensorModel
classes.doc: The noise of each sensor, declared. Nothing here is fitted: these are the numbers a datasheet would give.

classes.name: Sensors
classes.doc: One sample of everything the flight controller has.

classes.name: SensorObservatory
classes.sig: (sensors: SensorModel | None = None, seed: int = 0)
classes.doc:
Turns the truth into what the sensors report, including what the fault makes them lie about.

A physics fault never touches the sensors: a payload changes the truth, not the noise. The sensor faults
(:mod:`.faults`) are the ones that land here -- the fix jumps, the heading is wrong, the accelerometer vibrates.

methods.name: measure
methods.sig: (state: State, model: Multirotor, command: np.ndarray, telemetry, faults) -> Sensors

classes.name: Residual
classes.doc: The named disagreements at one instant.

classes.name: ResidualModel
classes.sig: (airframe: Airframe | None = None, *, window: int = 25, noise_floor: float = 0.06)
classes.doc: Newton-Euler on the nominal vehicle, evaluated against the sensors, every step.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multirotor.rotor
children.doc:
The rotor of a multirotor, from blade element momentum theory: thrust, torque and the power they cost.

A drone's dynamics change in flight because its rotors do -- a chipped blade, a degraded motor, a battery that sags.
Fitting a thrust curve hides that; solving the blades shows it, because every one of those faults walks into the same
three numbers a flight controller cannot measure directly.

The model is steady BEMT in axial flow, per annulus, with Prandtl tip loss and the inflow solved by bisection:

    phi = atan((Vc + v_i) / (Omega r))        alpha = theta(r) - phi
    dT/dr = 1/2 rho W^2 B c (Cl cos phi - Cd sin phi)      blade element
    dT/dr = 4 pi rho r F v_i (Vc + v_i)                    momentum
    dQ/dr = 1/2 rho W^2 B c r (Cl sin phi + Cd cos phi)

with ``Cl = cl_alpha alpha`` (clamped at ``cl_max``) and ``Cd = cd0 + k Cl^2``, and the geometric pitch giving
``theta(r) = atan(pitch / 2 pi r)``.

What it is checked against, in :mod:`tests.test_multirotor`:

* the figure of merit ``P_ideal / P`` -- the ideal being momentum theory's ``T^{3/2} / sqrt(2 rho A)`` -- lands in the
  published ``0.5-0.8`` band for a propeller of this size, which is what says the blade element and the momentum side
  agree instead of one of them being decoration;
* ``T ~ Omega^2`` to within 2 % over 2 000-8 000 rpm, the propeller law every bench measurement obeys;
* a chipped tip makes less thrust **at better efficiency** -- the tip is the part Prandtl's loss penalises most, so as
  the span goes the figure of merit rises, 0.650 to 0.787 between an intact blade and one missing 40 % of it. That is
  the *opposite* of what "a damaged prop works harder" suggests, which is why the ratio is measured here and not
  assumed.

classes.name: RotorState
classes.doc: What a rotor is producing at one instant.

classes.name: Rotor
classes.doc:
One propeller: its geometry, its airfoil, and the BEMT that turns a rotation rate into thrust and torque.

``chord_m`` is the blade chord at 75 % radius and ``taper`` the ratio of the tip chord to it, so a linear taper is
the blade: what a chipped tip removes is exactly the outer stations, which is the point.

methods.name: chord_at
methods.doc: The chord at radius ``r``: linear from the hub to the tip, ``taper`` times ``chord_m`` at the tip.

methods.name: inflow
methods.sig: (omega: float, r: float, climb: float = 0.0) -> float
methods.doc: The induced velocity at ``r``: where the blade element and the momentum annulus agree, by bisection.

methods.name: state
methods.doc: Thrust, torque, power and the figure of merit at ``omega``. Negative speed is refused, not mirrored.

methods.name: electrical_power
methods.doc: What the battery pays for that rotation, after the drivetrain's declared efficiency.

methods.name: omega_for_thrust
methods.doc: The rotation rate that produces ``thrust_n`` -- what a flight controller's mixer solves for, slowly.

functions.name: figure_of_merit
functions.sig: (thrust_n: float, power_w: float, radius_m: float, rho: float = 1.225) -> float
functions.doc: ``P_ideal / P`` for the thrust produced: 1.0 is an actuator disk with no losses, a real propeller is 0.5-0.8.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multirotor.sim
children.doc:
The flight loop: the truth with its faults, the sensors reading it, and the residual comparing the two.

One call is one flight. The controller flies the *nominal* model -- it is never told about the fault -- while the
dynamics of the flight carry the fault, so the vehicle drifts, the controller works harder, and the residual records by
how much. That is the whole experiment, and :func:`campaign` repeats it across faults, seeds and detectors.

classes.name: Flight
classes.doc: One flight's record: the residual per step, the truth, and what was flying at each instant.

methods.name: onset
methods.doc: When the first fault started, or ``None`` for a fault-free flight.

functions.sig: (faults = (), *, duration: float = DURATION_S, seed: int = 0, dt: float = DT, airframe: Airframe | None = None, trajectory: Trajectory | None = None, sensors: SensorModel | None = None) -> Flight
functions.doc: Fly once, with ``faults`` injected, and record what the residual saw.

functions.doc: Fly every named case over every seed: ``{case: [Flight, ...]}``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale
pinneapple_physics.multiscale.closures
children.doc:
Subfilter closures for 2-D large-eddy simulation in vorticity form, and the tests that tell whether a closure can
be trusted.

Filtering the momentum equations leaves the subfilter stress ``tau_ij = bar(u_i u_j) - bar(u_i) bar(u_j)``; in
vorticity form the filtered equation gets the tendency ``-curl(div tau) = -div(sigma)`` with the subfilter vorticity
flux ``sigma_j = bar(u_j omega) - bar(u_j) bar(omega)`` (the two are equal because the filter commutes with
derivatives). A closure models ``tau`` from the resolved field. In 2-D a deviatoric symmetric tensor has two
components, ``a = tau_xx = -tau_yy`` and ``b = tau_xy``, and the tendency is ``-(b_xx - b_yy - 2 a_xy)``.

Closures (each a callable ``closure(omega, solver) -> tendency`` for :class:`~.ns2d.VorticityNS2D`, with
``stress(omega, solver) -> (a, b)``):

* :class:`Smagorinsky` (Smagorinsky 1963; Lilly 1967): ``tau = -2 (Cs Delta)^2 |S| S``, ``|S| = sqrt(2 S_ij S_ij)``;
* :class:`DynamicSmagorinsky` (Germano, Piomelli, Moin & Cabot 1991; least squares of Lilly 1992): the coefficient
  from the Germano identity ``L_ij = C M_ij`` between the grid filter and a test filter of width ``alpha Delta``,
  averaged over the (homogeneous) domain and clipped at 0;
* :class:`GradientModel` (Clark, Ferziger & Reynolds 1979): ``tau = Delta^2 / 12 d_k u_i d_k u_j``, the leading term
  of the Taylor expansion for Gaussian or box filters. It correlates well with the true stress a priori and is
  known to be unstable a posteriori without extra dissipation;
* :class:`NoModel`, and learned closures through :mod:`.learned`.

Tests:

* :func:`apriori_test` (from a filtered fine field, no simulation): correlation of the modelled and true stress
  components and tendencies, mean subfilter energy transfer ``Pi = -tau_ij S_ij`` and the backscatter fraction
  (``Pi < 0``), which an eddy-viscosity model cannot represent;
* :func:`aposteriori_test` (run the LES and compare with the filtered reference): energy-spectrum error,
  resolved-energy dissipation rate, long-run stability;
* :func:`closure_health`: label-free checks on an LES prediction (no reference): resolved enstrophy must not grow in
  unforced 2-D flow, the spectrum near the cut-off must not pile up or collapse against the power law of the
  resolved range, the field must stay finite. Used by the ensemble as a prediction check.

classes.name: Smagorinsky
classes.doc: ``nu_t = (cs delta)^2 |S|``. ``delta`` defaults to the solver's implicit filter width.

classes.name: DynamicSmagorinsky
classes.doc:
Dynamic Smagorinsky: ``nu_t = C delta^2 |S|`` with ``C = <L_ij M_ij> / <M_ij M_ij>`` (domain average, clipped
at 0) from the test filter of width ``test_ratio * delta`` and kind ``test_kind``. The last coefficient is kept
in ``self.last_c``.

methods.name: coefficient
methods.sig: (w: np.ndarray, solver: VorticityNS2D, st: dict | None = None) -> np.ndarray

classes.name: GradientModel
classes.doc: Clark gradient (nonlinear) model ``tau_ij = coef * delta^2 / 12 * d_k u_i d_k u_j`` (deviatoric part).

classes.name: NoModel
classes.doc: No subfilter model (an under-resolved DNS).

functions.name: strain
functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, solver: VorticityNS2D) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Velocity gradients, strain ``S11 = u_x``, ``S12 = (u_y + v_x) / 2`` and ``|S| = sqrt(2 S_ij S_ij)``.

functions.name: stress_tendency
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, solver: VorticityNS2D) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Vorticity tendency ``-curl(div tau)`` of a deviatoric stress ``(tau_xx, tau_xy) = (a, b)``.

functions.name: true_subfilter
functions.sig: (w_fine: np.ndarray, filt: Filter, n_coarse: int | None = None, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Exact subfilter quantities of a resolved vorticity field for the filter ``filt``: the filtered field
``w_bar``, the deviatoric stress ``(a, b)``, the vorticity flux ``sigma`` and the tendency ``-div(sigma)``,
restricted to ``n_coarse`` points per axis (exact when the filter removes the modes the coarse grid lacks).

functions.name: apriori_test
functions.sig: (w_fine: np.ndarray, filt: Filter, closure: Any, n_coarse: int, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> AprioriReport
functions.doc:
A-priori test of ``closure`` on a resolved field: filter it with ``filt``, restrict to the LES grid of
``n_coarse`` points, and compare the closure's stress and tendency (computed from the filtered field) with the
exact subfilter terms.

functions.name: spectrum_error
functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, w_ref: np.ndarray, kmax: float, length: float = 2 * np.pi, kmin: int = 1) -> float
functions.doc:
Mean absolute difference of ``log10 E(k)`` over the shells ``kmin <= k <= kmax`` (0: same spectrum; 0.3: a
factor of 2 on average).

functions.name: aposteriori_test
functions.sig: (les: VorticityNS2D, w0_bar: np.ndarray, ref_bar: np.ndarray, times: Sequence[float], dt: float = 0.005, t_long: float | None = None) -> AposterioriReport
functions.doc:
Run the LES ``les`` (its closure included) from the filtered initial field ``w0_bar`` (on its grid) and compare
with the filtered reference ``ref_bar`` (``(len(times), n, n)``, same grid) at ``times``; then keep running to
``t_long`` (default 4 x the last time) for the long-run stability.

functions.name: closure_health
functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, w0: np.ndarray, kc: float, length: float = 2 * np.pi, *, forced: bool = False, max_enstrophy_growth: float = 1.05, tail_band: tuple[float, float] = (0.05, 5.0), closure: Any = None, solver: VorticityNS2D | None = None, germano_limit: float = 1.05) -> ClosureHealth
functions.doc:
Label-free health of an LES (or any filtered) prediction ``w`` at cut-off ``kc`` (shells), started from
``w0`` (same filter):

* finite values;
* resolved enstrophy ``Z(t) / Z(0) <= max_enstrophy_growth`` in unforced flow (2-D advection conserves
  enstrophy, viscosity and the forward enstrophy cascade only remove it: growth is a closure that injects
  enstrophy, e.g. an unstable gradient model);
* spectral tail: the energy in ``kc / 2 < k <= kc`` divided by the power law fitted on ``kc / 8 .. kc / 2`` and
  extrapolated, inside ``tail_band`` (above: pile-up at the cut-off, a closure too weak; below: a closure too
  dissipative).

* with ``closure`` and ``solver`` (the LES grid): the Germano-identity error :func:`germano_error` at most
  ``germano_limit`` (a closure that explains the resolved transfer between the grid and test filters worse than
  no model at all is inconsistent across scales).

``score`` is the product of soft scores (1 inside the limits, ``exp(-(log excess)^2)`` outside). Arrays may
carry leading axes (snapshots); every snapshot is checked and the worst counts.

functions.name: germano_error
functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, closure: Any, solver: VorticityNS2D, test_ratio: float = 2.0, test_kind: str = 'sharp', delta: float | None = None) -> float
functions.doc:
Label-free cross-scale check of a closure through the Germano identity: the resolved stress between the grid
filter and a test filter of width ``test_ratio * delta``, ``L_ij = hat(u_i u_j) - hat(u_i) hat(u_j)``, is known
exactly from the LES field; a consistent closure must reproduce it as ``tau(test width, hat field) -
hat(tau(delta, field))``. Compared through the vorticity tendency each stress produces (``-curl div``, the
term the resolved equation sees; in 2-D the stress components themselves are nearly orthogonal to any
eddy-viscosity stress, see :func:`apriori_test`). Returns ``||t(L) - t(L_model)|| / ||t(L)||``: 1 for no model,
below 1 when the closure explains part of the resolved transfer, above 1 when it makes things worse (e.g. a
fixed coefficient far too large for the flow). ``closure`` must accept a ``delta`` attribute (the classical
closures here do); it is restored afterwards.

classes.name: EnsembleConfig
classes.doc:
``aware``: scale-aware post-filtering (else blind); ``router``: :class:`~.scales.ScaleAwareRouter` with the
fidelity ladder; ``checks``: prediction checks and the closed multiscale residual (else the grid-scale residual);
``experts``: the experts it may use; ``error_tolerance``: escalate up the fidelity ladder when the awake

functions.name: evaluate_experts
functions.sig: (path: str | Path, queries: Sequence[dict], initial_states: np.ndarray, experts: Mapping[str, Callable[[np.ndarray, dict], Any]], checks: Mapping[str, Callable[[Any, np.ndarray, dict], tuple[float, str]]] | None = None, n_out: int | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]

Run every expert on every query once. ``experts[name](w0, query)`` returns the output on the common grid, or a
pair ``(output, internals)`` whose internals are handed to ``checks[name](internals, w0, query) -> (score,
reason)``. A failure (exception, non-finite values) is stored as NaN. Returns (and caches in ``path``) ``raw``
(queries, experts, ...), ``secs``, ``check`` (NaN where no check), ``reasons``, ``names``.

The answer to a query for ``target`` from an output that carries ``source``: blind (``target`` applied on top)
or scale-aware (:func:`~.filters.refilter`).

functions.name: raw_residual
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, nu: float, dt: float, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> float

functions.name: closed_multiscale_residual
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, nu: float, dt: float, filt: Filter, h: float, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> float

Residual of the filtered vorticity equation at the requested width and at twice it, with the subfilter
tendency estimated by the gradient model at each width removed; mean of the two relative residuals.

functions.name: run_ensembles
functions.sig: (queries: Sequence[dict], references: Sequence[np.ndarray], table: Mapping[str, np.ndarray], profiles: Mapping[str, Any], configs: Mapping[str, EnsembleConfig], *, dt: float, h: float, length: float = 2 * np.pi, cost_weight: float = 0.1, lookahead: float = 3.0, check_names: Sequence[str] | None = None, kmax_out: float | None = None) -> dict[str, dict]

Every configuration on the same stream, replaying the outputs of :func:`evaluate_experts`. Queries carry
``id``, ``nu``, ``re`` and ``filter``. Costs are the median measured wall times. ``check_names``: experts whose
stored checks are used as prediction checks (default: all that have one).

functions.name: summarise_runs
functions.sig: (runs: Mapping[Any, tuple[Sequence[dict], Mapping[str, dict]]], profiles: Mapping[str, Any], configs: Sequence[str], widths: Sequence[int], *, wrong_factor: float = 1.5, wrong_margin: float = 0.03, solver: str | None = None, oracle_config: str | None = None, target: float | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:

per requested width (with n), spectrum error, wrong selections (error above ``max(wrong_factor * best,
best + wrong_margin)``, best = best expert available to the configuration on that query), scale violations
(chosen model coarser than the request), cost of the chosen model and of the experts the policy ran, share of
queries sent to ``solver``; with ``target``, the queries whose error is above that accuracy target (the fair count
for policies that pick a cheaper model on purpose). Then two baselines: always ``solver`` and the oracle (best expert in hindsight, of
the experts of ``oracle_config``).

One line per configuration through its operating points ``(cost, error, label)`` (e.g. a sweep of the cost
weight or of the error tolerance); ``baselines`` as grey squares. Lower-left is better.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale.consistency
children.doc:
Cross-scale consistency: a fine and a coarse prediction of the same state must agree once both are brought to
the same scale.

The fine prediction is filtered to the coarse prediction's filter (with :func:`~.filters.refilter`, exact when the
fine filter is narrower and of a composable kind) and restricted to the coarse grid; then the two are compared on

* the field (relative L2),
* the energy spectrum over the shared wavenumbers (mean ``|log10 E_fine / E_coarse|``),
* integral quantities (mean, energy, enstrophy, or any ``{name: fn(field)}``), each with its own relative
  tolerance; the report names the integral that broke.

Tolerances can be scaled by the known discretisation error (``gci``: e.g. the grid-convergence index of the coarse
model, #437): a pair is only declared inconsistent beyond ``max(tol, safety * gci)``. Works for solver/solver,
surrogate/surrogate and surrogate/solver pairs.

methods.name: score
methods.doc: 1 when consistent, decaying with the worst excess over the tolerances (for ensemble checks).

functions.name: cross_scale_consistency
functions.sig: (fine: np.ndarray, coarse: np.ndarray, coarse_filter: Filter, fine_filter: Filter | None = None, *, length: float = 2 * np.pi, tol: float = 0.05, integrals: Mapping[str, Callable[[np.ndarray], float]] | None = None, integral_tol: float | Mapping[str, float] = 0.02, gci: float | None = None, safety: float = 1.25, spectrum: bool = True) -> ConsistencyReport
functions.doc:
Compare ``fine`` (filtered by ``fine_filter``, default unfiltered, on its grid) with ``coarse`` (filtered by ``coarse_filter``, on
a grid of equal or fewer points) after bringing the fine one to the coarse scale and grid. Arrays are ``(n, n)``
or with leading axes (e.g. snapshots). ``integrals`` default to :data:`VORTICITY_INTEGRALS` for 2-D fields.

children.summary: Cross-scale consistency: a fine and a coarse prediction of the same state must agree once both are brought to the same scale.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale.filters
children.doc:
Spatial filters for large-eddy simulation and multiscale checks on periodic grids.

A filter of width ``Delta`` turns a field ``u`` into ``u_bar = G_Delta * u`` (convolution). On a periodic domain it acts
on each Fourier mode by its transfer function ``G_hat(k)``, which is how it is applied here, so the transfer function
of the applied filter is exact (to round-off) and every filter commutes with derivatives as long as ``Delta`` is the
same everywhere. The three classical filters (Pope, *Turbulent Flows*, 2000, section 13.2, table 13.2):

=========  ===================================  =========================================================
kind       transfer function ``G_hat(k)``        notes
=========  ===================================  =========================================================
box        ``sin(k Delta / 2) / (k Delta / 2)``  top-hat average over ``Delta``; changes sign (zeros at
                                                  ``k = 2 pi n / Delta``)
gaussian   ``exp(-k^2 Delta^2 / 24)``            same second moment as the box filter; positive, smooth;
                                                  two Gaussians compose into one: ``Delta^2 = D1^2 + D2^2``
sharp      ``1`` if ``|k| <= pi / Delta`` else 0  spectral cut-off at ``k_c = pi / Delta``; idempotent
=========  ===================================  =========================================================

In several dimensions the filter is the tensor product of the 1-D filter in each direction (for the sharp filter this
is a square cut-off ``max(|k_x|, |k_y|) <= k_c``).

Also here: Fourier restriction / prolongation between grids (restriction keeps the mean exactly, so integrals are
preserved to round-off), the post-filter that turns a field already filtered at one width into one filtered at a
larger width (and how much of the requested filter cannot be reached from it), and filtering with a width that varies
in space, whose commutation error with derivatives is not zero (Ghosal & Moin 1995, J. Comput. Phys. 118:24).

classes.name: Filter
classes.doc:
A filter of width ``delta`` (physical length) and ``kind`` in :data:`FILTER_KINDS`. ``delta = 0`` is the
identity (a fully resolved field).

methods.name: cutoff
methods.doc: Wavenumber that separates resolved and subfilter scales, ``pi / delta`` (inf for the identity).

methods.name: transfer_nd
methods.doc: Tensor-product transfer on a grid of wavenumbers (``ks``: one array per axis, broadcastable).

functions.name: transfer
functions.sig: (kind: str, k: np.ndarray, delta: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: 1-D transfer function ``G_hat(k)`` of a filter of width ``delta`` (``delta = 0``: identity).

functions.name: wavenumbers
functions.sig: (n: int, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Angular wavenumbers of an ``n``-point periodic grid, in FFT order.

functions.name: apply_filter
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, filt: Filter, length: float = 2 * np.pi, axes: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Filter a periodic field over ``axes`` (default: the last two, or the last one for 1-D data).

functions.name: restrict
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, n: int | Sequence[int], axes: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Fourier restriction to a coarser periodic grid of ``n`` points per axis: keeps the modes ``|k| < n / 2`` (the
Nyquist mode of the coarse grid is dropped, so the result is real). The mean, hence the integral over the
domain, is preserved to round-off.

functions.name: prolong
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, n: int | Sequence[int], axes: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Fourier interpolation (zero padding) to a finer periodic grid of ``n`` points per axis.

functions.name: post_filter_transfer
functions.sig: (source: Filter, target: Filter, k: np.ndarray, max_gain: float = 2.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
1-D transfer of the post-filter that brings a field filtered by ``source`` to ``target``:
``G_target / G_source`` where that ratio is at most ``max_gain`` in magnitude, 0 elsewhere. A mild deconvolution
(gain up to 2 by default, e.g. a sharp cut-off at k = 4 from a slightly damped Gaussian output) is allowed;
beyond that the scales the source filter removed or damped are treated as lost: recovering them would only
amplify the source's errors.

functions.name: realizability_mismatch
functions.sig: (source: Filter, target: Filter, kmax: float, *, slope: float = -2.0, n: int = 4096, max_gain: float = 2.0, kmin: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Fraction (0 to 1, as an L2 ratio) of the ``target`` filter that cannot be obtained by post-filtering a field
already filtered by ``source``. The transfer functions are compared on ``kmin <= k <= kmax`` (``kmin``: the
fundamental wavenumber, 1 on a ``2 pi`` domain) weighted by a model
spectrum of the field, ``|k| ** slope`` per mode (default -2: a vorticity field with an energy spectrum
``k^-3`` per shell in 2-D). 0 when the target is reachable exactly (e.g. a wider Gaussian from a Gaussian, any
filter from an unfiltered field); 1 when nothing is (a finer target than the source cut-off).

functions.name: refilter
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, source: Filter, target: Filter, length: float = 2 * np.pi, axes: Sequence[int] | None = None, max_gain: float = 2.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Turn a field filtered by ``source`` into the ``target`` filter (as far as it can be, see
:func:`post_filter_transfer`).

functions.name: filter_variable_width
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, kind: str, delta: np.ndarray, length: float = 2 * np.pi, axes: Sequence[int] | None = None, decimals: int = 10) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Filter whose width varies in space: ``u_bar(x) = sum_k G_hat(k; delta(x)) u_hat(k) exp(i k x)``.

``delta`` has the shape of ``u``. Evaluated exactly by filtering the whole field once per distinct width and
taking each point from the field of its own width. With a uniform ``delta`` this is :func:`apply_filter`.

functions.name: spectral_derivative
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, axis: int, length: float = 2 * np.pi, order: int = 1) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Exact derivative of the trigonometric interpolant along ``axis`` (the Nyquist mode is dropped for odd
orders).

functions.name: commutation_error
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, kind: str, delta: float | np.ndarray, axis: int = -1, length: float = 2 * np.pi, axes: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``d(u_bar)/dx - (du/dx)_bar`` for a filter of width ``delta`` (scalar or a field). Zero to round-off for a
uniform width; for a width that varies in space it is the term that a residual of the filtered equations picks
up from filtering alone, not from the model (to leading order ``(d Delta / dx) d u_bar / d Delta``).

functions.name: low_modes
functions.sig: (kmax: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]
functions.doc:
Half-plane list of the 2-D integer wavenumbers with ``|kx|, |ky| <= kmax`` (sharp square cut-off), mean
excluded: one of each pair ``k, -k``.

functions.name: fourier_basis
functions.sig: (modes: Sequence[tuple[int, int]], n: int, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``(2 len(modes), n * n)`` real basis ``cos, sin(kx x + ky y)`` on an ``n x n`` grid (``k`` in units of
``2 pi / length``).

functions.name: fourier_coefficients
functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, modes: Sequence[tuple[int, int]], length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Coefficients of a periodic field on :func:`fourier_basis` (exact for modes below the grid's Nyquist).

children.summary: Spatial filters for large-eddy simulation and multiscale checks on periodic grids.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale.learned
children.doc:
Learned models that connect scales (PyTorch).

* :class:`ScaleConditionedFNO2d`: a 2-D Fourier neural operator that takes the filter width ``Delta`` as an input
  (FiLM: every Fourier layer is scaled and shifted by an embedding of ``log(Delta / delta_ref)``, Perez et al. 2018),
  trained on one fine dataset filtered at several widths. :func:`filtering_consistency_loss` ties its predictions at
  different widths together: the prediction at ``Delta_1``, filtered to ``Delta_2 > Delta_1``, must equal the
  prediction at ``Delta_2``. With ``conditioned=False`` it is the scale-blind version (same network, ``Delta``
  ignored), for comparison.
* :class:`TorchVorticityLES2D`: the 2-D vorticity LES of :class:`~.ns2d.VorticityNS2D`, differentiable (integrating
  factor RK4, dealiased), so a closure can be trained *a posteriori*, through the solver: the loss compares the
  LES trajectory with the filtered reference, and its gradient flows through every time step (as in the
  differentiable-physics training of subgrid models, e.g. Um et al. 2020; Kochkov et al. 2021; List et al. 2022).
* :func:`periodic_cnn2d`, :func:`torus_graph` (edges of a periodic graph for MeshGraphNet), :func:`fit_supervised`
  and :class:`FourierGalerkinPINN` (a physics-informed network for the large scales, trained on the residual of the
  Fourier-Galerkin truncated vorticity equation only): the surrogates of the multiscale benchmark.
* :class:`LearnedClosure`: a small periodic CNN that returns a subfilter vorticity *flux* ``sigma``; the tendency is
  ``-div(sigma)``, so the closure conserves circulation exactly whatever the network does.
  :func:`as_numpy_closure` plugs it into :class:`~.ns2d.VorticityNS2D`.

classes.name: ScaleConditionedFNO2d
classes.sig: (in_channels: int = 1, out_channels: int = 1, width: int = 32, modes: int = 12, layers: int = 4, conditioned: bool = True, delta_ref: float = 2 * math.pi / 64)
classes.doc:
FNO on a periodic grid whose layers are modulated by the filter width: ``x -> gelu(gamma(Delta) * (K x + W x)
+ beta(Delta))``. ``forward(x, delta)`` with ``x`` (B, C, n, n) and ``delta`` (B,) or a float. ``conditioned=False``
gives the scale-blind network (``gamma = 1``, ``beta = 0``).

methods.name: forward
methods.sig: (x: torch.Tensor, delta: torch.Tensor | float | None = None) -> torch.Tensor

classes.name: TorchVorticityLES2D
classes.sig: (n: int, length: float = 2 * math.pi, dtype = torch.float64)
classes.doc:
Differentiable dealiased pseudo-spectral 2-D vorticity solver (integrating-factor RK4) with an optional
closure ``closure(w (B, n, n), solver) -> tendency``. ``nu`` per sample in :meth:`rollout`.

methods.name: nonlinear_hat
methods.sig: (wh: torch.Tensor, closure = None, frozen: torch.Tensor | None = None) -> torch.Tensor

methods.name: rollout
methods.sig: (w0: torch.Tensor, nu: torch.Tensor, dt: float, save_steps: Sequence[int], closure = None, closure_per_step: bool = False) -> torch.Tensor
methods.doc:
Integrate ``w0`` (B, n, n) with viscosities ``nu`` (B,) and return the states after each number of steps
in ``save_steps`` (sorted): (B, len(save_steps), n, n). ``closure_per_step``: evaluate the closure once per
step and keep it fixed over the four Runge-Kutta stages (four times cheaper for a network closure; first
order in time for the closure term only).

classes.name: LearnedClosure
classes.sig: (hidden: int = 16, layers: int = 3, kernel: int = 5)
classes.doc:
Periodic CNN closure: inputs ``omega / rms``, ``u``, ``v`` (scaled) and the strain components; output the
subfilter vorticity flux ``sigma`` (2 channels), scaled by ``delta^2 * rms(omega)^2``; tendency ``-div(sigma)``.

classes.name: FourierGalerkinPINN
classes.sig: (kmax: int = 4, hidden: int = 256, scale: float = 5.0, t_ref: float = 0.3, length: float = 2 * math.pi)
classes.doc:
Physics-informed network for the large scales of 2-D vorticity, trained on the physics only.

The field is represented by the coefficients ``c`` of the modes ``|kx|, |ky| <= kmax`` (sharp square filter,
:func:`~.filters.low_modes`); ``c(t) = c0 + t * net(c0, z, t)`` is exact at t = 0 (``z``: a scalar feature of the
case, e.g. log Re). The loss is the residual of the Fourier-Galerkin truncated vorticity equation,
``dc/dt - P[-div(u w)] + nu k^2 c``, with ``dc/dt`` by forward-mode automatic differentiation in t and the
nonlinear term evaluated pseudo-spectrally on a grid fine enough to be exact for the retained modes. No solution
data. The truncation drops the subfilter term, so this is the large-scale model of a Galerkin truncation.

methods.name: coeffs
methods.sig: (c0: torch.Tensor, z: torch.Tensor, t: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor

methods.name: tendency
methods.doc: Galerkin-projected right-hand side for coefficients ``c`` (B, 2 * modes).

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (c0: np.ndarray, nu: np.ndarray, z: np.ndarray, steps: int, seed: int = 0, batch: int = 64, lr: float = 0.001, log: bool = True) -> list[float]
methods.doc:
Train on initial coefficients ``c0`` (N, 2 * modes), viscosities ``nu`` and features ``z`` (N,), with
times drawn uniformly in [0, t_ref].

methods.name: predict
methods.sig: (c0: np.ndarray, z: np.ndarray, times: Sequence[float]) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: (B, len(times), 2 * modes) coefficients.

methods.name: field
methods.doc: Coefficients to fields on an ``n x n`` grid.

functions.sig: (kind: str, k: torch.Tensor, delta: torch.Tensor | float) -> torch.Tensor

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale.ns2d
children.doc:
2-D incompressible Navier-Stokes in vorticity form on the periodic square ``[0, L)^2``, for resolved (DNS) and
large-eddy (LES) simulation, with the energy spectrum and the residual of the (filtered) vorticity equation.

    d(omega)/dt + u . grad(omega) = nu lap(omega) - mu omega + f + C(omega),
    lap(psi) = -omega,  u = d(psi)/dy,  v = -d(psi)/dx

``C`` is an optional subfilter closure (LES): any callable ``closure(omega, solver) -> tendency`` evaluated on the
resolved field, e.g. :class:`~.closures.Smagorinsky`. Pseudo-spectral in space with the 2/3 dealiasing rule (the
dealiased grid resolves ``|k| <= n / 3``, which is also the implicit sharp filter of an LES on that grid), ETDRK4 in
time (Cox & Matthews 2002; Kassam & Trefethen 2005, through
:class:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.etdrk4.ETDRK4`). Arrays are ``(n, n)`` or batched ``(batch, n, n)``,
axis -2 is x and axis -1 is y. Written from the equations; no third-party solver code was used.

classes.name: VorticityNS2D
classes.doc:
Pseudo-spectral 2-D vorticity solver. ``closure(omega, solver) -> tendency`` (physical space, same shape) adds
a subfilter model; ``forcing``: ``(n, n)`` time-independent vorticity forcing; ``drag``: linear friction ``mu``.

methods.doc: ``u . grad(w)`` in conservative form ``div(u w)`` (equal for divergence-free ``u``), dealiased.

methods.name: tendency
methods.doc: Right-hand side ``d(omega)/dt`` of the resolved equations (closure included).

methods.sig: (w0: np.ndarray, times: Sequence[float], dt: float = 0.005, check: bool = True) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Integrate from ``w0`` (at t = 0) and return the vorticity at each of ``times`` (sorted, >= 0):
``(len(times), n, n)`` or ``(batch, len(times), n, n)``. Raises ``FloatingPointError`` on blow-up when
``check``.

methods.sig: (w: np.ndarray, kmax: int | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]

fields: closure: Callable[[np.ndarray, VorticityNS2D], np.ndarray] | None = None

functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: ``(u, v)`` of a periodic vorticity field (zero mean velocity).

functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, length: float = 2 * np.pi, kmax: int | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Shell-summed kinetic energy spectrum ``E(k)`` from vorticity, ``sum_k E(k) = mean(u^2 + v^2) / 2``. Returns
integer shell wavenumbers (in units of ``2 pi / L``) and ``E`` (averaged over leading batch axes).

functions.sig: (rng: np.random.Generator, n: int, k0: float = 4.0, energy: float = 0.5, length: float = 2 * np.pi, batch: int | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Random vorticity with energy spectrum ``E(k) ~ k^4 exp(-2 (k / k0)^2)`` (peak at ``k0``), random phases, total
kinetic energy ``energy``.

functions.name: exact_advection
functions.sig: (w: np.ndarray, length: float = 2 * np.pi) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``div(u w)`` of the trigonometric interpolant of ``w``, without aliasing: the products are formed on a grid
3/2 times finer and truncated back (exact for the modes of the original grid).

functions.name: vorticity_residual
functions.sig: (w_prev: np.ndarray, w_next: np.ndarray, dt: float, nu: float, length: float = 2 * np.pi, forcing: np.ndarray | None = None, drag: float = 0.0, closure_tendency: np.ndarray | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float]
functions.doc:
Residual of the vorticity equation between two snapshots ``dt`` apart (trapezoidal in time, second order):
``R = (w_next - w_prev) / dt + mean(div(u w)) - nu lap(mean w) + mu mean(w) - f - C``, the means taken over the
two snapshots, where ``C`` is the subfilter tendency given in ``closure_tendency`` (0 for the resolved
equations). Returns ``(R, scale)``, where ``scale`` is the rms of the largest term, so ``rms(R) / scale`` is a
relative residual.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale.residuals
children.doc:
Physics residuals evaluated at several filter widths.

A residual computed at the grid scale only is one number: a field can satisfy the equations on average and violate
them at small scales, or be smooth at large scales and noisy at small ones. Filtering the field with ``G_Delta`` at
several widths and evaluating the residual of the *filtered* equations at each gives a curve against ``Delta``.

The filtered equations are not the original ones. For ``N(u)`` nonlinear, ``G * N(u) != N(G * u)``: the residual of an
exact field, filtered, is the subfilter term (the closure), not a model error. And when the width varies in space
the filter does not commute with derivatives, which adds a commutation term. Both are reported separately, so

    raw residual  =  subfilter term  +  commutation term  +  model residual

and only the last one is blamed on the model. The subfilter term is exact when the fine field is available
(``subfilter="exact"``, e.g. for a reference or a resolved prediction) and modelled otherwise (``"dynamic"``: the
dynamic Smagorinsky estimate from the filtered field itself, or any closure).

functions.name: multiscale_residuals
functions.sig: (state: np.ndarray, residual_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Filter], tuple[np.ndarray, float]], filters: Sequence[Filter], *, length: float = 2 * np.pi, subfilter_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Filter], np.ndarray] | None = None, commutation_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Filter], np.ndarray] | None = None, filter_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Filter], np.ndarray] | None = None) -> MultiscaleResidual
functions.doc:
Residual curve of any equation. ``residual_fn(filtered_state, filter) -> (R, scale)`` evaluates the residual
field of the filtered equations and a normalising scale; ``subfilter_fn(state, filter)`` the subfilter term
(from the unfiltered ``state``, or modelled); ``commutation_fn(state, filter)`` the commutation term;
``filter_fn`` (default: uniform filtering of the last two axes) how ``state`` is filtered.

functions.name: ns2d_multiscale_residuals
functions.sig: (w_prev: np.ndarray, w_next: np.ndarray, dt: float, nu: float, filters: Sequence[Filter], *, length: float = 2 * np.pi, forcing: np.ndarray | None = None, drag: float = 0.0, subfilter: str | Callable | None = 'exact') -> MultiscaleResidual
functions.doc:
Multiscale residual of the 2-D vorticity equation between two snapshots ``dt`` apart (see
:func:`~.ns2d.vorticity_residual`). ``subfilter``: ``"exact"`` (computed from the given, unfiltered snapshots:
for a resolved field, the model residual is then the true error of the filtered dynamics), ``"dynamic"``
(dynamic Smagorinsky with the filter's width and kind, from the filtered snapshots only), a closure object
(``closure(w, solver) -> tendency`` with a ``delta`` attribute), or None (raw residual only). The filters are
uniform, so the commutation term is zero; use :func:`multiscale_residuals` with
:func:`~.filters.commutation_error` for variable widths.

children.summary: Physics residuals evaluated at several filter widths.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale.scales
children.doc:
Scale-aware model selection: each model declares the scales it resolves, each query the scales it needs.

A model trained or run at grid spacing ``h`` with filter ``G_Delta`` represents ``G_Delta * u`` and nothing finer.
Asked for a field filtered at a smaller width it cannot answer, however small its validation error was; asked for a
larger width it can, by post-filtering its output (:func:`~.filters.refilter`), but only exactly when the requested
filter can be built from its own (a Gaussian from a narrower Gaussian, anything from a sharp cut-off below the
requested scales; a box filter has zeros a post-filter cannot undo). So:

* :class:`ScaleProfile` (per model): output filter (kind, width), grid spacing, closure model, valid Reynolds range,
  time resolution, fidelity rung (0 surrogate, 1 coarse LES with a closure, 2 resolved solver), cost;
* :class:`ScaleQuery` (per query): requested filter (kind, width) of the output, Reynolds number, time scale;
* :func:`scale_compatibility`: 0 (cannot answer: finer than its resolved scale or its time resolution) or
  ``exp(-(mismatch / tol)^2) x Re score``, with the mismatch of :func:`~.filters.realizability_mismatch`;
* :class:`ScaleAwareRouter`: the compatibility as a prior on the ensemble weights, sleeping experts that cannot
  answer, and a fidelity ladder: only the lowest rung that covers the query is awake; it escalates one rung when the
  query needs smaller scales than the rung resolves or when the prediction checks of every model on the rung fail
  (``escalate_from``). Same interface as :class:`~pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.PhysicsAwareRouter`
  (``prior``, ``awake``, ``escalate``, ``route``), so it plugs into
  ``PhysicsEnsemble(router=...)``, and it can wrap such a router (``base=``) to add the assumption audit.

classes.name: ScaleProfile
classes.doc:
Scales a model represents. ``filter``: the filter its output carries (``Filter("sharp", 0)`` for a resolved
field); ``grid_spacing``: its output grid; ``re_range``: Reynolds numbers it is valid for (training range of a
surrogate, resolution limit of a solver); ``time_step``: its time resolution (output interval); ``fidelity``: rung
in :data:`RUNGS`; ``closure``: the subfilter model (None for surrogates and resolved solvers).

methods.name: resolved_width
methods.doc:
Smallest width it can deliver: its filter width, or its grid spacing (a sharp cut-off at the grid's
Nyquist wavenumber), whichever is larger.

classes.name: ScaleQuery
classes.doc:
Scales a query needs: the filter of the requested output, the Reynolds number of the case and the time scale
of the requested quantity (None: not constrained). ``kmax``: largest wavenumber of the output grid (where the
filter comparison stops).

classes.name: ScaleAwareRouter
classes.sig: (profiles: Sequence[ScaleProfile] | Mapping[str, ScaleProfile], query_fn: Callable[[Any], ScaleQuery] | None = None, *, strength: float = 1.0, floor: float = 0.0001, abstain_below: float = 0.05, ladder: bool = True, rung_threshold: float = 0.3, cost_weight: float = 0.0, mismatch_tol: float = 0.25, re_band: float = 0.15, base: Any = None)
classes.doc:
``profiles``: one :class:`ScaleProfile` per expert (experts without one are always awake, score 1);
``query_fn(query) -> ScaleQuery`` (identity by default). ``strength``: exponent of the compatibility in the
prior; ``abstain_below``: compatibility under which an expert sleeps; ``ladder``: keep only the lowest
fidelity rung that has an expert with compatibility >= ``rung_threshold`` awake; ``cost_weight``: subtract
``cost_weight * cost / max cost`` from the log-prior; ``base``: another router whose prior and awake set are
combined with these (e.g. the assumption audit).

methods.name: awake
methods.sig: (query: Any, names: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, bool]

methods.doc:
Awake set after the experts in ``failed`` failed their prediction checks (e.g. a closure check): the

methods.name: covered

methods.doc: Experts that can answer the query at all (may be empty: the query is not covered).

Choose a model for one case with the reasons; ``chosen`` is None when no model covers the query (the

children.name: pinneapple_physics.multiscale.turbulence
children.doc:
Decaying 2-D turbulence as a multiscale benchmark: resolved reference data, filtered datasets at several widths,
query streams that shift the Reynolds number and the requested scale, and the closure benchmark.

:class:`DecayingTurbulence2D` holds the set-up (domain, output grid, output times, Reynolds bands, requested widths
and filter kinds, LES grid). Every case starts from a random vorticity field (energy spectrum peaked at ``k0``),
evolved for ``spinup`` time units at its own viscosity so the cascade is developed; the question is the vorticity
``t_out`` later, filtered at a requested width, on the ``n_out`` grid. Training data come from a pseudo-spectral DNS
at ``n_train``; the independent reference from a finer DNS at ``n_ref``. Data generation runs in parallel processes
(at low priority) and is cached in ``.npz`` files.

* :meth:`~DecayingTurbulence2D.generate_training_data`, :meth:`~DecayingTurbulence2D.generate_reference`;
* :meth:`~DecayingTurbulence2D.query_stream`: queries ``{"id", "seed", "nu", "re", "band", "width", "kind",
  "filter"}``; :meth:`~DecayingTurbulence2D.reference_output`: the filtered reference of a query;
* :meth:`~DecayingTurbulence2D.filtered_pairs`: (input, target) pairs at one filter for supervised surrogates;
* :func:`benchmark_closures`: a-priori, a-posteriori and label-free checks of several closures on held-out cases;
* :func:`scale_conditioning_study`: errors of a scale-conditioned model against fixed-width and scale-blind models,
  at trained and held-out widths, with its cross-scale self-consistency.

children.doc:
Multiscale physics for adaptive ensembles: filters, closures, multiscale residuals, cross-scale consistency and
scale-aware model selection.

=====================  ==========================================================================================
module                 contents
=====================  ==========================================================================================
:mod:`.filters`        box, Gaussian and sharp spectral filters with exact transfer functions; restriction and
                       prolongation; post-filtering from one width to another and its realizability; variable-width
                       filtering and the commutation error
:mod:`.ns2d`           pseudo-spectral 2-D vorticity DNS / LES, energy spectrum, residual of the vorticity equation
:mod:`.closures`       Smagorinsky, dynamic Smagorinsky, gradient (Clark) model; a-priori and a-posteriori tests;
                       label-free closure health (enstrophy growth, spectral pile-up, Germano-identity error)
:mod:`.residuals`      residuals of the filtered equations at several widths, split into subfilter, commutation
                       and model parts
:mod:`.consistency`    cross-scale consistency: filter(fine prediction) against the coarse prediction
:mod:`.scales`         scale profiles of models, scale queries, scale compatibility, :class:`ScaleAwareRouter`
                       with a fidelity ladder (surrogate -> LES with closure -> resolved solver)
:mod:`.learned`        (PyTorch, imported on demand) scale-conditioned FNO with a filtering-consistency loss,
                       differentiable LES and a closure trained a posteriori through the solver; periodic CNN,
                       torus graph and a Fourier-Galerkin PINN for the benchmark surrogates
:mod:`.turbulence`     decaying 2-D turbulence benchmark: DNS data, filtered pairs, query streams that shift Re
                       and scale, closure benchmark, scale-conditioning study
:mod:`.comparison`     cached expert evaluation, scale-blind vs scale-aware ensembles on one stream, metrics,
                       tables and the summary figure
:mod:`.viz`            animation of a run (requested scale, chosen model, spectra, weights)
=====================  ==========================================================================================

Plain numpy except :mod:`.learned`. See ``docs/core_concepts/multiscale_ensembles.md``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian
pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian.ep_tuning
children.doc:
Exceptional-point tuning: can a control parameter move the EP of a PT-symmetric dimer along a desired law?

Reference: "A No-Go Theorem for Exceptional-Point Tuning in PT-Symmetric Dimers: Pedagogical Structure and
Device-Design Constraints", Zenodo record 23287622 (Project Prometheus). For the reciprocal dimer the EP sits at
gamma_EP = |b(lam)|, so with a polynomial coupling b(lam) = J + c1 lam + ... + cn lam^n (lam real, cn != 0)

    gamma_EP^2(lam) = |b(lam)|^2,  a real polynomial of degree 2n with leading coefficient |cn|^2 > 0,

which can never equal the linear target J^2 + lam J <G> (degree 1) for a nontrivial perturbation: the no-go
theorem. The paper's classification and the three ways around it:

* phase-only coupling b = J exp(i phi(lam)): the EP does not move;
* reciprocal polynomial coupling: quadratic (or higher) corrections are unavoidable;
* Route A, non-polynomial coupling b = sqrt(J^2 + lam J <G>): exact linear tuning, PT symmetric;
* Route B, state-dependent feedback: a polynomial feedback map can have a non-polynomial fixed point (conjecture in
  the paper; :func:`feedback_coupling` shows one such map, which is not a proof);
* Route C, non-reciprocal hopping b_ab = J, b_ba = J + lam <G>: exact linear tuning, PT symmetry broken.

:func:`analyze_ep_tuning` checks any coupling law symbolically (sympy): the EP law, its degree, the residual against
the target, the class of the perturbation and which of the theorem's four assumptions (A PT symmetry, B dimension 2,
C polynomial coupling, D reciprocity) hold. :func:`theorem_profile` states the same assumptions for
:mod:`pinneapple_physics.physics_audit`, so a device design is audited like any model: when one assumption fails the
theorem no longer constrains it.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian.pt_dimer
children.doc:
PT-symmetric dimers and chains: Hamiltonian, spectrum, exceptional points (EPs) and how they coalesce.

The dimer

    H(gamma, lam) = [[eps + i gamma,  b_ab(lam)],
                     [b_ba(lam),      eps - i gamma]]

is PT symmetric (P = sigma_x, T = complex conjugation, P H* P = H) when ``b_ba = conj(b_ab)`` (reciprocal coupling).
Its eigenvalues are ``eps +/- sqrt(b_ab b_ba - gamma^2)``, so the eigenvalues *and* the eigenvectors coalesce at
``gamma_EP^2 = b_ab b_ba`` (= |b|^2 in the PT-symmetric case): an exceptional point. Below it the spectrum is real
(unbroken PT phase), above it complex conjugate (broken phase).

:class:`PTDimer` evaluates all of this for couplings given as numbers or functions of a control parameter ``lam``;
:meth:`PTDimer.ep_gamma_numeric` finds the EP from the matrix alone (eigenvalue splitting and eigenvector overlap),
an independent check of the closed form. :class:`PTChain` does the same for N sites (gain on the first, loss on the
last), where the EP can be of higher order (the trimer's is an EP3 at gamma = sqrt(2) |b|).

the origin of EP-enhanced sensitivity.

functions.doc: K_i = <L_i|L_i><R_i|R_i> / |<L_i|R_i>|^2 for each mode (1 for a Hermitian matrix, diverges at an EP).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.online_learning
children.doc:
Online learning with expert advice, shared by every adaptive method in the library (time-series forecasting in
``pinneapple_systems.time_series.adaptive`` and physics-model ensembles in ``pinneapple_physics.ensemble``).

* :class:`FixedShare`: exponentially weighted average with fixed share (Herbster & Warmuth 1998, Machine Learning
  32:151); tracks the best *sequence* of experts, so it can switch when the regime changes.
* :class:`AdaHedge`: parameter-free Hedge (de Rooij, van Erven, Grunwald & Koolen 2014, JMLR 15:1281); used to choose
  the learning and switching rates of a grid of Fixed-Share aggregators online.
* :class:`AdaptiveConformal`: adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs & Candes 2021, NeurIPS); interval level corrected
  after every observation so coverage holds under distribution shift.
* :class:`FixedShareGrid`: a grid of Fixed-Share aggregators weighted by AdaHedge, the combination used by both
  adaptive methods.

All decisions use only losses already observed (prequential), so they cannot overfit the evaluation period.

to Data-Driven Parameters Discovery of Epidemiological Compartmental Models" (arXiv:2008.05554v1): equations,

temperatures with PINNeAPPle's Ensemble Kalman Inversion.

``measurements``: [{"x_mm", "y_mm", "t_c", "side": "top"|"bottom"}] board

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pcb.solver
children.doc:
3D finite-volume thermal model of a populated PCB.

* The board is resolved layer by layer (one cell per copper or dielectric
  layer through the thickness, a structured grid in-plane), each layer with
  its own in-plane / through-plane conductivity (``pcb_thermal.Layer``).
* Components use the JEDEC two-resistor compact model: a junction node
  tied to the board cells under the footprint through theta_JB (split by
  overlap area) and to the air through theta_JC in series with the case-top
  convection. The footprint shields that part of the board face from the air.
* Thermal vias add plated copper through the dielectric under a component.
* Board faces lose heat by convection + radiation with coefficients from
  ``pcb_thermal.convection_coefficients``; those depend on the surface
  temperature, so the solve is iterated to a fixed point.
* Optional chassis contact along the board edges (card-edge / wedge-lock
  cooling) at a fixed temperature.

Unknowns are temperatures above ambient; the sparse system is solved with
AMG-preconditioned conjugate gradients (direct solve as fallback). Energy balance (heat to air + chassis = power) is returned.

functions.name: solve
functions.sig: (board: Board, comps: list[Component], env: Environment, *, n_cells: int = 60, h_override: dict[str, float] | None = None, k_xy_scale: float = 1.0, h_scale: float = 1.0, max_iter: int = 40, coarse_cells: int = 24) -> dict[str, Any]

Steady temperatures. ``h_override`` fixes {'top','bottom'} coefficients
(tests / calibration); ``k_xy_scale`` / ``h_scale`` scale the in-plane
conductivity and the surface coefficients (calibration / uncertainty).

The surface coefficients depend on the mean face temperatures only, so
their fixed point is found on a coarse grid, then the fine grid is solved
with them and the fixed point re-checked (one more fine solve if needed).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pde_environment
pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.builder
children.doc:
ProblemBuilder — fluent API for constructing ProblemSpec objects.

This module provides the researcher-facing interface for defining physics
problems without touching the raw dataclass constructors.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_physics.pde_environment import ProblemBuilder
>>> import numpy as np

>>> spec = (
...     ProblemBuilder("my_heat")
...     .domain(x=(0.0, 1.0), t=(0.0, 1.0))
...     .fields("u")
...     .pde("heat_1d", alpha=0.01)
...     .ic(field="u", fn=lambda X: np.sin(np.pi * X[:, 0:1]))
...     .bc("dirichlet", field="u", value=0.0, on="x_boundary")
...     .sample(interior=4000, boundary=800, ic=800)
...     .build()
... )

The resulting ``ProblemSpec`` is directly accepted by:
- ``Arena.from_spec(spec).run(...)``
- ``run_arena_experiment(...)`` via YAML
- ``generate_pinn_dataset(spec, ...)``

The builder can also register the spec as a named preset::

    builder.register("my_heat_preset")
    # now available via: get_preset("my_heat_preset")

classes.name: ProblemBuilder
classes.sig: (name: str) -> None
classes.doc:
Fluent builder for ``ProblemSpec``.

Every method returns ``self`` to allow method chaining.
Call ``.build()`` at the end to get a frozen ``ProblemSpec``.

Example
-------
>>> spec = (
...     ProblemBuilder("burgers_custom")
...     .domain(x=(-1.0, 1.0), t=(0.0, 1.0))
...     .fields("u")
...     .pde("burgers", nu=0.01)
...     .ic(field="u", fn=lambda X: -np.sin(np.pi * X[:, 0:1]))
...     .bc("dirichlet", field="u", value=0.0, on="x_boundary")
...     .sample(interior=4000, boundary=800, ic=800)
...     .solver(name="fdm", method="burgers_1d", nx=256, nt=256)
...     .build()
... )

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.condition_sampling
children.doc:
Sampling points for conditions whose region is given by a selector function.

Boundary and initial conditions live on a lower-dimensional set (``t == t0``, ``x == x_min``...). Drawing points
uniformly inside the box and keeping the ones a selector accepts almost never lands on that set: with
``np.isclose``-style selectors it returns zero points, and the condition is silently dropped. Here candidates are
drawn inside the box **and on every face of it** (one coordinate pinned to its lower or upper bound), and on the
plane where a coordinate is 0 when 0 lies inside its range (an initial condition at t = 0 on t in [-T, T]), so face-
and edge-type selectors find points, while interior selectors (data regions, sub-domains) still do.

functions.name: sample_condition_points
functions.sig: (select: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], domain_bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], coords: Sequence[str], n: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Up to ``n`` points (float32, shape ``(m, len(coords))``) accepted by ``select(X) -> bool mask``.

Returns an empty ``(0, d)`` array when the selector accepts none of the candidates; callers must treat that as
an error or skip explicitly, never pad with made-up points.

functions.name: box_face_normals
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, domain_bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], coords: Sequence[str], time_coord: str = 't') -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Outward unit normals of the bounding box at ``points`` (one column per coordinate, 0 for time).

Returns ``(normals, on_face)``: a point on one face gets that face's normal, a point on an edge or corner the
normalised sum of its faces' normals, and a point on no face (a curved boundary inside the box) gets zeros and
``on_face=False``; its normal cannot be known from a selector, so callers must not use it as if it were one.
