children.name: pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.monitor

methods.name: ratio
methods.doc: value / tolerance (> 1 means failed).

classes.name: ValidityCheck
classes.doc:
``fn(prediction, query) -> value``; passes when ``value <= tolerance``. ``critical``: a single failure is an
alarm (default for bounds: a negative density is never acceptable).

classes.name: PhysicsValidityMonitor
classes.sig: (checks: Sequence[ValidityCheck], persistence: int = 3, drift_ratio: float = 3.0, drift_alpha: float = 0.3, baseline_cases: int = 10, baselines: Mapping[str, float] | None = None)
classes.doc:
Run a set of checks on every prediction and keep their history.

``persistence``: a check failing this many cases in a row is an alarm. ``drift_ratio``: a residual check whose
value, smoothed (EWMA with ``drift_alpha``), reaches this multiple of its baseline (median of the first
``baseline_cases`` cases, or ``baselines[name]``) raises an alarm even before it crosses its tolerance.

functions.name: residual_check
functions.sig: (residual_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], float], tolerance: float, name: str = 'pde_residual', critical: bool = False) -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc: ``residual_fn(prediction, query)``: a residual norm (RMS of the PDE residual, for instance).

functions.name: conservation_check
functions.sig: (total_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], float], target_fn: Callable[[Any], float], rel_tol: float = 0.01, name: str = 'conservation', critical: bool = False, abs_tol: float = 0.0) -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc:
Relative imbalance ``|total(prediction) - target(query)| / |target(query)|``. ``total_fn`` is typically a
quadrature (``np.sum(cell_volumes * rho)``); ``target_fn`` the initial total plus sources minus outflow.
``abs_tol``: an absolute imbalance that is always accepted (needed when the target is zero); the value reported
is then ``|imbalance| / max(|target|, abs_tol / rel_tol)``.

functions.name: bounds_check
functions.sig: (lo: float | None = None, hi: float | None = None, name: str = 'bounds', select: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], np.ndarray] | None = None, max_fraction: float = 0.0, critical: bool = True) -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc: Fraction of values outside ``[lo, hi]`` (a field selected by ``select``, all of it by default).

functions.name: boundary_check
functions.sig: (predict_boundary: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], np.ndarray], boundary_value: Callable[[Any], np.ndarray], rel_tol: float = 0.01, name: str = 'boundary_condition', critical: bool = False, scale: float | None = None) -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc:
Relative RMS mismatch between the prediction on the boundary and the boundary condition: RMS(a - b) divided
by ``scale`` if given, else by the larger of the RMS of the boundary condition and the RMS of the whole
prediction. (Dividing by the RMS of the boundary prediction itself would make a homogeneous condition, b = 0,
fail for any non-zero value however small.)

functions.name: constitutive_check
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], float], tolerance: float, name: str = 'constitutive', critical: bool = False) -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc: Any relation the prediction must satisfy (equation of state, material law): ``fn`` returns its violation.

functions.name: invariant_check
functions.sig: (invariant_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, Any], float], expected: float | Callable[[Any], float], rel_tol: float = 0.01, name: str = 'invariant', critical: bool = False, abs_tol: float = 0.0) -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc:
Relative change of an invariant (energy of a conservative system, a symmetry measure). ``abs_tol`` as in
:func:`conservation_check`, for an invariant whose expected value is zero (an antisymmetry measure).

functions.name: envelope_check
functions.sig: (envelope: Envelope, features_fn: Callable[[Any], Mapping[str, float]], min_score: float = 0.5, name: str = 'training_envelope') -> ValidityCheck
functions.doc: Extrapolation: 1 - envelope score (0 inside the training ranges, -> 1 far outside).

children.summary: Physics validity monitor: is a prediction still physically plausible, when no ground truth is available?

children.name: pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.regime
children.doc:
Dimensionless numbers that tell which physics a case is in.

Every function takes plain floats (SI units) and returns a float, so the result can go straight into the feature
dictionary that the assumption auditor, the router and the knowledge graph read (``{"Re": ..., "Ma": ...}``).
:func:`regime_features` computes every number whose inputs are given and skips the rest.

functions.name: reynolds
functions.sig: (velocity: float, length: float, nu: float | None = None, *, rho: float | None = None, mu: float | None = None) -> float
functions.doc: Re = U L / nu (or rho U L / mu).

functions.name: mach
functions.sig: (velocity: float, sound_speed: float | None = None, *, gamma: float = 1.4, R: float = 287.05, T: float | None = None) -> float
functions.doc: Ma = U / a, with a given or a = sqrt(gamma R T) for an ideal gas.

functions.name: peclet
functions.sig: (velocity: float, length: float, diffusivity: float) -> float
functions.doc: Pe = U L / D (mass) or U L / alpha (heat).

functions.name: knudsen
functions.sig: (mean_free_path: float, length: float) -> float

functions.name: grashof
functions.sig: (g: float, beta: float, dT: float, length: float, nu: float) -> float

functions.name: prandtl
functions.sig: (nu: float, alpha: float) -> float

functions.name: rayleigh
functions.sig: (g: float, beta: float, dT: float, length: float, nu: float, alpha: float) -> float

functions.name: richardson
functions.sig: (g: float, beta: float, dT: float, length: float, velocity: float) -> float
functions.doc: Ri = Gr / Re^2 = g beta dT L / U^2.

functions.name: biot
functions.sig: (h: float, length: float, k: float) -> float

functions.name: froude
functions.sig: (velocity: float, length: float, g: float = 9.81) -> float

functions.name: strouhal
functions.sig: (frequency: float, length: float, velocity: float) -> float

functions.name: dominant_frequency
functions.sig: (signal, dt: float = 1.0, discard: float = 0.5, window: bool = True, refine: bool = True, pad: int = 1) -> float
functions.doc:
Frequency (1 / time unit of ``dt``) of the strongest spectral peak of a sampled signal, e.g. the
vortex-shedding frequency of a wake probe or a lift history, for :func:`strouhal`.

The first ``discard`` fraction of the record (start-up transient) is dropped and the mean removed; the rest is
optionally multiplied by a Hann window (Harris, Proc. IEEE 66, 1978) and zero-padded to ``pad`` times its
length, and the largest non-DC bin of ``|rfft|`` is taken. ``refine`` fits a parabola through the logarithms of
the peak bin and its two neighbours (Gaussian interpolation; Smith & Serra, "PARSHL", ICMC 1987), which brings the
estimate to a small fraction of a bin for a Hann-windowed sinusoid. Returns 0.0 for records too short to have
a non-DC bin.

functions.name: damkohler
functions.sig: (reaction_rate: float, length: float, velocity: float) -> float

functions.name: roughness_reynolds
functions.sig: (re: float, eps_d: float, f: float | None = None) -> float
functions.doc:
eps+ = Re (eps / D) sqrt(f / 8): roughness height in wall units. ``f`` (Darcy) defaults to the Haaland
estimate, so no solution is needed.

functions.name: regime_features
functions.sig: (*, velocity: float | None = None, length: float | None = None, nu: float | None = None, sound_speed: float | None = None, diffusivity: float | None = None, alpha: float | None = None, mean_free_path: float | None = None, g: float = 9.81, beta: float | None = None, dT: float | None = None, T: float | None = None, h: float | None = None, k: float | None = None, extra: Mapping[str, float] | None ...
functions.doc:
Every dimensionless number whose inputs are given (SI units). ``extra`` adds features computed elsewhere
(``strain``, ``stress_ratio``, ``alpha_deg``...).

children.summary: Dimensionless numbers that tell which physics a case is in.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.routing
children.doc:
Physics-aware model routing: weight each model by how well the *current* case fits its physical foundations, not
only by the errors it made on earlier cases.

For one case the router reads its features (dimensionless numbers, from ``features_fn(query)``) and, for each
model, the audit of its assumptions and training envelope (:func:`~.assumptions.audit_assumptions`). The
compatibility ``c_i`` in [0, 1] becomes a prior on the model's weight:

    w_i  proportional to  w_learned_i * max(c_i, floor) ** strength * exp(-cost_weight * cost_i / max cost)

A model whose assumptions the case violates is *asleep* (``c_i < abstain_below``): it is not used for this case
and, inside a :class:`~pinneapple_physics.ensemble.PhysicsEnsemble`, its weight is not changed by the case either
(the sleeping-experts rule: its loss is set to the mixture's). So a laminar correlation is not punished for the
turbulent cases it was never meant for, and is ready again when the flow returns to its regime, without waiting for
its weight to recover. When no model is compatible (best ``c_i < escalate_below``) the router escalates to the
reference solver named by ``escalate_to``.

Use standalone (:meth:`PhysicsAwareRouter.route`) or inside the ensemble: ``PhysicsEnsemble(experts,
router=PhysicsAwareRouter(profiles, features_fn))``. The learned weights and the residual look-ahead of the ensemble
still apply on top, so history and the current residual correct a compatibility that is wrong.

children.doc:
Physics audit: which model to use, when to trust it and when its physical formulation itself must be revisited.

"It is in the fundamental knowledge that we must look for the cause of a model's imperfections." The modules here
add, on top of the predictive models (PINN, FNO, GNN, DeepONet, CNN, solvers), the layers that judge them by their
physics:

========================  =====================================================================================
layer                     module
========================  =====================================================================================
physical evaluation       :mod:`.monitor` (residuals, conservation, bounds, boundary, invariants, extrapolation:
                          no ground truth needed), :mod:`.assumptions` (each model's assumptions and the
                          conditions they hold in), :mod:`.regime` (dimensionless numbers)
adaptive decision         :mod:`.routing` (compatibility of the current case with each model's physics, as a prior
                          on the weights of :class:`~pinneapple_physics.ensemble.PhysicsEnsemble`; sleeping
                          experts; escalation to the solver)
diagnosis and evolution   :mod:`.attribution` (probable cause of a failure, with evidence and confidence),
                          :mod:`.improvement` (next experiment or change of highest value), :mod:`.knowledge`
                          (graph of phenomena, equations, assumptions, parameters, mechanisms and models)
========================  =====================================================================================

:func:`diagnose` runs the evaluation and diagnosis layers on one case and returns a :class:`Diagnosis` with a
readable report. Plain numpy: nothing here imports torch.

Low residuals do not guarantee a correct prediction, and high residuals alone do not identify the cause: the
diagnosis combines physical evidence, observations, validity conditions and uncertainty, and says which of them
it had.

methods.name: trusted
methods.doc: No failure found, assumptions valid (or marginal at worst) and the validity checks passed.

functions.name: diagnose
functions.sig: (profile: ModelProfile, features: Mapping[str, float], prediction: Any = None, query: Any = None, monitor: PhysicsValidityMonitor | None = None, error: float | None = None, error_tolerance: float = 0.05, graph: PhysicsKnowledgeGraph | None = None, **attribution_kwargs) -> Diagnosis
functions.doc:
Audit the assumptions of ``profile`` for the case's ``features``, run ``monitor`` on ``prediction`` (if both
given), attribute the failure (``error``: relative error against a reference, if any; other evidence through
``attribution_kwargs``: ``resolution``, ``measurement_suspect``, ``spread``, ``residual_baseline``) and recommend
the next steps. ``graph`` (default: :func:`default_graph` with ``profile``) names the missing mechanisms.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.em_kinds
children.doc:
Electromagnetic PDE kinds of the problem compiler: Maxwell's equations in differential and integral form.

Every kind returns a list of residual tensors ``(N, 1)`` at the collocation points (the compiler squares and
averages them). Units are the caller's: ``eps``, ``mu``, ``sigma`` default to 1 (a non-dimensional problem); for
SI pass the SI values or, better, scale the problem (``x / L``, ``t c / L``, fields by a reference amplitude) so the
network sees O(1) numbers. Space- or field-dependent material maps come from ``ctx`` callables
``eps_fn(X, ctx)``, ``mu_fn``, ``nu_fn``, ``sigma_fn`` evaluated at the points (piecewise-constant maps are the
usual case; a preset may put them in the PDE ``params``, under the caller's ``ctx``; in the differential kinds
their jumps are not differentiated, so interface conditions are only
imposed by the integral kinds, which evaluate the maps on the edges of each control square).

Differential kinds (``fields`` in brackets):

``electrostatics`` [phi]               div(eps grad phi) + rho = 0, rho from ``ctx["rho_fn"]`` (or ``source_fn``)
``magnetostatics_az`` [Az]             div(nu grad Az) + Jz = 0, ``nu = 1/mu``, Jz from ``ctx["J_fn"]``
``eddy_current_az`` [Ar, Ai]           nu lap(A) - j omega sigma A + Js = 0 (phasor ``exp(+j omega t)``, A = Ar + j Ai)
``maxwell_tm`` [Ez, Hx, Hy] + t        eps dEz/dt - (dHy/dx - dHx/dy) + sigma Ez + Jz = 0, mu dHx/dt + dEz/dy = 0,
                                       mu dHy/dt - dEz/dx = 0 (2-D TMz; ``maxwell_te`` is the dual, in compile.py)
``maxwell_3d`` [Ex, Ey, Ez, Hx, Hy, Hz] + t
                                       eps dE/dt - curl H + sigma E + J = 0, mu dH/dt + curl E = 0; with
                                       ``params["gauss"] = True`` also div(eps E) - rho and div(mu H)
``maxwell_tm_frequency`` [Er, Ei]      lap(E) + k0^2 eps_r E = f for the phasor Ez = Er + j Ei; complex ``eps_r``
                                       from ``ctx["eps_fn"]`` (scatterers) or ``params["eps_r"]``, ``params["eps_i"]``

Integral kinds (2-D, each collocation point is the centre of a square control volume of half-width
``params["h"]``; Gauss-Legendre quadrature with ``params["quad"]`` points per edge, default 4; residuals divided by
the area so they have the units of the differential form and converge to it as ``h -> 0``):

``electrostatics_integral`` [phi]      oint eps grad(phi).n dl + int rho dA = 0 (Gauss: oint D.n = Q_enclosed)
``maxwell_tm_integral`` [Ez, Hx, Hy] + t
                                       oint H.dl = int (eps dEz/dt + sigma Ez + Jz) dA (Ampere-Maxwell) and, along x
                                       and y, the two Faraday line laws mu d/dt int Hy dx = Ez(x+h) - Ez(x-h) and
                                       mu d/dt int Hx dy = -(Ez(y+h) - Ez(y-h)) (per unit length in z)

References: Jackson, *Classical Electrodynamics* 3rd ed., sec. 6.1 (Maxwell's equations) and I.3 of the
introduction (integral forms); Jin, *The Finite Element Method in Electromagnetics* 3rd ed., ch. 4 (the 2-D
scalar formulations used by the static, eddy-current and TM-frequency kinds).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.integral_kinds
children.doc:
Integral equations of the second kind as PDE kinds of the problem compiler, in Nyström form.

The equations are Fredholm and Volterra of the second kind over an interval::

    Fredholm   u(x) = f(x) + lambda * int_a^b K(x, s) u(s) ds
    Volterra   u(x) = f(x) + lambda * int_a^x K(x, s) u(s) ds

The integral is replaced by a fixed quadrature on the collocation points themselves, so the residual is an algebraic
equation in the values the network already produces -- no extra model evaluations, no autograd through the kernel::

    r(x_i) = u(x_i) - f(x_i) - lambda * [ sum_j w_j K(x_i, x_j) u(x_j) + D_i u(x_i) ]

with ``w`` the composite-trapezoid weights on the nodes sorted by ``x`` and ``D_i`` the analytic integral of the
singular part of the kernel over the *self cell* of node ``i`` (see below). Because the coupling is a matrix-vector
product, the same assembly gives the classical direct solve, which is what makes the neural solution checkable
against something other than itself.

Weakly singular kernels
-----------------------
For ``K = ln|x - s|`` the diagonal of the matrix is infinite and the naive rule diverges. The standard remedy is
applied here: the kernel is split into a singular part, whose integral over the cell containing ``x_i`` is analytic,
and a remainder integrated numerically::

    int K u ~ sum_{j != i} w_j K(x_i, x_j) u(x_j) + D_i u(x_i),    D_i = int_{x_i - w_i/2}^{x_i + w_i/2} K(x_i, s) ds

The pair ``(kernel, diag)`` is what the caller supplies: ``diag`` is the analytic cell integral of the singular
part, and ``kernel`` is what is summed numerically. For a bounded kernel no ``diag`` is needed and the diagonal is
the trapezoid's own ``w_i K(x_i, x_i)``, which is the same rule.

``D`` is which for the cell of width ``w_i``; for ``ln|s|`` that integral is ``w (ln(w/2) - 1)`` exactly (see
:func:`log_diag`). For Volterra the integration stops at ``x_i``, so only the left half of the self cell counts and
``D`` is halved -- exact for the distance kernels used here, which are even in the local coordinate.

Nodes
-----
The collocation points **are** the Nyström nodes. That is what makes the kind cheap, and it also means a resampled
collocation set turns the quadrature error into noise: for a deterministic quadrature, hand the compiler a fixed
grid. ``nystrom_matrix`` sorts the nodes internally, so the batch may arrive in any order.

Scope of this module: one spatial coordinate, real kernels with one field and complex kernels with two (the
``Er``/``Ei`` convention of :mod:`~pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.em_kinds`), and a dense ``(N, N)``
assembly -- adequate up to a few thousand nodes, beyond which a fast method is the right tool and is not here.
Integral equations of the first kind and hypersingular kernels are refused rather than approximated.

References: Atkinson, *The Numerical Solution of Integral Equations of the Second Kind* (Cambridge, 1997), ch. 3-4
(Nyström methods) and Delves & Mohamed, *Computational Methods for Integral Equations* (Cambridge, 1985), ch. 6
(product integration and the cell-integral diagonal).

functions.name: trapezoid_weights
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Composite-trapezoid weights on sorted nodes ``x`` (N,): ``(x[i+1] - x[i-1]) / 2`` inside, half a cell at
the ends. The weights sum to ``x[-1] - x[0]``, which is also the width of each node's self cell in the sense the
diagonal replacement needs.

functions.name: nystrom_matrix
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, kernel_fn: Callable, ctx: dict[str, Any] | None = None, *, diag_fn: Callable | None = None, volterra: bool = False) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Assemble ``(A, D)`` such that ``int K(x_i, s) u(s) ds ~ (A @ u)_i + D_i u_i`` on the nodes ``x``.

``A`` has the column weights folded in and a zero diagonal; ``D`` is the self-cell contribution. The pairing
``A + diag(D)`` is the Nyström matrix, so the direct solve of ``u = f + lambda K u`` is
``np.linalg.solve(np.eye(N) - lambda * (A + np.diag(D)), f_sorted)``. Nodes are sorted internally and the
returned matrices are in that sorted order; :func:`integral_residuals` maps back.

``kernel_fn(X, S, ctx) -> (N, M)`` takes the sorted nodes as two arrays of shape ``(N, 1)`` and ``(M, 1)`` and
must be finite on the diagonal (return 0 there when the singular part is carried by ``diag_fn``). ``diag_fn
(width, ctx) -> (N,)`` returns the analytic self-cell integral of the singular part for cell widths ``width``.

functions.name: constant_kernel
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray, ctx: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``K = 1``: the bounded kernel of the textbook Fredholm examples. Finite on the diagonal, so no ``diag_fn``.

functions.name: product_kernel
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray, ctx: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``K(x, s) = x s``: the degenerate (rank-one) kernel, finite on the diagonal, so no ``diag_fn``.

functions.name: log_kernel
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray, ctx: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``ln|x - s|`` with a zero diagonal: the singular part is carried by :func:`log_diag`.

functions.name: log_diag
functions.sig: (width: np.ndarray, ctx: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``int_{-w/2}^{w/2} ln|s| ds = w (ln(w/2) - 1)``: the exact self-cell integral of :func:`log_kernel`.

functions.name: helmholtz2_kernel
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray, ctx: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``(j/4) H_0^(2)(k r)`` with a zero diagonal: the two-dimensional Helmholtz kernel under ``exp(+j omega t)``
(outgoing waves are ``H_0^(2)``, the convention of ``pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics``). Reads ``k`` from
``ctx``; complex, so the equation needs two fields.

functions.name: helmholtz2_diag
functions.sig: (width: np.ndarray, ctx: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Self-cell integral of :func:`helmholtz2_kernel` from the small-argument expansion
``H_0^(2)(z) ~ 1 - (2j/pi)(ln(z/2) + gamma)``::

    int_{-w/2}^{w/2} (j/4) H_0^(2)(k|s|) ds ~ w [ j/4 + (ln(k w / 4) + gamma - 1) / (2 pi) ]

The expansion is the ``k w << 1`` limit, which is the regime where the kernel is resolvable at all; the diagonal
is the only place it is used and the trapezoid carries the rest. Raises when ``k w >= 1``.

functions.name: integral_residuals
functions.sig: (kind: str, *, fields: dict[str, torch.Tensor], xcol: torch.Tensor, coords: Sequence[str], params: dict[str, Any], ctx: dict[str, Any], model: Callable, field_names: Sequence[str], split_fields: Callable) -> list[torch.Tensor]
functions.doc:
Residuals of a second-kind integral equation at the collocation points, in the compiler's ``(N, 1)`` form.

``params``: ``lambda`` (alias ``lam``, default 1), and ``singular`` -- set it to ``True`` to demand a ``diag_fn``
and refuse to run without one, since a singular kernel silently integrated through its diagonal produces
plausible garbage. ``ctx`` (or the callables in ``params``): ``kernel_fn``, the optional ``diag_fn``, and
``f_fn`` (alias ``source_fn``) for the free term, which defaults to zero.

classes.name: AdaptiveWeights
classes.doc:
Self-normalising weights for a multi-term PINN loss, keyed by
arbitrary term names (unlike :class:`LossWeights`'s four fixed
``w_pde``/``w_bc``/``w_ic``/``w_data`` fields, which ``compile_problem``
reads directly by attribute and is unaffected by this addition -- this
class is a standalone utility for training loops that manage their own
named loss-term dict, e.g. from ``compile_problem``'s own per-term
output keys (``"pde"``, ``"bc_<name>"``, ``"ic_<name>"``,
``"data_<name>"``) or from a hand-rolled residual/loss set entirely).

Tracks a lagged exponential moving average of each term's *raw* loss
value and rescales that term's configured base weight *relative to the
currently hardest (largest-EMA) term*: every term's multiplier is
``max_j(ema_j) / (ema_i + eps)``, clamped to ``[1, max_ratio]``.
"Lagged" matters -- the multiplier used for step *n* is computed from
the EMA *before* step *n*'s losses are folded in via :meth:`update`, so
the weights are plain Python floats with no gradient path of their own.

Why relative-to-hardest and not a plain per-term ``base / (ema + eps)``
inverse magnitude (a natural first attempt): a PDE with a trivial exact
solution is a real trap for the naive version. Incompressible
Navier-Stokes with no-slip walls, for instance, has ``U ≡ 0, p ≡ const``
as an exact solution of the momentum/continuity residual and the wall
BC simultaneously -- if the network drifts anywhere near that
degenerate field, a physics/BC term's EMA collapses toward zero, its
*per-term* inverse weight blows up to the configured cap, and any
data-fit term is left floating down near the cap's reciprocal. The
optimiser is then explicitly rewarded for finishing the collapse to the
trivial solution and ignoring the data entirely (observed in practice:
a per-term-inverse-weighted run on exactly this problem converged to a
uniformly-zero velocity field instead of the real, highly
non-uniform mean profile). Rescaling relative to the *hardest* term
instead of each term's own history removes the failure mode: a term's
multiplier can only ever be pulled *up* to match the hardest term,
never pulled *down* below its base weight, so no term can be abandoned
just because it became easy (possibly trivially, possibly
degenerately) to satisfy.

Examples
--------
>>> aw = AdaptiveWeights(base_weights={"pde": 1.0, "bc": 10.0, "data": 5.0})
>>> for step in range(n_steps):
...     w = aw.current()
...     loss = sum(w[k] * raw_losses[k] for k in raw_losses)
...     loss.backward(); opt.step()
...     aw.update({k: float(v.item()) for k, v in raw_losses.items()})

Effective weights for *this* step, from the EMA state left by

methods.doc:

the *next* step's :meth:`current`.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.domino
children.doc:
DoMINO: Domain Decomposition for Physics-Informed Neural Networks.

Splits a large domain into overlapping subdomains, trains a separate PINN per
subdomain, and enforces interface continuity conditions.

Reference: Li et al. 2020 "D3M: A Deep Domain Decomposition Method for PDE"

classes.name: Subdomain
classes.sig: (bounds: list[tuple[float, float]], overlap: float = 0.1)
classes.doc:
Rectangular subdomain with overlap.

Parameters
----------
bounds : list of (lo, hi) tuples, one per spatial dimension.
overlap : fractional overlap added on each side of the subdomain boundary.
          E.g. overlap=0.1 means 10 % of each axis width is added on each
          side to form the extended/interface region.

methods.name: contains
methods.doc: Boolean mask: which rows of x (shape [N, D]) are in this subdomain.

methods.name: contains_strict
methods.doc: Boolean mask using the *non-extended* (strict) bounds.

methods.name: is_interface
methods.doc: Points that lie inside the overlap/interface strip.

classes.name: SubdomainPINN
classes.sig: (subdomain: Subdomain, model: nn.Module)
classes.doc:
PINN for a single subdomain.

Parameters
----------
subdomain : Subdomain
model     : any nn.Module that maps (N, D) inputs → (N, out_dim) outputs.

classes.name: DoMINO
classes.sig: (subdomains: list[Subdomain], model_factory: Callable[[], nn.Module], interface_weight: float = 10.0)
classes.doc:
Domain-decomposition PINN trainer.

Each subdomain gets its own network (created by ``model_factory``).
In the overlap region the outputs are combined using a distance-weighted
average (soft-partition-of-unity blending).

Usage
-----
::

    subdomains = DoMINO.partition(bounds=[(0,1),(0,1)], n_splits=(2,2), overlap=0.1)
    domino = DoMINO(subdomains, model_factory=lambda: MLP(2, 1, 64, 4))
    history = domino.train(residual_fn, bc_fn, n_epochs=5000)

Parameters
----------
subdomains        : list of Subdomain instances.
model_factory     : zero-argument callable that returns a fresh nn.Module.
interface_weight  : weight multiplier applied to the interface continuity loss.

methods.name: partition
methods.sig: (bounds: list[tuple[float, float]], n_splits: tuple[int, ...], overlap: float = 0.1) -> list[Subdomain]
methods.doc: Create a regular grid of overlapping subdomains.

methods.name: forward
methods.doc: Evaluate PINN across all subdomains (weighted average in overlap).

methods.name: interface_loss
methods.doc: Continuity loss at subdomain interfaces.

classes.name: PINNProblemSpec
classes.doc:
A model-agnostic PINN specification.

pde_residuals: list of equations that should be ~0 on collocation points
conditions: list of dicts like:
  {
    "name": "ic_u",
    "equation": "u - sin(pi*x)",
    "weight": 1.0
  }
independent_vars: e.g. ["t","x"] or ["t","lat","lon","lev"]
dependent_vars: e.g. ["u"] or ["T","U","V"]
inverse_params: optional list of trainable scalars used in equations
loss_weights: weights for loss buckets: {"pde":1.0,"conditions":1.0,"data":1.0}
constants: named numbers used in equations, e.g. {"T0": 0.25}. A condition dict may
  also carry its own "constants" (they override these for that condition). A bare name
  that is declared nowhere (e.g. "T(t) - T0" with no T0 anywhere) is accepted as a
  *runtime constant*: listed in ``PINNFactory.runtime_constants`` and read at loss time
  from the condition entry's "constants", then ``batch["constants"]``.
exogenous: providers for known input signals written as functions of the independent
  variables, e.g. "a*S(t) - b*(T(t) - Tamb(t))" with {"S": ..., "Tamb": ...}. A provider
  is a callable f(*inputs) -> Tensor (see ``signals.TabulatedSignal``) or a Tensor with one
  row per collocation point. Undeclared functions are detected automatically from the
  equations; ``PINNFactory.exogenous_vars`` lists them. Providers can also be passed per
  batch (``batch["exogenous"]``) and per condition.

classes.name: PINNFactory
classes.sig: (spec: PINNProblemSpec)
classes.doc:
Factory that compiles symbolic equations (SymPy) into torch-callable residuals,
then creates a unified loss function.

Data contract for the generated loss(model, batch):
  batch can contain:
    - "collocation": Tuple[Tensor,...]  # for PDE residuals
    - "conditions": List[Tuple[Tensor,...]]  # one per condition equation (same length as spec.conditions)
    - "data": (Tuple[Tensor,...], Tensor)  # supervised data pairs
    - "exogenous": {name: Tensor | callable}  # optional; known signals such as S(t), Tamb(t)
    - "constants": {name: float | Tensor}  # optional; values of runtime constants (e.g. T0)
  A condition entry may also be a dict {"inputs": (Tensor, ...), "exogenous": {...}}.
  Exogenous providers are looked up in: the condition entry, then batch["exogenous"],
  then spec.exogenous. Tensors must have one row per point of that bucket; callables
  are evaluated on the bucket's inputs, so one TabulatedSignal serves every bucket.

methods.name: generate_loss_function
methods.sig: () -> Callable[[PINN, dict[str, Any]], tuple[Tensor, dict[str, float]]]
methods.doc:
Returns (loss_fn) where:
  loss_fn(model, batch) -> (total_loss, components_dict)

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.factory.signals
children.doc:
Exogenous signal providers for ``PINNFactory``: known inputs such as sensor data or forcing.

An equation like ``Derivative(T(t), t) - a*S(t) + b*(T(t) - Tamb(t))`` uses ``S`` and ``Tamb``
as *known* functions of time (weather data), not as network outputs. The factory needs their
values at whatever points it evaluates the residual (collocation, conditions, data). A provider
is either a tensor with one row per point of that batch, or a callable ``f(*inputs) -> Tensor``
that can be evaluated anywhere -- ``TabulatedSignal`` is the usual choice for sampled data.

classes.name: TabulatedSignal
classes.sig: (x: ArrayLike, values: ArrayLike, *, input_index: int = 0, extrapolate: str = 'clamp')
classes.doc:
Piecewise-linear interpolation of a sampled signal, evaluated in torch.

Parameters
----------
x : sample locations (strictly increasing) along ``input_index`` of the model inputs.
values : sample values, same length as ``x``.
input_index : which model input the signal depends on (0 = first independent variable).
extrapolate : ``"clamp"`` (hold the end values, default) or ``"linear"``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.factory.sympy_backend
children.doc:
SymPy-based compiler for symbolic equations to torch-callable lambdas.

Design note — two SymPy→PyTorch compilation paths exist in this codebase:

* **This module** (``SympyTorchCompiler``): uses ``sympy.lambdify`` to emit a
  fast Python lambda.  Gradients do *not* flow through the symbolic evaluation
  itself; the lambdified call is opaque to autograd.  Suitable when PDE losses
  are evaluated at fixed collocation points and runtime speed is the priority.

* ``pinneapple_symbolic.SymbolicPDE``: walks the expression tree with
  ``torch.autograd.grad``, so gradients *do* flow through the evaluation.
  Use that path when you need the symbolic expression to participate in the
  autograd graph (e.g. differentiating the residual w.r.t. model weights for
  meta-learning, or computing higher-order cross derivatives).

classes.name: CompiledEquation
classes.doc:
A compiled symbolic equation.

- expr: SymPy expression
- derivatives: set of SymPy Derivative atoms appearing in expr
- call: torch-compatible callable from sympy.lambdify
- args_order: stable argument order for call(...)

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.stochastic
children.doc:
Latent-conditioned (stochastic) PINN training utilities.

A deterministic PINN, ``f(x) -> y``, is the wrong tool for a chaotic
system with only a handful of real observed snapshots to fit against: with
too few, decorrelated snapshots to learn genuine dynamics from, a
pointwise-MSE-trained deterministic network is pushed towards either an
over-smoothed, near-constant predictor (nothing left to distinguish
different points) or an overfit one that memorises the specific noisy
values of whatever snapshots it saw, at the cost of any coherent spatial
structure (observed in practice on a wall-bounded turbulent-channel LES
surrogate: a deterministic model trained on two real, 36-time-units-apart
instantaneous snapshots produced non-physical, spatially disconnected
low-velocity blobs scattered through the flow's core, rather than the
wall-hugging streaky structure the real LES has).

This module instead makes the model take an additional latent code ``xi``
(typically ``xi ~ N(0, I)``), turning ``f(x) -> y`` into a family
``f(x, xi) -> y`` -- a *distribution* of physically-plausible outputs at
each ``x``, trained so that:

- every ``(x, xi)`` still satisfies the governing PDE residual and any
  boundary conditions (physics must hold for *every* plausible
  realisation, not just an average one) -- pass ``xi`` straight through to
  whatever residual function you already use, since the residual only
  needs `torch.autograd.grad` w.r.t. the coordinates ``x``, never ``xi``;
- one or more *known* real observations can be anchored to a fixed
  reference code (e.g. ``xi = 0``), so the model reproduces at least the
  literal trajectories you actually have data for;
- the *ensemble* mean and covariance over many random ``xi`` draws
  (:func:`ensemble_forward`, :func:`mean_covariance_loss`) are matched
  against real time/plane-averaged statistics (a mean field and, e.g., a
  Reynolds-stress-like covariance tensor for CFD) -- i.e. the model is
  trained to match the real system's *statistics*, not to hit one noisy
  pointwise value.

``xi`` can be sampled two ways:

- **per-point i.i.d.** (:func:`sample_latent`, the default when no
  ``latent_sampler`` is given to :func:`ensemble_forward`) -- simple, but
  every point's latent code is independent, so individual generated
  realisations are spatially disconnected noise, not coherent structure
  (see below).
- **as a spatially-correlated field** (:class:`CorrelatedLatentField`) --
  draws one or more smooth 3D Gaussian random fields (per-axis anisotropic
  correlation length, periodic- or reflect-padded per axis as appropriate)
  and looks them up at query coordinates, so nearby points share
  correlated ``xi`` and a generated realisation can look like an actual
  coherent flow feature (e.g. a streak) instead of per-point noise. This
  was validated on a real wall-bounded turbulent-channel LES surrogate:
  switching from i.i.d. to a correlated field turned scattered noise into
  streamwise-elongated structure resembling the real flow's streaks (the
  correct anisotropy -- x much longer than y/z -- had to be found
  empirically; an isotropic length scale produced wrongly-oriented,
  wall-normal-elongated streaks instead).

Historical note: this per-point-only limitation used to be a "known,
documented simplification" here with no fix implemented -- :func:`
ensemble_forward`'s optional ``latent_sampler`` parameter and
:class:`CorrelatedLatentField` close that gap while staying fully
backward compatible (``latent_sampler=None`` reproduces the old
per-point-i.i.d. behaviour exactly).

classes.name: LatentConditionedModel
classes.sig: (base: nn.Module, latent_dim: int) -> None
classes.doc:
Wrap any ``model(x) -> y`` so it additionally accepts a latent code
``xi``, concatenated onto ``x`` before the wrapped model's own forward.

``latent_dim=0`` degenerates to calling the base model unchanged
(``xi`` is accepted but ignored), so wrapping is a no-op for anyone not
using the stochastic mechanism. The wrapped model's ``in_dim`` must be
``x.shape[1] + latent_dim``.

Examples
--------
>>> base = ModelRegistry.build("modified_mlp", in_dim=4+8, out_dim=4, ...)
>>> model = LatentConditionedModel(base, latent_dim=8)
>>> xi = sample_latent(x.shape[0], latent_dim=8, device=x.device)
>>> y = model(x, xi)

methods.name: forward
methods.sig: (x: torch.Tensor, xi: torch.Tensor | None = None) -> torch.Tensor

classes.name: CorrelatedLatentField
classes.sig: (bounds: dict[str, Sequence[float]], coord_order: Sequence[str], spatial_axes: Sequence[str], periodic_axes: Sequence[str], latent_dim: int, grid_res: Sequence[int] = (64, 24, 32), length_scale = 0.75)
classes.doc:
Spatially-correlated replacement for per-point :func:`sample_latent`.

Draws ``n_fields`` independent 3D Gaussian random fields (one per
latent channel, per field) by convolving white noise with a Gaussian
kernel -- circular padding along axes named in ``periodic_axes``,
reflect padding along the rest -- which is exactly the covariance-
kernel-via-convolution construction of a GRF. :meth:`lookup` then
trilinearly interpolates a drawn field at arbitrary physical query
coordinates, so every point in a batch queried against the *same*
field draw gets correlated ``xi`` -- nearby points get similar values,
so the network can learn to associate a smoothly-varying ``xi`` region
with a coherent output structure, instead of only ever seeing
per-point noise (see :func:`sample_latent`/module docstring).

``length_scale`` sets the correlation length per axis (same physical
units as ``bounds``) -- either one scalar (isotropic) or a
``{axis: value}`` dict / sequence matching ``spatial_axes`` order.
Real turbulent flow features are often strongly anisotropic (e.g. a
channel flow's streamwise streak length is roughly an order of
magnitude longer than its spanwise spacing or wall-normal extent) --
an isotropic scale gives structure the wrong shape/orientation, not
just the wrong size, so prefer per-axis values whenever known.

Parameters
----------
bounds : ``{axis: (lo, hi)}`` for every axis in ``spatial_axes``.
coord_order : full column order of query points passed to
    :meth:`lookup` (may include a time axis; only entries also present
    in ``bounds``/``spatial_axes`` are used for the lookup).
spatial_axes : the (exactly 3) spatial axis names this field spans, in
    the order its grid dimensions are laid out.
periodic_axes : subset of ``spatial_axes`` treated as periodic.
latent_dim : number of independent latent channels per field.
grid_res : coarse grid resolution per spatial axis.

methods.name: sample_field
methods.doc: Draw ``n_fields`` independent correlated fields: (n_fields, latent_dim, *grid_res).

methods.name: lookup
methods.doc:
Trilinear interpolation of ``field`` (n_fields, latent_dim, *grid_res)
at physical query points ``x`` (N, len(coord_order)). Returns
(N, n_fields, latent_dim).

methods.name: sample_xi
methods.doc:
Draw fresh field(s) and return ``xi`` at every point in ``x``:
(N, n_samples, latent_dim). One call = one set of coherent
realisation(s) shared across all points in ``x``.

functions.name: sample_latent
functions.sig: (n: int, latent_dim: int, device = None, dtype = torch.float32) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc: ``N(0, I)`` latent codes, shape ``(n, latent_dim)``.

functions.name: ensemble_forward
functions.sig: (model, x: torch.Tensor, latent_dim: int, n_samples: int, latent_sampler: CorrelatedLatentField | None = None) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Evaluate ``n_samples`` latent draws at every point in ``x`` (N, D) in
a single batched forward pass. Returns ``(N, n_samples, out_dim)``.

``latent_sampler=None`` (default): each point gets its own independent
set of draws -- see the module docstring for why that is a real
limitation for generating individually-coherent realisations (the
ensemble mean/covariance losses are unaffected either way, since they
are simple Monte Carlo point statistics regardless of spatial
correlation).

``latent_sampler`` given (a :class:`CorrelatedLatentField`): the
``n_samples`` draws are ``n_samples`` independent *coherent fields*,
each queried at every point in ``x`` -- nearby points share correlated
``xi`` within one realisation.

functions.name: mean_covariance_loss
functions.sig: (model, x: torch.Tensor, latent_dim: int, n_samples: int, mean_target: torch.Tensor, cov_target: torch.Tensor | None = None, cov_index_pairs: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] | None = None, field_slice: slice = slice(None), latent_sampler: CorrelatedLatentField | None = None, ens: torch.Tensor | None = None) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]
functions.doc:
Monte-Carlo mean and (optionally) covariance of the model's own
latent ensemble at ``x``, matched (MSE) against externally supplied
real statistics.

Parameters
----------
mean_target : (N, k) real time/plane-averaged field, ``k`` = the
    number of output components selected by ``field_slice``.
cov_target : (N, len(cov_index_pairs)) optional real covariance-like
    target -- e.g. a Reynolds-stress tensor's independent components.
cov_index_pairs : which (component_i, component_j) pairs of the
    selected fields to compute covariance for, in the same order as
    ``cov_target``'s columns. Defaults to every unique pair
    (upper-triangular, including the diagonal / variances) if
    ``cov_target`` is given but this is not.
field_slice : which output columns of the model count as "the field"
    being matched (e.g. ``slice(0, 3)`` for a 3-component velocity out
    of a ``(u, v, w, p)`` output) -- everything else is still computed
    by the ensemble forward pass but ignored by this loss.
latent_sampler : optional :class:`CorrelatedLatentField` -- forwarded
    to :func:`ensemble_forward` unchanged; ``None`` (default) keeps the
    original per-point-i.i.d. ensemble. Ignored if ``ens`` is given.
ens : optional pre-computed ``(N, n_samples, out_dim)`` ensemble (from
    a prior :func:`ensemble_forward` call) -- skips this function's own
    internal ``ensemble_forward`` call when given. Useful when a
    caller needs several different statistics (e.g. a velocity mean +
    covariance here, plus some other field's mean matched separately)
    from the *same* ensemble draw: calling this twice without ``ens``
    would draw two independent ensembles, which is both wasteful and
    statistically inconsistent between the two matched quantities.

Returns
-------
dict with key ``"mean"`` (always) and ``"covariance"`` (only if
``cov_target`` is given).

Examples
--------
Matching a CFD mean velocity + Reynolds-stress tensor (OpenFOAM's own
``symmTensor`` component order: xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz)::

    stats = mean_covariance_loss(
        model, x, latent_dim=8, n_samples=8,
        mean_target=u_mean,                        # (N, 3)
        cov_target=reynolds_stress,                 # (N, 6)
        cov_index_pairs=[(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,2)],
        field_slice=slice(0, 3),
    )
    loss = stats["mean"] + stats["covariance"]

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential
pinneapple_physics.potential.co2_study
children.doc:
Measured study: a potential-based surrogate against a direct multi-output surrogate on CO2 near its critical point.

Data: CoolProp's Helmholtz-energy equation of state for CO2 (HEOS backend, Span & Wagner, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data
25 (1996) 1509-1596), the same backend ``pinneapple_systems.process_components.real_gas_eos`` wraps. Six specific
properties at given ``(T, rho)``: ``p, s, u, c_v, c_p, w``.

Protocol (same for every model):

* training region ``T`` in [305, 335] K (just above ``T_c`` = 304.13 K), ``rho`` in [100, 800] kg/m3, where ``c_p``
  peaks along the Widom line; ``n_per_prop`` random points per property, each point carrying one property (mixed
  data);
* the same data, loss (:func:`~pinneapple_physics.potential.surrogate.fit`: per-property standardised squared error,
  log for the heat capacities), optimiser (Adam, cosine decay), number of steps, width and depth for every model;
* scores on a held-out grid inside the training region (``interp``) and on two extrapolation regions: hotter
  (``T`` in [335, 365] K) and denser (``rho`` in [800, 950] kg/m3); normalised RMS error per property (RMS error over
  the standard deviation of the property in the training region), the thermodynamic identities of
  :func:`~pinneapple_physics.potential.thermo.identities_T_rho` checked by
  :func:`~pinneapple_physics.potential.relations.consistency_check`, and the share of points with ``(dp/drho)_T > 0``
  and ``c_v > 0`` (thermodynamic stability);
* several seeds; intervals are 95 % Student-t intervals over seeds, and the comparison is paired by seed.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.core
children.doc:
A potential and its derivative tree.

A potential is one scalar function of its natural variables, ``Phi(x_1, ..., x_n)``. Its derivatives, organised by
order, are the tree: depth 1 gives the "forces" (entropy and pressure from a Helmholtz energy, stress from a strain
energy, momenta from a Lagrangian), depth 2 the response functions (heat capacity, compressibility, elastic tangent,
mass matrix), and so on. Every quantity of the tree comes from the same function, so the mixed partials agree and
the quantities are consistent with one another by construction.

    import torch
    from pinneapple_physics.potential import Potential, tree

    A = Potential(lambda T, V: -8.314 * T * torch.log(V) - 1.5 * 8.314 * T * torch.log(T),
                  {"T": "K", "V": "m3/mol"}, name="A", unit="J/mol",
                  names={("T",): ("S", -1, "J/(mol K)"), ("V",): ("p", -1, "Pa")})
    t = tree(A, depth=2, at={"T": 300.0, "V": 0.025})
    t["p"], t["S"], t[("T", "T")]                  # 8.314 * 300 / 0.025, ..., -1.5 * 8.314 / 300

Derivatives are taken by reverse-mode automatic differentiation in float64 (``torch.autograd``), batched over the
evaluation points. A potential written as a SymPy expression (:meth:`Potential.from_sympy`) also carries its
symbolic derivatives; :meth:`DerivativeTree.symbolic_agreement` compares the two.

Variables may be tensors (a deformation gradient ``F`` of shape ``(3, 3)``): the node ``("F",)`` then has the shape
of ``F`` and ``("F", "F")`` the shape ``(3, 3, 3, 3)``, per point.

classes.doc: A natural variable: its unit (free text, e.g. ``"K"``) and its shape per point (``()`` for a scalar).

classes.doc: The physical name of a raw derivative: ``quantity = sign * d^k Phi / dx...``, with its unit.

``fn(d, x)`` receives ``d``, a mapping from derivative keys (tuples of variable names in variable order, ``()``
for the potential itself) to tensors, and ``x``, the variables as tensors; it returns a tensor. ``depth`` is the
highest derivative order it reads.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.hyperelastic
children.doc:
Hyperelastic strain-energy potentials ``W(F)``: stress and tangent from one function.

The first Piola-Kirchhoff stress is ``P = dW/dF`` (depth 1) and the material tangent ``A_iJkL = d2W/dF_iJ dF_kL``
(depth 2, shape ``(3, 3, 3, 3)`` per point). The tangent of a potential has the major symmetry
``A_iJkL = A_kLiJ``; :func:`major_symmetry` measures it for any tangent (from a potential, a material routine or a
learned model).

Neo-Hookean (compressible, Ogden form): ``W = mu/2 (I_1 - 3) - mu ln J + lam/2 (ln J)^2``, with the closed forms
``P = mu (F - F^-T) + lam ln J F^-T`` and ``A_iJkL = mu d_ik d_JL + (mu - lam ln J) Fi_Li Fi_Jk + lam Fi_Ji Fi_Lk``
(``Fi = F^-1``); Bonet & Wood, *Nonlinear Continuum Mechanics for Finite Element Analysis*, 2nd ed. (2008), sections
6.4.3 and 6.5. At ``F = I`` the tangent is the isotropic linear-elastic one, ``mu (d_ik d_JL + d_iL d_Jk) +
lam d_iJ d_kL``.

Mooney-Rivlin (compressible, isochoric invariants): ``W = c10 (I1b - 3) + c01 (I2b - 3) + kappa/2 (J - 1)^2`` with
``I1b = J^(-2/3) I_1``, ``I2b = J^(-4/3) I_2``; small-strain shear modulus ``2 (c10 + c01)``, bulk modulus ``kappa``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.legendre
children.doc:
Legendre transforms between potentials, with a convexity check.

``legendre(Phi, swap={"x": "y"})`` replaces the natural variable ``x`` by its conjugate ``y = s dPhi/dx`` and
returns ``Psi(y, ...) = Phi - x dPhi/dx`` evaluated at the ``x`` that solves ``s dPhi/dx(x, ...) = y``:

* Helmholtz to Gibbs: ``legendre(A, swap={"V": "p"}, conjugate_sign=-1)`` gives ``G(T, p) = A + p V``;
* Lagrangian to Hamiltonian: ``legendre(L, swap={"qd": "p"}, negate=True)`` gives ``H(q, p) = p qd - L``.

The transform is one-to-one only where ``Phi`` is strictly convex (or strictly concave) in the swapped variables.
:func:`legendre` checks that on a grid (``bounds=``) and reports where it fails: for a van der Waals fluid below its
critical temperature the Helmholtz energy is not convex in ``V`` between the two spinodals, the region where the
homogeneous fluid is unstable; the report gives that interval at each temperature of the grid.

Numerically, ``x`` is found by Newton's method (bracketed when bounds are given), without a graph; then two Newton
steps are repeated inside the autodiff graph from that root. Each step doubles the order to which ``x(y, ...)`` is
exact, and ``Psi`` is stationary in ``x``, so derivatives of the transformed potential are exact to order seven at a
converged root. When the potential has a SymPy expression and ``s dPhi/dx = y`` has one solution, the symbolic
transform is used (``method="auto"``).

shape, ``indexing="ij"`` in the order of ``axes``); ``stable``: where that block is definite with the expected
sign (``expect="convex"``: positive definite).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.machines
children.doc:
Electromechanical co-energy ``W'(i, theta)`` as a potential: torque, flux linkages and inductances from one map.

At constant currents the torque on the rotor is ``T = dW'/dtheta`` and the flux linkage of phase ``k`` is
``psi_k = dW'/di_k``; the differential inductances are ``L_jk = d2W'/di_j di_k`` (symmetric by construction) and
the reciprocity ``dpsi_k/dtheta = dT/di_k`` is the Maxwell relation of the co-energy.

A finite-element solver gives the co-energy at chosen points. :func:`local_polynomial` fits a polynomial potential to
such samples (least squares in scaled variables); :func:`machine_coenergy` samples a machine of
``pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics`` (any object with ``coenergy(theta, currents)``, e.g. ``SPMMachine`` or
``IPMMachine``) around an operating point -- ``2 n + 1`` rotor angles at the operating currents, nine current
perturbations at the operating angle -- and returns the local co-energy potential. With ``n = 2`` and angles on the
moving-band grid the torque is the same fourth-order virtual-work estimate as ``machine.torque_coenergy``; the map
adds the flux linkages and inductances from the same potential. Cross terms between angle and current are not
sampled, so the map does not carry ``dpsi/dtheta``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.mechanics
children.doc:
Analytical mechanics from a Lagrangian ``L(q, qd)``.

Depth 1 of the tree gives the generalised momenta ``p_i = dL/dqd_i`` and forces ``Q_i = dL/dq_i``; depth 2 the mass
matrix ``M_ij = d2L/dqd_i dqd_j`` and the coupling ``d2L/dqd_i dq_j``. The Euler-Lagrange equations
``d/dt dL/dqd = dL/dq`` give ``M qdd = Q - (d2L/dqd dq) qd`` (:func:`accelerations`), and the Hamiltonian is the
Legendre transform ``H(q, p) = p qd - L`` (:func:`hamiltonian`), defined where ``L`` is convex in ``qd``
(positive-definite mass matrix).

:func:`double_pendulum` is the planar double pendulum of two point masses on massless rods (angles from the
downward vertical); its equations of motion in closed form are in Goldstein, Poole & Safko, *Classical Mechanics*,
3rd ed. (2002), and in most textbooks.
