children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.relations
children.doc:
Maxwell relations and consistency checks of data or models against a potential family.

A potential gives equal mixed partials, ``d2Phi/dx_i dx_j = d2Phi/dx_j dx_i``. Written with the named first
derivatives these are the Maxwell relations (``(dS/dV)_T = (dp/dT)_V`` from the Helmholtz energy), the reciprocity
of an electromechanical converter (``dpsi/dtheta = dT/di`` from the co-energy) or the symmetry of a mass matrix.
Response functions add identities between second derivatives (``c_p - c_v = T V alpha^2 / kappa_T``, the speed of
sound from ``c_v`` and the pressure derivatives).

:func:`consistency_check` evaluates such identities on anything that predicts the quantities separately: a
surrogate with one output per property, a table, or measurements on a grid. Each identity is reported with its
relative violation; a potential satisfies them all to rounding, a model fitted property by property in general does
not. Satisfying the identities is necessary for the quantities to come from one potential (and, on a simply
connected domain, sufficient for the first-derivative ones).

    from pinneapple_physics.potential import consistency_check
    rep = consistency_check(model, "helmholtz_T_rho", at={"T": T, "rho": rho})
    print(rep)                    # one line per identity: median, 95th percentile and largest relative violation

classes.name: Identity
classes.doc:
An identity ``lhs(D) = rhs(D)`` between quantities and their derivatives.

``D(q, *vars)`` is the derivative of quantity ``q`` with respect to the listed natural variables (the others
held constant); ``D.x(var)`` is the value of a variable. ``needs`` lists the quantities it reads. ``scale(D)``,
when given, is the natural magnitude the violation is measured against (for identities whose two sides can both
vanish, like ``(dc_v/dv)_T = T (d2p/dT2)_v`` for a van der Waals fluid); otherwise the typical size of the two
sides is used.

classes.name: MaxwellRelation
classes.doc: Equality of the mixed partials of a potential in ``pair``, written with its named first derivatives.

classes.name: Derivatives
classes.sig: (values: Callable[[dict], Mapping[str, np.ndarray]] | None, point: Mapping[str, np.ndarray], variables: Sequence[str], step: float = 0.0001, grid: Mapping | None = None)
classes.doc:
Derivatives of predicted quantities, by central finite differences of a callable or ``np.gradient`` on a
grid. Results are cached per (quantity, variables).

classes.name: ConsistencyReport
classes.doc: Violation of each identity: relative to the typical magnitude of its two sides.

functions.name: maxwell_relations
functions.sig: (potential: Potential) -> list[MaxwellRelation]
functions.doc:
The mixed-partial identities of ``potential`` for every pair of scalar variables, in terms of its named
first derivatives (raw derivatives where unnamed), with their engineering names where the potential gives them.

Each relation is an :class:`Identity` usable by :func:`consistency_check` on a model that predicts the first
derivatives separately.

functions.name: identities
functions.sig: (family: str) -> list[Identity]
functions.doc: The identity set of a named potential family (see :data:`FAMILIES`).

functions.name: consistency_check
functions.sig: (model, family, at: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, *, variables: Sequence[str] | None = None, tol: float = 0.001, step: float = 0.0001) -> ConsistencyReport
functions.doc:
How far ``model`` is from being generated by one potential of ``family``.

Parameters
----------
model:
    ``model(point) -> {quantity: array}`` (``point`` maps variable names to arrays); a :class:`Potential` (its
    named quantities); or grid data ``{"axes": {var: 1-D array}, "values": {quantity: grid array}}`` (then
    ``at`` is not needed and derivatives come from ``np.gradient``, second order).
family:
    a family name (:data:`FAMILIES`), a :class:`Potential` (its :func:`maxwell_relations`), or a list of
    :class:`Identity`.
at:
    evaluation points ``{var: array}`` for a callable or potential model.
tol:
    pass when the 95th percentile of the relative violation is below ``tol``.
step:
    relative finite-difference step for callables.

children.summary: Maxwell relations and consistency checks of data or models against a potential family.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.surrogate
children.doc:
Potential-based surrogates: a network learns the potential, every property is a derivative of it.

:class:`PotentialSurrogate` holds a network ``a(T, rho)`` (specific Helmholtz energy, J/kg) and predicts pressure,
entropy, internal energy, heat capacities and speed of sound from its derivative tree
(:func:`~pinneapple_physics.potential.thermo.helmholtz_T_rho`, or :func:`~.thermo.helmholtz` in ``(T, v)`` for the
convex option), so the predictions satisfy the Maxwell relation and the response identities by construction.
``convex=True`` makes the network input-convex in the specific volume (a partially input-convex network, Amos, Xu &
Kolter, ICML 2017): ``(dp/dv)_T < 0`` everywhere, the mechanical stability of a single phase.

:class:`DirectSurrogate` is the usual alternative: one network with one output per property.

Both are trained by :func:`fit` on *mixed* data -- each sample carries one property (some give ``p``, others
``c_p``, others ``w``) -- with the same loss, optimiser and number of steps, so a comparison at equal budget is one
loop over the two classes.

classes.name: MixedData
classes.doc: Samples ``(T_k, rho_k)`` each carrying one property ``prop[k]`` with value ``y[k]``.

classes.name: Scaling
classes.doc:
Centres and scales of the inputs and the per-property loss transform.

The loss compares ``(g(pred) - g(y)) / sigma`` per property, with ``g = log`` for the heat capacities (they span a
decade near the critical point) and the identity otherwise; ``sigma`` is the spread of ``g(y)`` in the training
data.

methods.name: g
methods.doc:
Loss transform: ``log`` for the heat capacities, continued linearly below ``floor`` (a tenth of the
smallest training value) so that a negative prediction is a large error with a useful gradient.

classes.name: MLP
classes.sig: (n_in: int, n_out: int, hidden: int = 32, layers: int = 3, act: str = 'tanh')
classes.doc: Fully connected network with a smooth activation (needed for second derivatives).

classes.name: PICNN
classes.sig: (n_x: int, n_y: int, hidden: int = 32, layers: int = 3)
classes.doc:
Partially input-convex network ``f(x, y)``, convex in ``y`` for every ``x``.

``z_{k+1} = softplus(W^z_k z_k + W^y_k y + U_k u_k + b_k)`` with ``W^z_k >= 0`` (softplus of free weights) and
``u_{k+1} = tanh(V_k u_k + c_k)`` the unconstrained path in ``x``; the output ``w . z_K + a(x) . y + c(x)`` with
``w >= 0``. Non-negative combinations and non-decreasing convex activations of convex functions are convex.

classes.name: PotentialSurrogate
classes.sig: (scaling: Scaling, hidden: int = 32, layers: int = 3, convex: bool = False, a_scale: float | None = None, init_scale: float = 0.01)
classes.doc:
A network for the specific Helmholtz energy; properties are derivatives of it.

``a(T, rho) = c0 + c1 (T - T0) - c2 (T ln(T/T0) - (T - T0)) + a_scale net(x)``. The first three terms are a
reference with constant heat capacity: ``c0`` and ``c1`` are the free reference of energy and entropy, ``c2`` a
constant ``c_v``; they start at the training means of ``u``, ``s`` and ``c_v`` (the counterpart of the per-output
centring of :class:`DirectSurrogate`) and are trained with the network. The network's last layer starts small
(``init_scale``), so training starts from that reference. ``a_scale`` (J/kg) defaults to ``mean(p)/mean(rho)`` of
the training data, the size of ``a`` variations that ``p = rho^2 da/drho`` needs.

``convex=False``: an :class:`MLP` of the standardised ``(T, rho)`` (tanh). ``convex=True``: a :class:`PICNN`
convex in the specific volume ``v = 1/rho``, so ``(dp/dv)_T < 0`` everywhere (mechanical stability).

methods.name: properties
methods.sig: (T: torch.Tensor, rho: torch.Tensor, create_graph: bool = False) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]
methods.doc: ``p, s, u, cv, cp, w`` (specific, SI) at ``(T, rho)`` from the depth-2 tree.

classes.name: DirectSurrogate
classes.sig: (scaling: Scaling, hidden: int = 32, layers: int = 3, props: Sequence[str] = PROPERTIES)
classes.doc: One network ``(T, rho) -> (p, s, u, cv, cp, w)``, each output scaled back from the training spread.

methods.name: properties
methods.sig: (T: torch.Tensor, rho: torch.Tensor, create_graph: bool = False) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]

functions.name: n_parameters
functions.sig: (model: nn.Module) -> int

functions.name: fit
functions.sig: (model: nn.Module, data: MixedData, *, epochs: int = 3000, lr: float = 0.003, seed: int = 0, lr_final: float = 1e-05, robust: bool = True, clip: float | None = 1.0, log_every: int = 0) -> dict
functions.doc:
Full-batch Adam with a cosine learning-rate decay from ``lr`` to ``lr_final``, the same for every model;
soft-L1 loss on the standardised errors (``robust``) and gradient-norm clipping (``clip``).
Returns ``{"loss": [...], "seconds": wall-clock, "steps": epochs, "parameters": n}``. The network's initial
weights are whatever it was built with: seed ``torch.manual_seed`` before building it.

children.summary: Potential-based surrogates: a network learns the potential, every property is a derivative of it.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.potential.thermo
children.doc:
Thermodynamic potentials: Helmholtz energy builders, closed-form equations of state and their identities.

* :func:`helmholtz` names the tree of ``A(T, V)`` (molar or specific): ``S = -dA/dT``, ``p = -dA/dV``; responses
  ``U, H, G`` (depth 1) and ``c_v, c_p, kappa_T, alpha_p, w, (dp/dT)_V, (dp/dV)_T`` (depth 2).
* :func:`helmholtz_T_rho` does the same for a specific energy ``a(T, rho)`` (the variables of most reference
  equations of state): ``p = rho^2 da/drho``, ``s = -da/dT``.
* :func:`ideal_gas`, :func:`van_der_waals`, :func:`peng_robinson`: SymPy potentials with closed-form properties
  (symbolic and autodiff trees agree).
* :func:`gibbs`: ``G(T, p)`` by Legendre transform, with ``c_p = -T d2G/dT2``, ``kappa_T``, ``alpha_p``.
* :func:`identities_T_v`, :func:`identities_T_rho`: the Maxwell relation and the response identities used by
  :func:`~pinneapple_physics.potential.relations.consistency_check` on property-by-property models.

Units are SI; molar potentials in J/mol with ``V`` in m3/mol, specific ones in J/kg with ``v`` in m3/kg and ``rho``
in kg/m3. Sources: Callen, *Thermodynamics and an Introduction to Thermostatistics*, 2nd ed. (1985), ch. 3, 5 and 7
(potentials, Maxwell relations, response functions); Peng & Robinson, Ind. Eng. Chem. Fundam. 15 (1976) 59-64.

functions.name: helmholtz
functions.sig: (fn, variables = ('T', 'V'), *, molar_mass: float = 1.0, mass: bool = False, name: str = 'A', expr = None, symbols = None) -> Potential
functions.doc:
A Helmholtz energy ``A(T, V)`` with its thermodynamic names and responses.

``fn(T=..., V=...)`` in torch (or pass a SymPy ``expr`` with ``symbols``). ``mass=True``: specific energy
(J/kg, ``v`` in m3/kg); otherwise molar, and ``molar_mass`` (kg/mol) is needed for the speed of sound.

functions.name: helmholtz_T_rho
functions.sig: (fn, *, name: str = 'a', T: str = 'T', rho: str = 'rho') -> Potential
functions.doc:
A specific Helmholtz energy ``a(T, rho)`` (J/kg) with ``p = rho^2 da/drho``, ``s = -da/dT``, ``u``, ``h``,
``c_v``, ``c_p``, ``w`` and the pressure derivatives as responses.

functions.name: ideal_gas
functions.sig: (c: float = 1.5, R: float = R_GAS, T0: float = 298.15, V0: float = 0.024789570296023, molar_mass: float = 1.0) -> Potential
functions.doc:
Ideal gas with constant ``c_v = c R`` (``c = 3/2`` monatomic): ``A = c R T (1 - ln(T/T0)) - R T ln(V/V0)``.
Closed forms: ``p = R T / V``, ``S = c R ln(T/T0) + R ln(V/V0)``, ``c_p = (c + 1) R``, ``kappa_T = 1/p``,
``alpha_p = 1/T``, ``w = sqrt((c + 1)/c R T / M)``.

functions.name: van_der_waals
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, c: float = 1.5, R: float = R_GAS, T0: float = 298.15, V0: float = 0.024789570296023, molar_mass: float = 1.0) -> Potential
functions.doc: Van der Waals fluid, ``A = A_ideal - R T ln(1 - b/V) - a/V``, so ``p = R T/(V - b) - a/V^2``.

functions.name: vdw_critical_point
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, R: float = R_GAS) -> dict[str, float]

functions.name: vdw_spinodal
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, T: float, R: float = R_GAS) -> tuple[float, float] | None
functions.doc: The two volumes where ``(dp/dV)_T = 0`` (``R T V^3 = 2 a (V - b)^2``) for ``T < T_c``; None above.

functions.name: peng_robinson_constants
functions.sig: (Tc: float, pc: float, omega: float, R: float = R_GAS) -> dict[str, float]

functions.name: peng_robinson
functions.sig: (Tc: float, pc: float, omega: float, c: float = 2.5, R: float = R_GAS, T0: float = 298.15, V0: float = 0.024789570296023, molar_mass: float = 1.0) -> Potential
functions.doc:
Peng-Robinson fluid with a constant ideal-gas ``c_v = c R``:
``A = A_ideal - R T ln(1 - b/V) - a alpha(T)/(2 sqrt2 b) ln((V + (1+sqrt2) b)/(V + (1-sqrt2) b))``,
``alpha = (1 + kappa (1 - sqrt(T/Tc)))^2``; ``p = R T/(V - b) - a alpha/(V^2 + 2 b V - b^2)``.

functions.name: gibbs
functions.sig: (A: Potential, bounds = None, guess = None, method: str = 'auto', **kw) -> LegendreResult
functions.doc:
``G(T, p) = A + p V`` by Legendre transform of a Helmholtz energy ``A(T, V)``, with ``S = -dG/dT``,
``V = dG/dp`` and responses ``cp = -T d2G/dT2``, ``kappa_T = -(d2G/dp2)/(dG/dp)``,
``alpha_p = (d2G/dTdp)/(dG/dp)``. ``bounds={"T": .., "V": ..}`` runs the convexity check in ``V``.

functions.name: identities_T_v
functions.sig: () -> list[Identity]
functions.doc: Identities between specific properties in ``(T, v)``: quantities ``p, s, u, cv, cp, w``.

functions.name: identities_T_rho
functions.sig: () -> list[Identity]
functions.doc: Identities between specific properties in ``(T, rho)``: quantities ``p, s, u, cv, cp, w``.

children.summary: Thermodynamic potentials: Helmholtz energy builders, closed-form equations of state and their identities.

children.doc:
Derivative trees from a potential (``pp.potential``): one scalar function of its natural variables generates every
property by differentiation, consistently.

* :class:`Potential`, :func:`tree` -- a potential (torch or SymPy) and its derivative tree (autodiff, plus symbolic
  where the potential is a SymPy expression);
* :func:`legendre` -- transforms between potentials with a convexity check (:func:`convexity`);
* :func:`maxwell_relations`, :func:`consistency_check` -- the mixed-partial identities, and how far data or a
  property-by-property model is from one potential;
* domain adapters: :mod:`.thermo` (Helmholtz / Gibbs, ideal gas, van der Waals, Peng-Robinson), :mod:`.hyperelastic`
  (Neo-Hookean), :mod:`.mechanics` (Lagrangian, double pendulum), :mod:`.machines` (co-energy of an electric machine
  from FEA samples).

Guide: ``docs/guides/derivative_trees.md``.
children.summary: Derivative trees from a potential (pp.potential): one scalar function of its natural variables generates every property by differentiation, consistently.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.pretrained
children.doc:
Bring your own foundation model: wrap a pre-trained model as an ``Expert`` of :class:`PhysicsEnsemble` and let the
same residual, measurement and horizon checks decide when to trust it.

Nobody will train a better global model than the large pre-trained ones; the value is in knowing **when** to trust
them and **where** they leave their domain. This module puts one next to the models trained here:

* :data:`REGISTRY` knows the open models worth wrapping — the forecasts published in WeatherBench2 (IFS HRES,
  Pangu-Weather, GraphCast, NeuralGCM), Prithvi for satellite imagery, SAM 2 and Depth-Anything for vision — with
  the source, the grid and variables each was trained on, and the **licence**, with the place and date it was read
  (``Licence.verified``) or an explicit "not stated upstream" (``NOASSERTION``);
* **adapters** load the weights and map the query to the model's input and back to the common output:
  :class:`WeatherBench2Adapter` (the published archive), :class:`TorchCheckpointAdapter` (a checkpoint of a network
  trained here or elsewhere), :class:`ArrayArchiveAdapter` (a ``.npz`` of fields: the offline path) and
  :class:`HuggingFaceAdapter` (weights from the Hub). An adapter that cannot get its weights raises
  :class:`PretrainedUnavailable` saying what is missing and how to point it at a local copy: it never silently
  pretends to have run, and :class:`PhysicsEnsemble` then counts that expert as failed for the case;
* the **cost estimate** per call (seconds, the unit ``cost_weight`` uses) comes from the adapter's payload and
  latency or from a per-step time measured on the checkpoint, and the provenance says which of the two it was;
* :func:`from_pretrained_expert` returns an :class:`~pinneapple_physics.ensemble.Expert` whose ``provenance``
  carries the model, the licence and the cost method, and :func:`licence_report` collects them for a whole ensemble.

Weather queries are ``{"i0": <index into the Era5Store>, "steps": int, "variable": "z500"}`` and the prediction is
``(steps + 1, lat, lon)`` in physical units — exactly what :mod:`pinneapple_physics.weather.evaluate` scores, so an
expert built here can be compared case by case with the published skill curves. The physics checks that say where
each model leaves its domain are in :mod:`pinneapple_physics.domain_checks`.

classes.name: PretrainedUnavailable
classes.doc:
The model could not be loaded (no weights, no network, no optional dependency). The message says what is
missing and how to point the adapter at a local copy; nothing is guessed in its place.

classes.name: UnknownPretrainedModel
classes.doc: The name is not in :data:`REGISTRY` and the caller gave no licence record for it.

classes.name: LicenceError
classes.doc: The licence is missing, or it does not allow the use the caller declared.

classes.name: Licence
classes.doc:
What the model's licence allows, with the evidence: ``verified`` says where and when it was read
(``"2026-11-26: huggingface.co/api/models/<id>, cardData.license"``), and is empty when the upstream states
nothing — in that case ``spdx`` is ``"NOASSERTION"`` and the record says so instead of guessing.

classes.name: PretrainedModel
classes.doc:
A model this repository knows how to wrap: where the weights are, what they were trained on (its envelope),
what it costs and what its licence allows.

classes.name: Adapter
classes.doc:
Loads a pre-trained model and maps a query to its input and its output back to the common shape.

``predict(query)`` returns the prediction in the same shape and units as the other experts of the ensemble.
``cost(query)`` returns the estimated cost of that call in **seconds** (the unit the ensemble's ``cost_weight``
expects), and ``cost_method`` says how it was obtained. ``open()`` loads the weights and raises
:class:`PretrainedUnavailable` with a message that says what is missing.

methods.name: cost
methods.doc: Estimated seconds for one call (a declared constant when the adapter cannot do better).

classes.name: WeatherBench2Adapter
classes.sig: (store: Any, name: str, forecast: Callable | None = None, latency_s: float = NET_LATENCY_S, throughput_mb_s: float = NET_MB_S)
classes.doc:
The forecasts published in WeatherBench2 (IFS HRES, Pangu-Weather, Keisler, NeuralGCM) as one expert, read
through :class:`pinneapple_physics.weather.evaluate.PublishedForecasts` (the same loader the skill curves use).

``forecast`` injects the source instead of opening the archive (a test, or a local mirror with the same
``fn(i0, steps) -> (steps + 1, channel, lat, lon)`` contract); without it the archive is opened on first use and
a missing one is reported with the reason :class:`PublishedForecasts` recorded.

methods.name: cost
methods.doc:
Latency plus payload: one field per lead and per channel the archive provides (the request fetches the
whole set, so asking one variable does not make it cheaper).

classes.name: TorchCheckpointAdapter
classes.sig: (store: Any, checkpoint: str, name: str = 'pinneapple-weather', per_step_seconds: float | None = None, weights: Callable | None = None)
classes.doc:
A ``torch.nn.Module`` checkpoint with the arithmetic of :mod:`pinneapple_physics.weather.train`
(:class:`~pinneapple_physics.weather.train.Forecaster`): the network trained here, or any checkpoint saved with
the same ``{"state_dict", "config"}`` layout. The prediction is rolled out autoregressively from the two states
before ``i0`` and de-normalised, so it comes out in the same units as the published forecasts.

``per_step_seconds``: measured seconds per 6-hour step (the cost estimate); ``None`` uses the declared default
and refines it with every call, which ``cost_method`` reports.

classes.name: ArrayArchiveAdapter
classes.sig: (path: str, store: Any = None, name: str = '')
classes.doc:
A local ``.npz`` archive of fields laid out like a published forecast: ``fields`` (n_init, steps + 1,
channel, lat, lon) in physical units, ``times`` (datetime64 of the initialisations) and ``channels`` (str).

This is the offline path: a subset of WeatherBench2 saved once (or a model's output), scored with the same code
and the same checks as the archive it came from, on a machine with no network.

methods.name: who
methods.doc: How this adapter names itself in a message: its own name when the caller gave one, else the archive's.

methods.name: save
methods.sig: (path: str, fields: np.ndarray, times: np.ndarray, channels: list[str]) -> str
methods.doc: Write the archive an :class:`ArrayArchiveAdapter` reads (``fields`` in physical units).

classes.name: HuggingFaceAdapter
classes.sig: (repo_id: str, name: str = '', to_input: Callable | None = None, from_output: Callable | None = None, family: str = 'vision', local_path: str | None = None, loader: Callable | None = None, cost_s: float = 0.1)
classes.doc:
Weights from the Hugging Face Hub (Prithvi, SAM 2, Depth-Anything...): ``to_input(query)`` builds the model
input, ``from_output(out, query)`` maps it back to the common shape, and ``predict`` runs under ``no_grad``.

The model is loaded with ``transformers`` (or ``timm`` for Prithvi's ViT backbone) on first use.
``local_path`` skips the Hub entirely: the only way to run without network, and the reason the failure message
names it. A missing package, a gated repository or no network all raise :class:`PretrainedUnavailable` with the
specific cause: an adapter that cannot load never returns a prediction.

functions.name: register
functions.sig: (model: PretrainedModel) -> PretrainedModel
functions.doc: Add or replace an entry of :data:`REGISTRY` (a new pre-trained model, or a local mirror of a known one).

functions.name: spec
functions.sig: (name: str) -> PretrainedModel

functions.name: known_models
functions.sig: (family: str | None = None) -> list[str]

functions.name: from_pretrained_expert
functions.sig: (name: str, adapter: Adapter | None = None, *, licence: Licence | None = None, cost: float | Callable | None = None, kind: str = '', commercial: bool = False, require_verified: bool = False, lazy: bool = False) -> Expert
functions.doc:
Wrap a pre-trained model as an :class:`~pinneapple_physics.ensemble.Expert`, with its licence in the provenance.

``name`` is a key of :data:`REGISTRY` (its licence and envelope are picked up from there) or any name given
together with ``licence`` — the way to wrap a model this repository does not know without losing the record.
``adapter`` does the loading and the mapping; without one the expert is built for a model whose prediction is the
query itself mapped by an adapter bound later (not useful on its own, so the common case gives one).

``commercial``: the caller declares a commercial use, and a licence that forbids it raises :class:`LicenceError`
instead of being ignored; ``require_verified`` does the same for a licence nobody read at the source
(``NOASSERTION``). ``cost`` overrides the adapter's estimate; ``lazy`` defers :meth:`Adapter.open` to the first
prediction, so building an ensemble does not download anything.

The expert is named after the adapter when the adapter was given a name of its own, and after ``name`` -- the
model -- when it was not: the archive adapters keep an empty name by default, so wrapping one for
``"pangu-weather"`` puts the *model* in the ensemble and in :func:`licence_report`, while
``HuggingFaceAdapter(..., name="depth")`` puts the adapter's label there. Both records stay in the provenance.

functions.name: provenance_of
functions.sig: (expert: Expert) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: The provenance record of one expert (empty for an expert that declares none).

functions.name: licence_report
functions.sig: (expert_or_ensemble: Any) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``{expert: licence record}`` plus the two lists a deployment asks about: the experts whose licence nobody read
at the source (``unverified``) and those that forbid commercial use (``non_commercial``).

children.summary: Bring your own foundation model: wrap a pre-trained model as an Expert of PhysicsEnsemble and let the same residual, measurement and horizon checks decide when to trust it.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.reactors
pinneapple_physics.reactors.design
children.doc:
Closed-loop reactor design: the reactor model, a learned model only when it pays off, optimisation, and the optimum
re-verified with the model (#1179).

1. **Measure** what one solve of the reactor model costs.
2. **Ask** :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.architecture_recommendation.recommend_architecture` whether a
   surrogate pays off for the evaluations the optimiser will make (``none`` when the model is cheap enough; a
   Gaussian process for a few scalar outputs otherwise), with the checks the chosen model must pass.
3. **Optimise** the design variables (volume, coolant temperature, heat-transfer coefficient, inlet temperature) for
   the smallest volume subject to the conversion, selectivity and hot-spot limits, with differential evolution
   on the model directly or on the surrogate. With a surrogate, the design is re-solved by the model; while it
   misses a limit there, the solve joins the training set and the loop repeats (active learning).
4. **Verify** the final design with the model: the limits, the integration re-run ten times tighter, the Levenspiel
   area against the volume (PFR), the element balance through the stoichiometry (the change of the flows lies in
   the span of the reactions), and safety: Semenov's number and the parametric-sensitivity margin of a cooled PFR.

Every number in the result is computed by the run; the surrogate never grades itself.

functions.name: evaluate
functions.sig: (spec: ReactorSpec, x: dict[str, float], *, rtol: float = 1e-08) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: The reactor model at design ``x``: conversion, selectivity and yield, peak temperature, outlet.

functions.name: design_reactor
functions.sig: (spec: ReactorSpec, *, n_doe: int = 40, maxiter: int = 60, popsize: int = 12, seed: int = 0, force_surrogate: bool = False, active_rounds: int = 6, sensitivity: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Run the closed loop and return a JSON-ready record (see the module docstring).

functions.name: to_json
functions.sig: (record: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]

children.summary: Closed-loop reactor design: the reactor model, a learned model only when it pays off, optimisation, and the optimum re-verified with the model (#1179).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.reactors.kinetics
children.doc:
Reaction networks: stoichiometry, Arrhenius power-law rates, heats of reaction with their temperature dependence.

A :class:`Reaction` has stoichiometric coefficients (negative for reactants), a rate

    r = A exp(-Ea / (R T)) prod_i c_i ** n_i          [mol/(m^3 s) of extent, per reactor volume]

on a concentration basis (``c_i`` in mol/m^3) or a partial-pressure basis (``c_i`` replaced by ``p_i`` in Pa), and a
heat of reaction ``dH`` [J/mol of extent] at ``T_ref`` (default 298.15 K). With constant species heat capacities the heat of reaction
at ``T`` is ``dH + dcp (T - T_ref)`` with ``dcp = sum_i nu_i cp_i`` (Kirchhoff's law), so the energy balances that
use it are exact for constant ``cp``, not the ``dcp = 0`` shortcut.

A rate on a catalyst-mass basis (mol/(kg s)) enters as ``A * rho_bed`` (the bulk density of the bed).

methods.doc: Stoichiometric matrix, (species, reactions).

methods.name: rates
methods.sig: (c: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray, T: float) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Extent rates of every reaction, mol/(m^3 s), from concentrations (mol/m^3) and partial pressures (Pa).

methods.name: dH_at
methods.doc: Heats of reaction at ``T`` (Kirchhoff, constant cp), J/mol of extent.

classes.doc:
Molar flows (mol/s) at temperature ``T`` (K). A liquid keeps its volumetric flow ``v`` (m^3/s); a gas is ideal
at pressure ``P`` (Pa), so its concentrations follow the local temperature, pressure and total molar flow.

Conversion of an isothermal plug-flow reactor with a first-order Arrhenius reaction,
``X = 1 - exp(-A exp(-Ea / (R T)) tau)`` (Levenspiel, 3rd ed., eq. 5.17 with k(T) of Arrhenius): ``T`` in K,
``tau`` residence time in s, ``A`` in 1/s, ``Ea`` in J/mol.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.reactors.models
children.doc:
Steady plug-flow (PFR, packed bed) and stirred-tank (CSTR) reactors with mole, energy and momentum balances.

PFR (Fogler, *Elements of Chemical Reaction Engineering*, 5th ed., ch. 11-12), along the reactor volume ``V``:

    dF_i/dV = sum_j nu_ij r_j
    dT/dV   = [Ua (Tc - T) + sum_j r_j (-dH_j(T))] / sum_i F_i cp_i
    dP/dV   = -(G / (rho Dp)) (1 - phi) / phi^3 [150 (1 - phi) mu / Dp + 1.75 G] / Ac      (Ergun, packed bed only)

``Ua`` is the heat-transfer coefficient times the wall area per reactor volume (4 U / D for a tube), ``Tc`` the
coolant temperature (constant: a boiling or well-mixed coolant). ``rho`` is the local gas density from the ideal
gas law, so the Ergun term follows the pressure, the temperature and the molar flow.

CSTR, with the volume ``V`` and the total heat-removal ``UA``:

    F_i0 - F_i + V sum_j nu_ij r_j = 0
    sum_i F_i0 cp_i (T0 - T) + UA (Tc - T) + V sum_j r_j (-dH_j(T)) = 0

Every steady state is found (an exothermic CSTR can have three): at each temperature the mole balances are solved,
which gives the heat generated ``G(T)`` and removed ``R(T)`` (van Heerden's construction); the steady states are the
roots of ``G - R``, refined by Brent's method. A state is stable only if ``dR/dT > dG/dT`` there (the slope
condition, necessary for stability). :func:`cstr_startup` integrates the transient from a reactor full of feed to
say which state a start-up reaches (liquid phase).

A liquid keeps its volumetric flow (its density is taken as constant along the reactor: state it when it is not).

classes.name: Cooling
classes.doc:
Heat removal: ``Ua`` per reactor volume (W/(m^3 K), a PFR) or ``UA`` in total (W/K, a CSTR), coolant at
``Tc``. ``Ua = UA = 0`` is adiabatic.

classes.name: Bed
classes.doc:
A packed bed (Ergun pressure drop): tube ``diameter`` (m), particle diameter ``particle`` (m), ``voidage``
(-), gas viscosity ``mu`` (Pa s). Needs the species' molar masses in the network.

classes.name: Profile
classes.doc: A PFR solution along the volume: flows ``F`` (n, species), ``T``, ``P``, and the rates at each point.

CSTRs in series: each tank's outlet feeds the next; per tank, every steady state and the one a start-up from

children.name: pinneapple_physics.reactors.presets
children.doc:
Two reactors from the textbooks, converted to SI, as starting points (replace the kinetics with your own measured
ones; every value says where it comes from).

* :func:`propylene_glycol_cstr`: hydrolysis of propylene oxide to propylene glycol in a cooled CSTR, water in excess
  and methanol as an inert (Fogler, *Elements of Chemical Reaction Engineering*, 5th ed., Examples 12-3 and 12-4;
  kinetics of Furusawa, Nishimura & Miyauchi, *J. Chem. Eng. Data* 14 (1969) 211). Liquid phase, first order in the
  oxide. It has several steady states, the case for the CSTR's multiplicity and start-up.
* :func:`phthalic_anhydride_bed`: partial oxidation of o-xylene to phthalic anhydride in a cooled multitubular
  packed bed, the classical parametric-sensitivity case (Froment & Bischoff, *Chemical Reactor Analysis and Design*,
  2nd ed., Example 11.7.A.1; Froment, *Ind. Eng. Chem.* 59 (1967) 18). The rate is written with both partial
  pressures (not pseudo-first-order: the oxygen consumed is followed); the Ergun pressure drop is added when the
  catalyst's particle size and voidage are given.

functions.name: propylene_glycol_cstr
functions.sig: () -> dict
functions.doc: ``{"network", "feed", "V", "cooling", "key", "desired", "source"}`` in SI.

functions.sig: (p_xylene_atm: float = 0.011, T0: float = 625.0, bed: Bed | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
One tube of the bed: ``{"network", "feed", "V", "cooling", "bed", "key", "desired", "source", "assumptions"}``
in SI. The example has no pressure drop: ``bed=None`` keeps it so and says so; pass a :class:`Bed` with the
catalyst's particle size and voidage to add the Ergun term.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.reactors.sizing
children.doc:
Sizing and safety of a reactor: the volume for a conversion, the Levenspiel plot, yield and selectivity, the
number of tanks in series, the adiabatic temperature rise, Semenov's runaway number and the parametric sensitivity
of a cooled PFR.

* **Volume for a conversion**: a PFR is integrated until the key species reaches it (an event of the integration,
  not a search); a CSTR's volume is found by Brent's method on the stable steady state a start-up reaches.
* **Levenspiel plot**: ``F_A0 / (-r_A)`` against ``X`` along the PFR; its area is the PFR volume and the rectangle at
  the outlet the CSTR volume (Levenspiel, *Chemical Reaction Engineering*, 3rd ed., ch. 5).
* **Yield and selectivity** of a desired product ``D`` from the key reactant ``A``: ``Y = (F_D - F_D0) / F_A0`` and
  ``S = (F_D - F_D0) / (F_A0 - F_A)`` (Fogler, 5th ed., sec. 8.1).
* **Adiabatic rise** ``dT_ad = sum_j (-dH_j) xi_j / sum_i F_i0 cp_i`` for full conversion of the key reactant by
  each reaction.
* **Semenov number** of a cooled reactor at its inlet: ``psi = (-dH) r(c0, Tc) Ea / (Ua R Tc^2)``; a zeroth-order
  exothermic reaction runs away when ``psi > 1/e`` (Semenov 1928). For reactions of positive order it is a
  conservative bound (consumption of the reactant helps).
* **Parametric sensitivity** (Morbidelli & Varma, *AIChE J.* 34 (1988) 1863-1877): the normalized sensitivity of the
  hot spot to the coolant temperature, ``s = (Tc / T_max) dT_max/dTc``; the runaway boundary is the coolant
  temperature where ``s`` peaks. The margin is the distance from the operating ``Tc`` to it.

functions.sig: (net: Network, feed: Feed, key: str, X: float, cooling: Cooling | None = None, bed: Bed | None = None, *, V_max: float = 1000.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The PFR (or packed-bed) volume at which ``key`` reaches conversion ``X``: ``{"V", "reached", "profile"}``. Not
reached within ``V_max`` (equilibrium, a reactant running out, the bed losing its pressure): ``reached=False``
with the conversion it got to.

functions.sig: (net: Network, feed: Feed, V: float, cooling: Cooling, bed: Bed | None = None, *, Tc_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None, n: int = 41, inlet_follows: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]

children.name: pinneapple_physics.relativity
pinneapple_physics.relativity.warp
children.doc:
The Alcubierre warp drive, measured: the expansion, the energy density and where the physics says "impossible".

The metric (Alcubierre 1994), in Cartesian ``(t, x, y, z)`` with ``c = G = 1``::

    ds^2 = -dt^2 + (dx - v_s f(r_s) dt)^2 + dy^2 + dz^2

so :math:`g_{tt} = -1 + v_s^2 f^2`, :math:`g_{tx} = -v_s f`, and the spatial part is flat. ``f`` is a shape function that
is 1 inside the bubble and 0 outside, ``r_s = |x - x_s(t)|``, and ``v_s`` is the bubble's speed -- superluminal if you
like, because nothing *inside* the bubble moves.

Two things this module computes and one it refuses to hide:

* **the expansion** (the York time) :math:`\theta = \nabla \cdot \vec v = v_s (x - x_s)/r_s \, f'(r_s)` -- negative
  ahead of the bubble, positive behind it, exactly the "contract in front, expand behind" the picture claims;
* **the energy density** :math:`T^{00} = G^{00}/8\pi`, computed from the metric by differentiating it -- the Einstein
  tensor of the metric as written, not a quoted formula. It is **negative** wherever the wall is and the observer is off
  the axis, which is the whole problem: the drive needs exotic matter;
* **the energy conditions** -- both of them, since the weak one is where the sign of ``T^{00}`` already settles the
  matter and the null one is the stronger statement: :math:`T_{\mu\nu} u^\mu u^\nu` over unit timelike vectors and
  :math:`T_{\mu\nu} k^\mu k^\nu` over null ones, evaluated on the same grid. This is where the "impossible" is
  written down rather than asserted. The null vectors are built as ``n + s`` (the Eulerian
  normal plus a unit spatial direction) and checked to satisfy ``g(k, k) = 0`` to roundoff -- ``k = (1, n)``, the obvious
  guess, is *not* null in this metric and silently measures nothing.

How it is checked (:mod:`tests.test_warp_bubble`):

* the energy density reproduces Alcubierre's closed form
  :math:`T^{00} = -(v_s^2/32\pi)\,(y^2+z^2)/r_s^2\,(df/dr_s)^2` to 1e-6 relative, on random points in the wall;
* it is **zero on the axis** (``y = z = 0``), which is what that closed form says and what a curvature routine
  assembled from the wrong index permutation does not;
* where ``f`` is exactly zero the Riemann tensor vanishes: the metric is flat outside the bubble, and the curvature
  lives in the wall;
* integrating it gives the total, and the total is what a mission would have to supply: for a 10 m bubble at
  ``v_s = 1`` it comes out at ``-1.89e27 kg`` of *negative* energy -- ``-9.5e-4`` solar masses, about the mass of
  Jupiter -- and the drive needs it, which is the whole problem.

What this is not: a solution of the quantum inequalities (Pfenning-Ford) or a proposal for how to build one. It is the
metric, its curvature, and the sign of the answer.

classes.name: WarpMetric
classes.doc: One bubble: how fast it moves, how big it is, how thick the wall is, and where it is at ``t = 0``.

methods.name: radius_at
methods.doc: ``r_s``: the distance from the bubble's centre, which moves at ``v_s`` along ``x``.

methods.name: metric
methods.doc: ``g_{mu nu}`` with ``mu, nu`` in ``(t, x, y, z)``, shape ``(N, 4, 4)``.

classes.name: Curvature
classes.doc: The Einstein tensor and the energy it implies, sampled at points.

functions.name: shape
functions.sig: (r: np.ndarray, radius: float, wall: float, kind: str = 'alcubierre') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
The shape function ``f``: 1 inside the bubble, 0 outside, a wall of thickness ~``wall`` in between.

``"alcubierre"`` is the smooth ``tanh`` wall used in numerical work (it is what Alcubierre's own top-hat becomes once
you ask for a differentiable function); ``"tophat"`` is his original, which is 1 for ``r < radius`` and 0 beyond and
is kept because it makes the closed form easy to recognise.

functions.name: shape_derivative
functions.sig: (r: np.ndarray, radius: float, wall: float, kind: str = 'alcubierre') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``df/dr``, analytically -- the expansion and the energy both need it and differentiating a ``tanh`` by hand is
cheaper and more accurate than finite differences.

functions.name: expansion
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, time: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: The York time ``theta = div v = v_s (x - x_s)/r_s f'(r_s)``: contraction ahead, expansion behind.

functions.name: einstein_tensor
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, time: float = 0.0, step: float | None = None) -> Curvature
functions.doc: ``G_{mu nu}`` of the metric as written, in the frame that moves with the bubble.

functions.name: energy_density
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, time: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: null_vector
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, direction: tuple[float, float, float], time: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
A vector that really is null: ``k = n + s``, the Eulerian normal plus a unit *spatial* direction.

``n^mu = (1, v_s f, 0, 0)`` is the 4-velocity of the observers the ADM split uses (unit lapse, shift
``-v_s f``), and the spatial frame is flat, so ``n + s`` is null for any unit ``s``. Writing ``k = (1, n)``
instead -- the obvious thing, and what this module used to do -- is **not** null in this metric, and the
"null energy" it produces is meaningless. :func:`null_energy` checks ``g(k, k) = 0`` before returning.

functions.name: null_energy
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, direction: tuple[float, float, float] = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0), time: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``T_{mu nu} k^mu k^nu`` along the null direction ``k = n + s`` (see :func:`null_vector`).

The null energy condition is this quantity being non-negative for *every* null direction. One negative value
anywhere is a violation, and :func:`worst_null_energy` looks for it rather than trusting a single guess.

functions.name: worst_null_energy
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, *, samples: int = 16, time: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
The most negative ``T_{mu nu} k^mu k^nu`` over a sphere of null directions, and where it is.

A negative minimum is the null energy condition being violated at that point -- measured over a grid of
directions, not asserted from the sign of ``T^{00}``.

functions.name: timelike_vector
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, direction: tuple[float, float, float], speed: float = 0.0, time: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
A *unit* timelike vector ``u = (n + speed * s) / sqrt(1 - speed^2)``, with ``n`` the Eulerian normal.

``n = (1, v_s f, 0, 0)`` is the 4-velocity of the ADM observers and the spatial frame is flat and orthogonal to
it, so this is a unit vector with ``g(u, u) = -1`` for every ``|speed| < 1``. ``speed = 0`` is the Eulerian
observer itself, which is where :func:`weak_energy` starts.

functions.name: weak_energy
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, direction: tuple[float, float, float] = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0), speed: float = 0.0, time: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``T_{mu nu} u^mu u^nu`` for the unit timelike ``u`` of :func:`timelike_vector`.

The weak energy condition is this non-negative for *every* timelike direction; ``speed = 0`` alone is the energy
density an Eulerian observer measures, which is the term Alcubierre's closed form gives.

functions.name: worst_weak_energy
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, points: np.ndarray, *, samples: int = 12, speeds: tuple[float, ...] = (0.0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9), time: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
The most negative ``T_{mu nu} u^mu u^nu`` over timelike directions and speeds, and where it is.

``speeds`` includes 0, the Eulerian observer, so a negative result at ``speed = 0`` is the statement that the
energy density itself is negative for the observers the ADM split uses.

functions.name: integrated_energy
functions.sig: (metric: WarpMetric, *, extent: float | None = None, samples: int = 41, time: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
The total ``T^{00}`` over a box: negative, and the number a mission would have to supply.

Units: the density comes out of the geometry in ``1/length^2`` (``G = c = 1``), so the integral is a length. It is
converted to kilograms with ``c^2/G`` and reported in solar masses.

functions.name: solar_masses
functions.sig: (kilograms: float) -> float

children.name: pinneapple_physics.solid
pinneapple_physics.solid.axisymmetric
children.doc:
Axisymmetric linear elasticity in cylindrical coordinates ``(r, z)``, by autograd.

A displacement field ``u(x)`` with ``x = [r, z]`` (``(N, 2)``, ``requires_grad``) and ``u = [u_r, u_z]`` or
``[u_r, u_z, u_theta]`` (``(N, 2)`` or ``(N, 3)``, computed from ``x``) is independent of ``theta``. With the
optional torsional component ``u_theta`` (torsion of a solid of revolution) the small strains are

    e_rr = du_r/dr,   e_tt = u_r / r,   e_zz = du_z/dz,   e_rz = (du_r/dz + du_z/dr) / 2,
    e_rt = (du_t/dr - u_t / r) / 2,     e_tz = (du_t/dz) / 2          (tensor shear strains),

Hooke's law ``sigma = lambda tr(e) I + 2 mu e`` with ``lambda = E nu / ((1 + nu)(1 - 2 nu))``,
``mu = E / (2 (1 + nu))``, and the equilibrium equations without body force are

    R_r = d s_rr/dr + d s_rz/dz + (s_rr - s_tt) / r
    R_z = d s_rz/dr + d s_zz/dz + s_rz / r
    R_t = d s_rt/dr + d s_tz/dz + 2 s_rt / r.

The meridional (``u_r, u_z``) and torsional (``u_theta``) problems decouple. Reference: S. P. Timoshenko and
J. N. Goodier, *Theory of Elasticity*, 3rd ed., McGraw-Hill (1970): equilibrium and strain-displacement relations in
cylindrical coordinates, the solid of revolution under axisymmetric load and torsion of shafts of variable diameter;
the thick-walled cylinder (Lame) solution ``u_r = A r + B / r`` is the test case of ``tests/test_axisymmetric.py``.

Units are whatever ``x``, ``u`` and ``E`` use (``E`` in Pa with ``u`` and ``x`` in the same length unit gives Pa).

functions.name: lame_parameters
functions.sig: (E: float, nu: float) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc: ``(lambda, mu)`` from Young's modulus ``E`` and Poisson's ratio ``nu`` (isotropic).

functions.name: strains_rz
functions.sig: (u: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor, *, r_min: float | None = None, create_graph: bool = True) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]
functions.doc:
Small strains ``e_rr, e_tt, e_zz, e_rz`` (and ``e_rt, e_tz`` when ``u`` has ``u_theta``), each ``(N, 1)``.

Shear entries are tensor components (half the engineering shear strain). ``r_min`` clamps ``r`` in ``u_r / r``
(points on the axis). ``create_graph=True`` keeps the result differentiable (needed for residuals and training).

functions.name: stresses_rz
functions.sig: (u: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor, E: float, nu: float, *, r_min: float | None = None, create_graph: bool = True) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]
functions.doc: Stresses ``s_rr, s_tt, s_zz, s_rz`` (and ``s_rt, s_tz`` with torsion), each ``(N, 1)``, by Hooke's law.

functions.name: equilibrium_residual_rz
functions.sig: (u: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor, E: float, nu: float, *, r_min: float | None = None) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Pointwise equilibrium residual ``[R_r, R_z]`` (``(N, 2)``), plus ``R_theta`` (``(N, 3)``) with torsion.

Units of stress per length; zero for an exact elastic solution without body force. Differentiable in the model
parameters (use ``(R ** 2).mean()`` as a physics loss; divide ``R_theta`` by ``mu`` for the torsion equation
``d2u/dr2 + (1/r) du/dr - u/r^2 + d2u/dz2 = 0`` in displacement form).

children.name: pinneapple_physics.solving
children.doc:
``pp.solve`` and ``pp.compare``: one entry point to solve a problem by any method and compare methods.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> sol = pp.solve("burgers_1d", method="pinn", epochs=2000)          # a PINN
>>> exact = pp.solve("burgers_1d", method="analytic")                 # Cole-Hopf closed form
>>> print(pp.compare("burgers_1d", methods=["pinn"], reference="analytic", options={"pinn": {"epochs": 2000}}))

``problem`` may be a ``PhysicalProblem``, a PDE ``ProblemSpec`` or a preset name. Built-in methods:

* ``"reference"`` -- the classical solver named in the problem's ``reference_solver`` (a preset's ``solver_spec``).
  Its grid output is interpolated linearly in between grid points. If that solver does not produce a field on a
  grid over **every** coordinate of the problem, ``solve`` raises ``MethodNotAvailable`` instead of returning a
  partial answer (for example a transient solver that keeps only the last time step).
* ``"pinn"`` -- a physics-informed network from the model registry trained with ``solve_pde``.
* ``"analytic"`` -- a closed-form solution the library knows for this problem (``list_analytic()``), for example the
  Cole-Hopf solution of the ``burgers_1d`` preset. Raises ``MethodNotAvailable`` when none is registered.
* ``"exact"`` -- a closed-form or manufactured solution passed as ``fn=lambda X: ...``.

* ``"fem"`` -- a classical P1 finite-element solve of steady ``poisson`` / ``laplace`` problems on a box with
  Dirichlet conditions (1D, 2D or 3D). The source ``f`` of ``laplace(u) = f`` comes from ``ctx={"source_fn": fn}``,
  the same ``ctx`` the PINN reads, so both backends solve the same problem through the same call.
* ``"external"`` -- any code that returns a field on a grid: ``runner=callable(problem) -> {"coords": {...}, field: array}``.

Every method has a ``kind`` (``classical``, ``neural``, ``analytic``, ``external``, ``reference`` or ``custom``) and every
``Solution`` has ``metadata()``, one dictionary with the same keys for all of them.

Add your own with ``@register_method("name", kind="classical")``; the function receives ``(problem, **options)`` and returns a
``Solution``. Every ``Solution`` has ``predict(X)`` with ``X`` of shape ``(N, len(problem.coords))`` returning
``(N, len(problem.fields))``, plus the wall time of the solve.

classes.name: MethodNotAvailable
classes.doc: The requested method cannot solve this problem (missing solver output, missing option, ...).

methods.name: metadata
methods.doc:
The same keys for every backend: what was solved, by which method, how long it took, and the
backend's own details under ``info``.

methods.doc:
Save the result as an experiment manifest (``path``: a folder or an ``experiment.json``) and, with
``register=True``, import it into the Lab for curation. Returns the manifest path.

methods.doc: All grid points ``(N, dim)`` of a grid solution, else ``None``.

methods.name: best
methods.doc: Method with the lowest mean (over fields) value of ``metric`` among the methods that ran.

methods.name: to_experiment
methods.sig: (path: str, *, title: Optional[str] = None, register: bool = False, lab: Any = None)
methods.doc:
Save the comparison as an experiment manifest (every metric of every method that ran, against the stated
reference) and, with ``register=True``, import it into the Lab. Returns the manifest path.

functions.sig: (problem: Union[PhysicalProblem, Any, str], **preset_kwargs) -> PhysicalProblem
functions.doc: ``PhysicalProblem`` from a ``PhysicalProblem``, a PDE ``ProblemSpec`` or a preset name.

functions.doc:
Decorator registering ``fn(problem, **options) -> Solution`` under ``name`` for ``solve``/``compare``.
``kind`` labels the family of the method (``classical``, ``neural``, ...) in every Solution it returns.

functions.doc: Registered method names, optionally only those of one ``kind``.

functions.sig: () -> Dict[str, List[str]]

functions.sig: (name: str, matcher: Callable[[PhysicalProblem], bool])
functions.doc: Decorator: ``factory(problem) -> fn(X)`` is the exact solution for every problem where ``matcher`` is True.

functions.sig: (problem: Union[PhysicalProblem, Any, str]) -> Optional[str]
functions.doc:
Name of the closed-form solution this library knows for ``problem``, or ``None``.

Lets a caller answer "can I get an exact answer before training anything?" without catching an
exception from :func:`solve`. ``problem`` is anything :func:`solve` accepts: a name, a PDE spec
or a :class:`PhysicalProblem`.

>>> from pinneapple_physics.solving import analytic_for
>>> analytic_for("burgers_1d")
'burgers_sine_cole_hopf'
>>> analytic_for("poisson_2d") is None
True

functions.name: solve
functions.sig: (problem: Union[PhysicalProblem, Any, str], method: Union[str, Callable[..., Solution]] = 'pinn', *, preset_kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None, **options) -> Solution
functions.doc:
Solve ``problem`` with ``method`` (a registered name or a callable ``(problem, **options) -> Solution``).

Raises ``MethodNotAvailable`` when the method cannot handle the problem, and ``ValueError`` when
``problem.validate()`` finds inconsistencies (a broken problem is never solved silently).

functions.name: compare
functions.sig: (problem: Union[PhysicalProblem, Any, str], methods: Sequence[Union[str, Callable[..., Solution], Solution]], *, reference: Union[str, Solution] = 'reference', options: Optional[Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]]] = None, points: Optional[np.ndarray] = None, n_points: int = 4096, seed: int = 0, metric_names: Sequence[str] = ('relative_l2', 'rmse', 'max_abs'), preset_kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, A...
functions.doc:
Solve or reuse each method and score it against ``reference`` at the same points.

Points: ``points`` if given; else up to ``n_points`` points of the reference grid (when the reference is a grid
solution); else ``n_points`` uniform random points in ``domain_bounds``. A method that fails is reported with
its error and does not stop the others. Entries can be registered method names, solver callables, or precomputed
``Solution`` objects. Precomputed solutions must have the same coordinates and fields as ``problem``.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde
pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.bc
children.doc:
Boundary condition enforcement for PINNeAPPle symbolic PDE module.

Provides hard (by-construction) and soft (penalty) BC implementations:

- HardBC    : distance-function ansatz — BCs are satisfied exactly at every step.
- PeriodicBC: coordinate-embedding trick to enforce periodicity exactly.
- DirichletBC: soft Dirichlet penalty loss.
- NeumannBC : soft Neumann penalty loss via autograd normal derivative.

classes.name: HardBC
classes.sig: (distance_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor], bc_value_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]) -> None
classes.doc:
Hard boundary condition enforcement via a distance-function ansatz.

The network output is modified so that the BC is satisfied *exactly* at
every evaluation, without any penalty term in the loss:

    u(x) = phi(x) * net(x) + g_bc(x)

where

* ``phi(x)`` is a smooth distance function that is 0 on the boundary
  (and positive inside the domain).
* ``g_bc(x)`` is the boundary value lifted into the domain (can be the
  function that equals the BC on the boundary; a simple choice is the BC
  value extended by any smooth function, or just a constant).

Parameters
----------
distance_fn : callable(x: Tensor) -> (N, 1) Tensor
    Smooth function that is 0 on Gamma and positive inside the domain.
    Example for the unit square [0,1]^2::

        distance_fn = lambda x: x[:, 0:1] * (1 - x[:, 0:1]) * x[:, 1:2] * (1 - x[:, 1:2])

bc_value_fn : callable(x: Tensor) -> (N, 1) Tensor
    The known boundary value extended to the full domain.
    For homogeneous Dirichlet BCs (u=0) this is simply ``lambda x: 0``.

Examples
--------
>>> import torch
>>> from pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.bc import HardBC
>>> phi = lambda x: x[:, 0:1] * (1 - x[:, 0:1]) * x[:, 1:2] * (1 - x[:, 1:2])
>>> bc = HardBC(distance_fn=phi, bc_value_fn=lambda x: torch.zeros(x.shape[0], 1))
>>> wrapped = bc.wrap_model(model)
>>> u = wrapped(coords)   # automatically satisfies u = 0 on the boundary

methods.name: apply
methods.doc: Apply hard BC transformation.

methods.name: wrap_model
methods.doc: Return a new Module whose forward() applies the hard BC ansatz.

classes.name: PeriodicBC
classes.sig: (period: float, dim: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Periodic boundary condition enforcement via coordinate transformation.

Maps one coordinate dimension x_i to (cos(2*pi*x_i/L), sin(2*pi*x_i/L)),
replacing a scalar coordinate with two features on the unit circle.
This guarantees that the model output at x_i = 0 and x_i = L are
identical (by construction), without any penalty term.

Parameters
----------
period : float
    Period L of the coordinate.
dim : int
    Index of the coordinate dimension that should be periodic (0-based).

Examples
--------
>>> pbc = PeriodicBC(period=1.0, dim=0)
>>> wrapped = pbc.wrap_model(model)
>>> u = wrapped(coords)   # coords[:,0] is the periodic coordinate

Warning
-------
Chaining two ``PeriodicBC``\ s to make more than one axis periodic --
e.g. ``PeriodicBC(Lx, dim=0).wrap_model(PeriodicBC(Lz, dim=2).wrap_model(model))``
for a channel-flow-style ``(x, y, z, t)`` input periodic in both ``x``
and ``z`` -- is unsound: each ``wrap_model`` inserts one extra column,
so the *second* wrap's ``dim`` index is computed against a channel
ordering the *first* wrap has already shifted (after wrapping ``dim=0``,
column 2 of the 5-column intermediate tensor is ``y``, not ``z``, so
``dim=2`` on the outer wrap silently embeds the wrong axis). Use
:class:`MultiPeriodicBC` for more than one periodic axis -- it applies
every axis's transform in a single pass against the original,
unshifted coordinate ordering.

methods.name: transform
methods.doc: Transform coordinates: replace column *dim* with (cos, sin) pair.

methods.name: wrap_model
methods.doc: Return a new Module that applies the coordinate transformation before forward.

classes.name: MultiPeriodicBC
classes.sig: (periods: dict) -> None
classes.doc:
Exact periodic-BC embedding for two or more coordinate axes at once.

Same ``(cos(2*pi*x_i/L_i), sin(2*pi*x_i/L_i))`` construction as
:class:`PeriodicBC`, but computed for every periodic axis in a single
pass against the *original* column ordering, so it is correct for
however many axes are periodic (unlike chaining several
``PeriodicBC.wrap_model`` calls -- see the warning on ``PeriodicBC``).

Parameters
----------
periods : dict[int, float]
    Maps a 0-based input-column index to its period. Every other
    column passes through unchanged, in its original position.

Examples
--------
>>> # (x, y, z, t) input, periodic in x (period Lx) and z (period Lz):
>>> pbc = MultiPeriodicBC(periods={0: Lx, 2: Lz})
>>> wrapped = pbc.wrap_model(model)  # model must accept (N, D + len(periods))
>>> u = wrapped(coords)  # -> (cos x, sin x, y, cos z, sin z, t)

methods.name: wrap_model
methods.doc:
Return a new Module that applies every axis's periodic
transform before calling *model*. *model* must accept
``(N, D + len(periods))`` input.

classes.name: DirichletBC
classes.sig: (value_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor], boundary_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor] | None = None, weight: float = 1.0) -> None
classes.doc:
Soft Dirichlet boundary condition via an MSE penalty term.

Computes: loss = weight * mean((u(x_bc) - g(x_bc))^2)

Parameters
----------
boundary_fn : callable(x: Tensor) -> bool mask Tensor  [optional]
    If provided, applied to filter which points in x_bc are on this boundary.
    When None, all points in x_bc are used.
value_fn : callable(x: Tensor) -> (N, 1) Tensor
    Target boundary value.
weight : float
    Loss weight (default 1.0).

Examples
--------
>>> dbc = DirichletBC(value_fn=lambda x: torch.zeros(x.shape[0], 1), weight=100.0)
>>> loss = dbc.loss(model, x_boundary)

methods.name: loss
methods.doc: Compute the Dirichlet BC penalty loss.

classes.name: NeumannBC
classes.sig: (flux_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor], normal_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor], boundary_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor] | None = None, weight: float = 1.0) -> None
classes.doc:
Soft Neumann boundary condition via autograd normal derivative.

Computes: loss = weight * mean((n·∇u(x_bc) - g(x_bc))^2)

Parameters
----------
flux_fn : callable(x: Tensor) -> (N, 1) Tensor
    Target normal flux value g(x).
normal_fn : callable(x: Tensor) -> (N, D) Tensor
    Outward unit normal at each boundary point.
boundary_fn : callable(x: Tensor) -> bool mask Tensor  [optional]
    If provided, used to filter boundary points.
weight : float
    Loss weight (default 1.0).

Examples
--------
>>> # Zero Neumann on a boundary where the normal is +x direction
>>> nbc = NeumannBC(
...     flux_fn=lambda x: torch.zeros(x.shape[0], 1),
...     normal_fn=lambda x: torch.cat([torch.ones(x.shape[0],1), torch.zeros(x.shape[0],1)], dim=1),
... )
>>> loss = nbc.loss(model, x_boundary)

methods.name: loss
methods.doc: Compute the Neumann BC penalty loss.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.compiler
children.doc:
Symbolic PDE compiler for PINNeAPPle.

Converts SymPy PDE residual expressions into callable PyTorch autograd functions.

Design note — two SymPy→PyTorch compilation paths exist in this codebase:

* **This module** (``SymbolicPDE``): walks the expression tree recursively using
  ``torch.autograd.grad``.  Gradients flow *through* the evaluation, so you can
  differentiate the residual loss with respect to model weights.  Use this when
  you need higher-order autograd or want the symbolic expression to participate
  directly in the training graph.

* ``pinneapple_pinn.factory.sympy_backend.SympyTorchCompiler``: uses
  ``sympy.lambdify`` to emit a Python lambda; faster to evaluate but the
  lambdified call is opaque to autograd (no gradient tape through the symbolic
  tree).  Use that path when the PDE loss is evaluated at fixed collocation
  points and speed matters more than differentiability through the expression.

``SymbolicPDE`` also supports a pluggable ``grad_method`` (default
``"autograd"``, unchanged from the original behavior above): pass
``grad_method="finite_difference"`` or ``"spectral"`` plus a ``grid``
(``GridAxisSpec``) to evaluate the SAME symbolic residual over grid-shaped
field tensors (e.g. an FNO's output) instead of a continuous model's output
at scattered points — see ``gradient_backends.py`` and
``to_grid_residual_fn``. Note: this module's ``compile_problem``-based
sibling, ``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.compile`` (the actual
engine behind the registered preset catalog in ``pde_environment/presets/``,
string-``kind``-dispatched rather than SymPy-expression-based), is a
different code path and is not affected by this parameter.

Usage example::

    import sympy as sp
    from pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde import SymbolicPDE

    x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
    u = sp.Function("u")
    pi = sp.pi

    # Poisson: u_xx + u_yy + 2*pi^2*sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y) = 0
    expr = u(x, y).diff(x, 2) + u(x, y).diff(y, 2) + 2 * pi**2 * sp.sin(pi * x) * sp.sin(pi * y)
    pde = SymbolicPDE(expr, coord_syms=[x, y], field_syms=[u])
    residual_fn = pde.to_residual_fn(model)
    # residual_fn(coords_tensor) -> (N,1) tensor

classes.name: SymbolicPDE
classes.sig: (expr: sp.Expr, coord_syms: list[sp.Symbol], field_syms: list[sp.Function], param_syms: list[sp.Symbol] | None = None, grad_method: GradMethod = 'autograd', grid: GridAxisSpec | None = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Symbolic PDE residual — compile to a PyTorch autograd callable.

Parameters
----------
expr : sympy expression equal to 0 (the PDE residual).
coord_syms : list of SymPy symbols for independent variables (e.g. [x, y, t]).
field_syms : list of SymPy *Function* objects for dependent variables (e.g. [u, v]).
param_syms : optional list of SymPy symbols for (possibly learnable) parameters,
    e.g. an unknown diffusivity in an inverse PDE problem. Their numeric values
    are not fixed at construction time — supply them via ``to_residual_fn(model,
    params={...})`` (or per-call via ``residual_fn(coords, params={...})``) so
    that a ``torch.nn.Parameter`` can be optimized jointly with the model.
grad_method : how derivatives are computed from the underlying data — see
    ``gradient_backends.py``. One of:

    * ``"autograd"`` (default) — ``torch.autograd.grad`` through a
      continuous model's output at scattered collocation points. This is
      ``SymbolicPDE``'s original (and only, before this parameter existed)
      behavior; the default preserves it unchanged. Use ``to_residual_fn``.
    * ``"finite_difference"`` / ``"spectral"`` — grid-based derivatives
      (e.g. an FNO's structured-grid output), reusing
      ``pinneapple_neural``'s PINO derivative backends. Requires ``grid``.
      Use ``to_grid_residual_fn`` instead of ``to_residual_fn``.

    The SAME symbolic PDE (``expr``) can be reused unmodified across all
    three — only the derivative *computation* changes with the data's shape.
grid : required when ``grad_method`` is ``"finite_difference"`` or
    ``"spectral"`` — a ``GridAxisSpec`` mapping ``coord_syms`` to the grid
    tensor's axes/extents. Ignored for ``"autograd"``.

methods.name: to_residual_fn
methods.sig: (model: nn.Module, params: dict[str, torch.Tensor] | None = None) -> Callable[..., torch.Tensor]
methods.doc: Return a callable that computes the PDE residual using autograd.

methods.name: to_grid_residual_fn
methods.sig: (params: dict[str, torch.Tensor] | None = None) -> Callable[..., torch.Tensor]
methods.doc:
Return a callable that computes the PDE residual on grid-shaped
field tensors, using this instance's grid-based ``grad_method``
(``"finite_difference"`` or ``"spectral"``).

methods.name: compile
methods.doc: Compile the symbolic expression (currently a no-op for 'torch' backend).

functions.name: pde_from_sympy
functions.sig: (expr: sp.Expr, coords: list[sp.Symbol], fields: list[sp.Function], params: list[sp.Symbol] | None = None, grad_method: GradMethod = 'autograd', grid: GridAxisSpec | None = None) -> SymbolicPDE
functions.doc:
Create a SymbolicPDE from a SymPy residual expression.

Parameters
----------
expr : sympy expression equal to 0 (the PDE residual).
coords : list of SymPy symbols for independent variables.
fields : list of SymPy Function objects for dependent variables.
params : optional list of parameter symbols.
grad_method, grid : forwarded to ``SymbolicPDE`` — see its docstring.

Returns
-------
SymbolicPDE instance.

Example::

    x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
    u = sp.Function("u")
    expr = u(x, y).diff(x, 2) + u(x, y).diff(y, 2)  # Laplace
    pde = pde_from_sympy(expr, [x, y], [u])

functions.name: auto_residual
functions.sig: (model: nn.Module, coords_tensor: torch.Tensor, derivative_fns: dict[str, Callable[[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]]) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]
functions.doc:
Compute field values and named derivative quantities via autograd.

This is a lower-level helper intended for users who prefer to wire
derivative operators manually rather than through SymPy expressions.

Parameters
----------
model : nn.Module taking (N, D) -> (N, F) tensors.
coords_tensor : (N, D) input coordinates tensor (grad will be enabled).
derivative_fns : dict mapping name -> callable(field, coords) -> tensor.
    Each callable receives the raw model output and the coords tensor
    (with grad enabled) and should return a (N, *) tensor.

Returns
-------
dict with keys:
    "fields" : (N, F) raw model output
    + one key per entry in derivative_fns.

Example::

    from pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.autograd_ops import laplacian

    result = auto_residual(
        model, x_col,
        {"laplacian_u": lambda u, x: laplacian(u, x)}
    )
    res = result["laplacian_u"] - f_source

children.summary: Symbolic PDE compiler for PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.gradient_backends
children.doc:
Pluggable derivative backends for :class:`SymbolicPDE`.

Design note -- this mirrors a pattern found in PhysicsNeMo's
``PhysicsInformer(grad_method=...)`` (see ``physicsnemo/sym/eq/phy_informer.py``
upstream, Apache-2.0; this module reimplements the *architecture pattern*,
not their code): separate "what is the PDE" (the SymPy expression, unchanged)
from "how do we compute a derivative given the shape of the data". The same
symbolic residual can then be evaluated either

* over scattered collocation points from a continuous model (PINN-style),
  differentiated via ``torch.autograd.grad`` -- the ``"autograd"`` backend,
  which is exactly ``SymbolicPDE``'s original (and still default) behavior, or
* over a structured grid (e.g. an FNO's output), differentiated via
  finite-difference or spectral (FFT) stencils -- the ``"finite_difference"``
  / ``"spectral"`` backends below.

The finite-difference and spectral math here is **not reimplemented**: it
calls straight through to ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators
.pino``'s ``fd_derivative`` / ``spectral_derivative``, the same functions
already used (and exercised) by the PINO wrapper. This module only adds the
bookkeeping to (a) map SymPy coordinate names to grid tensor axes/extents and
(b) compose repeated/mixed partial derivatives (e.g. ``u_xx``, or a mixed
``u_xy``) out of those single-axis primitives.

classes.name: GridAxisSpec
classes.doc:
Maps SymPy coordinate names to axes of a structured-grid field tensor.

Parameters
----------
coord_names : coordinate symbol names, e.g. ``("x", "t")`` for a 1D
    time-dependent PDE like Burgers'.
dims : which tensor dimension of the (grid-shaped) field each entry of
    ``coord_names`` corresponds to, e.g. ``(-2, -1)`` for a field tensor
    shaped ``(..., n_x, n_t)``. Same convention as ``pino.GridSpec.dims``.
L : physical extent spanned by each axis (same convention as
    ``pino.GridSpec.L``) -- used to derive finite-difference spacing
    (``dx = L / n``) and spectral wavenumbers.

functions.name: grid_derivative
functions.sig: (field: torch.Tensor, wrt: List[str], *, grid: GridAxisSpec, method: GridGradMethod) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Compute an arbitrary-order partial derivative of a grid-shaped field.

``wrt`` lists coordinate names in differentiation order (the same
convention ``compiler.py`` already expands SymPy's
``Derivative.variable_count`` into for the autograd backend), e.g.
``["x", "x"]`` for ``u_xx`` or ``["x", "y"]`` for a mixed ``u_xy``.

Repeated differentiation along the SAME axis is composed into a single
``order=count`` call to the underlying primitive. Differentiation along
DIFFERENT axes is applied sequentially, one axis at a time -- exact for
the spectral case (differentiation along different axes commutes; each
is an independent per-axis multiplication in Fourier space) and the
standard way to build higher-dimensional finite-difference stencils out
of 1D ones for the FD case.

children.summary: Pluggable derivative backends for SymbolicPDE.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.pinn
children.doc:
A parsed equation system (:mod:`.text`) as a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.validation.pinn.PINNProblem`.

The residual is evaluated by autograd from the same SymPy expressions the finite-difference solver uses, so a PINN
and a classical solution of one edited system are comparable point for point. Dirichlet and initial conditions
become the problem's ``boundary`` / ``initial`` samplers (checked by ``validate_pinn``); conditions with derivatives
(Neumann, Robin, ``u_t = ...`` at ``t = 0``) become ``constraints``. Coefficients listed in ``unknowns`` are trainable
scalars (an inverse PINN, with ``train_pinn(..., data=(X, Y))``).

    P, model = pinn_problem(system, {"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)})
    net, info = train_pinn(P, model, adam_steps=2000, lbfgs_steps=200)
    report = validate_pinn(net, P)

children.name: pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.text
children.doc:
Equations as text, parsed safely into SymPy: ``"u_t = alpha*lap(u) + sin(pi*x)"``.

The text is read with :mod:`ast` and translated node by node into SymPy objects; nothing is handed to ``eval`` or
``sympify``. Allowed: numbers, ``+ - * / ** ^``, parentheses, coordinates, fields, coefficient names and the
functions in :data:`FUNCTIONS`, plus three operators:

==================  ===========================================================================================
``u_t``, ``u_xx``   derivative shorthand: a field, an underscore, then one coordinate letter per derivative
``d(f, x, ...)``    derivative of any expression (chain rule applied), e.g. ``d(u**2, x)`` or ``d(u, x, x)``
``lap(f)``          Laplacian over the *spatial* coordinates (so the same text works in 1-D, 2-D and 3-D)
==================  ===========================================================================================

Any other name is a coefficient: it needs a value (``coefficients={"alpha": 0.1}``) before the system is solved, or
it is declared unknown (an inverse problem). Attribute access, subscripts, keywords, strings, lambdas, comprehensions
and calls of anything not listed are refused with :class:`EquationSyntaxError`.

    sys_ = parse_system(["u_t = alpha*lap(u)"], [{"kind": "dirichlet", "on": "x_min", "equation": "u = 0"}],
                        coords=["x", "t"], fields=["u"], coefficients={"alpha": 0.1})
    sys_.classify()["family"]       # "heat"

children.doc:
pinneapple_symbolic — Symbolic PDE compiler for PINNeAPPle.

Converts SymPy PDE residual expressions into callable PyTorch autograd functions
and provides hard / soft boundary condition implementations.

Quick start::

    import sympy as sp
    from pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde import SymbolicPDE, HardBC

    x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
    u = sp.Function("u")

    # Poisson: u_xx + u_yy + 2*pi^2 * sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y) = 0
    expr = (
        u(x, y).diff(x, 2)
        + u(x, y).diff(y, 2)
        + 2 * sp.pi**2 * sp.sin(sp.pi * x) * sp.sin(sp.pi * y)
    )
    pde = SymbolicPDE(expr, coord_syms=[x, y], field_syms=[u])

    # Hard BC: u = 0 on unit-square boundary via distance-function ansatz
    phi = lambda pts: pts[:,0:1]*(1-pts[:,0:1])*pts[:,1:2]*(1-pts[:,1:2])
    import torch
    hard_bc = HardBC(phi, lambda pts: torch.zeros(pts.shape[0], 1, device=pts.device))
    wrapped_model = hard_bc.wrap_model(base_model)

    residual_fn = pde.to_residual_fn(wrapped_model)
    res = residual_fn(x_col)   # (N, 1) PDE residual tensor

children.name: pinneapple_physics.tribology
pinneapple_physics.tribology.archard
children.doc:
Sliding wear of a bar end pressed against a rigid, flat counterface.

Archard's law, local form: the wear depth grows as dh/ds = K p, with K = k / H the specific wear rate
(mm³ / (N·m)), p the contact pressure (MPa = N/mm²) and s the sliding distance (m). The bar end is crowned (a
cylinder of radius R across the sliding direction), so at first only its middle touches; the pressure comes from an
elastic (Winkler) layer, p = E' / t · max(0, δ - g(x) - h(x)), with the approach δ set by the load at every step. Wear
removes the crown, the contact spreads and the pressure tends to the flat-punch value F / A: running-in, then
steady wear at dh/ds = K F / A.

Exact facts the solver must keep (checked in the lab experiment ``bar_wear``):

* worn volume = K F s at every moment (global Archard, any pressure distribution);
* the initial contact is the closed-form Winkler solution for a parabolic gap (``winkler_parabolic_contact``);
* after running-in the wear rate is K F / A.

The materials are the classic pin-on-ring data of Archard and Hirst (1956), as tabulated in Hutchings and Shipway,
*Tribology* (2nd ed., 2017), table 5.2 (k dimensionless, H Vickers hardness): order-of-magnitude values for dry
sliding at low load, not design data for a specific pair.

methods.name: K
methods.doc: Specific wear rate, mm³ / (N·m).

classes.name: BarWear
classes.doc: A bar of section length (along sliding, crowned) x width, end radius R, pressed with load F.

methods.name: pressure
methods.doc:
Contact pressure (MPa) and approach δ (mm) that carry the load on the current profile. With ``ds_m`` the
pressure is the one at the end of a wear step of that length (implicit: p = k (δ - gap - K ds p), i.e. an
effective stiffness k / (1 + k K ds)), which keeps the wear update stable for any step.

methods.sig: (distance_m: float, n_save: int = 60, max_step_um: float = 0.2) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
methods.doc:

fraction) and saved profiles / pressures.

methods.name: running_in_distance_m
methods.doc: Distance to wear the whole crown away at the flat-punch rate (an estimate of the running-in).

functions.name: winkler_parabolic_contact
functions.sig: (F_N: float, width_mm: float, R_mm: float, k_w: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Closed form for a parabolic gap g = x² / (2R) on a Winkler layer of modulus k_w (MPa/mm), load F over a
width b: p = k_w (δ - x²/2R) on |x| < a, a = sqrt(2 R δ), F = (4/3) b k_w a δ.

children.name: pinneapple_physics.weather
pinneapple_physics.weather.cyclones
children.doc:
A tropical cyclone end to end on real data: the official best track, the vortex at the centre of a gridded
pressure field, and the three numbers a hurricane showcase has to quote — track error in kilometres, intensity error
in knots, and the lead at which the model stops being able to follow the storm.

Two kinds of data, both public and both cited where they are used:

* **Best track** — the NHC North Atlantic Hurricane Database (HURDAT2), the official 6-hourly position, maximum wind
  and minimum central pressure of every storm, reanalysed after the season (Landsea & Franklin, 2013). US Government
  work, public domain, downloaded from the NHC at run time and never stored in the repository.
* **Gridded fields** — any ``(n, lat, lon)`` array of sea-level pressure in hPa: an analysis (ERA5 through the ARCO
  bucket), a published forecast (IFS HRES, Pangu-Weather through WeatherBench2), or a model of this library.

The centre of the storm in a gridded field is the deepest pressure minimum within a search radius of the previous
position — the continuity tracker used in operational verification — refined to the sub-grid minimum by a parabola
through the three cells along each axis. A minimum shallower than ``deepest_hpa`` is reported as *not found*: on a
grid too coarse for the core, that is the honest outcome, and it is counted rather than hidden.

Intensity is compared three ways, because a grid minimum and a best track do not measure the same thing: the central
pressure directly (hPa), and the maximum wind through the empirical wind-pressure relation of Atkinson & Holliday
(1977), ``W = 6.7 (1010 - p)^0.644`` knots, which turns a grid minimum into an *equivalent* wind. The relation is
named wherever it is used; it is not a model wind.

The scale is the story. ERA5 and the 0.25-degree forecast archives place the centre of a hurricane to a few tens of
kilometres and are still 20-40 hPa too shallow; a 5.625-degree grid (WeatherBench2's 64 x 32) has cells wider than a
hurricane and cannot hold one at all. The same code measures both, which is why a showcase can say *where* the chain
has to hand over to a finer model instead of asserting it.

classes.name: BestTrack
classes.doc:
One storm of HURDAT2: its 6-hourly (plus landfall) records, in the units the file publishes.

Attributes
----------

    ATCF identifier: basin letter, storm number, year (``AL092022`` is the Atlantic's ninth storm of 2022).
name : str
times : np.ndarray
    ``datetime64[h]`` of every record.
lat, lon : np.ndarray [degrees]
    Centre position; ``lon`` in [-180, 180], as the file publishes it.
wind_kt : np.ndarray [kt]
    Maximum sustained wind (1-minute mean) of each record.
pressure_hpa : np.ndarray [hPa]
    Minimum central pressure (NaN where the file has none).
status : np.ndarray [str]
    Two-letter code of each record: TD, TS, HU (hurricane), EX, LO, ...
record : np.ndarray [str]
    Record identifier: ``L`` landfall, ``P`` minimum pressure, empty for a routine synoptic record.
source : dict
    Where the records came from: the file, its SHA-256 and the citation, filled in by
    :func:`load_best_track` so that a figure or a JSON can quote it.

methods.doc: Index of an exact record, or None.

methods.doc: (lat, lon, wind_kt, pressure_hpa) linearly interpolated to ``times``; NaN outside the storm's life.
